## `html/tel-non-breaking` — Phone numbers don't wrap

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the text then contains non-breaking characters, which copy and search keep)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/tel-non-breaking.md

### What it checks

The text of a `tel:` link uses non-breaking spaces and hyphens.

**Why:** A phone number broken over two lines is hard to read and to copy.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignoreClasses` | `string[]` | `[]` | classes that already prevent wrapping |
| `ignoreStyle` | `boolean` | `true` | skip links styled `white-space: nowrap` or `pre` |

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<a href="tel:5551234">555 1234</a>
```

##### Do

```html
<a href="tel:5551234">555&nbsp;1234</a>
```

## `html/text-content` — Buttons have text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the button's name needs a human)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/text-content.md

### What it checks

A `<button>` has text a screen reader can announce: content, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or an image with `alt`.

**Why:** Without it the button is announced as just "button".

### How to fix

1. Add visible text, or an `aria-label` that says what the button does.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<button type="button"><svg width="16" height="16"></svg></button>
```

##### Do

```html
<button type="button" aria-label="Close"><svg width="16" height="16"></svg></button>
```

## `html/th-scope` — Header cells in complex tables have scope

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether each header labels a row or a column is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/th-scope.md

### What it checks

In a table whose headers are not just the first row or just the first column, every `<th>` has `scope` (`row`, `col`, `rowgroup` or `colgroup`).

**Why:** Screen readers announce each cell with its headers; `scope` tells them which headers belong to which cells.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `strict` | `boolean` | `false` | check simple tables too |

### How to fix

1. Add `scope="col"` to column headers and `scope="row"` to row headers.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<table>
  <tr><th>Name</th><th>Age</th></tr>
  <tr><th>Ada</th><td>36</td></tr>
</table>
```

##### Do

```html
<table>
  <tr><th scope="col">Name</th><th scope="col">Age</th></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Ada</th><td>36</td></tr>
</table>
```

## `html/unique-landmark` — Repeated landmarks have distinct names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the names need a human)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/unique-landmark.md

### What it checks

When a landmark appears more than once (two `<nav>`, two `<aside>`, …), each has a unique, non-empty `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

**Why:** Screen-reader users jump between landmarks by name; two unnamed `<nav>` are indistinguishable.

### How to fix

1. Give each landmark of the same kind its own `aria-label`, or point `aria-labelledby` at its heading.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<nav><a href="/">Home</a></nav>
<nav><a href="/help">Help</a></nav>
```

##### Do

```html
<nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/">Home</a></nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer"><a href="/help">Help</a></nav>
```

## `html/unrecognized-char-ref` — Character references exist and are terminated

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended character is not always clear)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/unrecognized-char-ref.md

### What it checks

Every named character reference (`&name;`) is one HTML defines, and ends with `;`.

**Why:** An unknown reference is shown literally, and an unterminated one may be read with the text after it.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignoreCase` | `boolean` | `false` | compare names without case |
| `requireSemicolon` | `boolean` | `true` | report references without `;` |

### How to fix

1. Correct the name, or escape the `&` as `&amp;` if no reference was meant.
2. End the reference with `;`.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<p>Price: 5&euros; &copy 2024</p>
```

##### Do

```html
<p>Price: 5&euro; &copy; 2024</p>
```

## `html/valid-autocomplete` — autocomplete values are valid

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right field name depends on what the field collects)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:html/a11y` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-autocomplete.md

### What it checks

`autocomplete` holds a valid token list: optional `section-*`, then `shipping`/`billing`, then `home`/`work`/… for contact fields, then one field name that fits the input type, then optional `webauthn`. `<form>` takes only `on` or `off`.

**Why:** Browsers ignore an invalid value, so autofill and password managers can't help the user.

### How to fix

1. Pick the field name that describes the data (the WHATWG autofill list).
2. Order the tokens as described above, or use `off`.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="mail">
<input type="number" name="n" autocomplete="email">
```

##### Do

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="number" name="n" autocomplete="off">
```

## `html/valid-for` — A label points at a control

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (either the id or the element is wrong, and only the author knows which)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-for.md

### What it checks

A `<label for>` refers to the id of a form control a label can name (`input`, `select`, `textarea`, `button`, `meter`, `output`, `progress`).

**Why:** Pointed at a `<div>` or `<span>`, the label names nothing, and clicking it does nothing.

### How to fix

1. Point `for` at the control's id, or make the target a form control.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<label for="name">Name</label>
<div id="name"></div>
```

##### Do

```html
<label for="name">Name</label>
<input type="text" id="name">
```

## `html/valid-id` — Ids are well-formed

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming an id breaks the CSS, scripts and links that use it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/valid-id.md

### What it checks

An `id` is not empty and has no whitespace; it starts with a letter and uses only letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

**Why:** Whitespace makes the id unusable; other characters need escaping in CSS selectors and are easy to get wrong.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relaxed` | `boolean` | `false` | only require a non-empty id without whitespace |

### How to fix

1. Rename the id, and update everything that refers to it.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<div id="1st item"></div>
```

##### Do

```html
<div id="first-item"></div>
```

## `html/void-content` — Void elements have no end tag

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-html` · `codelaw-rules-html` · **Languages:** HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`</br>` is read as a second line break, so removing it changes the rendering)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/html/void-content.md

### What it checks

Void elements (`<br>`, `<img>`, `<input>`, `<meta>`, …) are written without an end tag.

**Why:** They can't have content; browsers ignore most such end tags, and read `</br>` and `</p>` as new elements.

### Examples

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<input type="text" name="q"></input>
```

##### Do

```html
<input type="text" name="q">
```

## `js/constructor-super` — A derived class's constructor calls super(); a base class's does not

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what `super()` must receive depends on the base class)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/constructor-super.md

### What it checks

A class that extends another must call `super()` in its constructor before it returns, and a class
that extends nothing must not call `super()` at all.

**Why:** Without `super()` the instance is never initialised and the constructor throws; in a base
class `super()` is a syntax error.

### How to fix

1. In a class with `extends`, call `super(...)` with the arguments the base class expects, before any use of `this`.
2. In a class without `extends`, remove the `super()` call.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

### Differences from the source

Paths are followed in straight-line order: a `super()` on any branch counts as called.

## `js/exports-at-end` — Exports are gathered at the end of the file

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/exports-at-end.md

### What it checks

Declarations are written without `export`, and the module's exports are listed in one `export { … }`
(and `export type { … }`) block at the end of the file.

**Why:** A reader or an agent sees the module's whole public API in one place.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const zero = 0;
```

##### Do

```js
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
const zero = 0;
export { add, zero };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const zero = 0;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
const zero = 0;
export { add, zero };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
export interface Point {
  x: number;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
interface Point {
  x: number;
}
export { add };
export type { Point };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
export interface Point {
  x: number;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}
interface Point {
  x: number;
}
export { add };
export type { Point };
```

### Differences from the source

`export default`, namespaces and `declare` blocks are left alone.

## `js/for-direction` — A for loop's counter moves toward its end condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the condition or the update is wrong needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/for-direction.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop whose condition tests `i < n` counts up, and one that tests `i > n` counts down.

**Why:** A counter that moves the wrong way never meets its end condition, so the loop never ends.

### How to fix

1. Decide which way the loop should count.
2. Fix the update (`i++` or `i--`) or the comparison to match.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i--) {
  draw(i);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  draw(i);
}
```

## `js/getter-return` — A getter returns a value on every path

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the value a getter should return is the author's decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/getter-return.md

### What it checks

Every path through a getter ends in `return <value>` or a `throw`.

**Why:** A getter that falls off its end returns `undefined`, which is almost always a forgotten
`return`.

### How to fix

1. Find the path that ends without a `return`.
2. Return the value the property should have there, or throw.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const box = {
  get size() {
    return this.items ? this.items.length : 0;
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const box = {
  get size() {
    if (this.items) {
      return this.items.length;
    }
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const box = {
  get size() {
    return this.items ? this.items.length : 0;
  },
};
```

## `js/import-groups` — Imports are grouped builtin, external, internal, relative

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/import-groups.md

### What it checks

The file's leading imports come in four groups, in order — Node.js built-ins, packages, internal
aliases (the `internal` option, `@/` and `~/` by default), relative paths — with a blank line
between groups.

**Why:** Grouped imports show at a glance what a module depends on, and keep diffs of the import
block small.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `internal` | `string[]` | `["@/", "~/"]` | prefixes of internal imports |

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```js
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```ts
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
import fs from "node:fs";
import React from "react";
helper(fs, React);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import fs from "node:fs";

import React from "react";

import { helper } from "./helper";
helper(fs, React);
```

### Differences from the source

A block of imports with a comment inside is left alone, so no comment is moved away from the import
it describes. A side-effect import (`import './polyfills'`, a stylesheet) stays where it is, since moving it
changes what runs first; only the imports between two of them are ordered.

## `js/max-lines` — A file stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting a file changes its structure; which exports belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-lines.md

### What it checks

A file has at most `max` lines (300 by default). Blank lines and lines that hold only a comment (a `{/* … */}`
in JSX is one) are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`; a line that holds code and a
comment counts as code. `skip_imports` leaves the import block out too. The rule reports once, on the first line over
the limit, with the measured count: `412 lines (max 300; blank lines and comments not counted)`.

**Why:** A long file is hard to hold in your head, slow to review and the usual place a second responsibility hides. The
limit is a prompt to split, not a goal in itself: raise `max` for a file that is long on purpose, or put
a generated file where `[files] lint_generated = false` skips it. Only the host file is measured, never a `<script>` in
HTML or a code block in Markdown.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `300` | the most lines a file may have |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_imports` | `boolean` | `false` | the import block does not count |

### How to fix

1. Find a cohesive group of exports (a component and its helpers, one feature's types) and move it to a new module next to the file.
2. Import it back where it is used, or re-export it from the old file so callers do not change.
3. If the file is long on purpose, raise `max` for it in an `[[overrides]]` entry, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule js/max-lines`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
const c = 3;
const d = 4;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
import { d } from "./more.js";
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
const a = <i />;
const b = <b />;
const c = <u />;
const d = <s />;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
import { d } from "./more.jsx";
const a = <i />;
const b = <b />;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
const a: number = 1;
const b: number = 2;
const c: number = 3;
const d: number = 4;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
import { d } from "./more";
const a: number = 1;
const b: number = 2;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
const a: JSX.Element = <i />;
const b: JSX.Element = <b />;
const c: JSX.Element = <u />;
const d: JSX.Element = <s />;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
import { d } from "./more";
const a: JSX.Element = <i />;
const b: JSX.Element = <b />;
```

## `js/max-lines-per-function` — A function stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (extracting part of a function changes its structure; where to cut and what to call the piece is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-lines-per-function.md

### What it checks

A function spans at most `max` lines (50 by default), from its first line to its last. Every function form counts:
declarations, expressions, arrows, methods, getters and setters, and class `static` blocks. Blank lines and comment-only
lines are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`. With `include_nested` (the default) an
inner function's lines count toward the outer function as well; with `include_nested = false` they do not, from the
inner function's first line to its last. An immediately invoked function is not measured on its own unless
`include_iife` is `true`; its lines belong to the function around it. `ignore_names` is a regular expression for names
to exempt, such as `"^(test|it|describe)"`. The rule reports on the function's name: `renderOrders is 84 lines (max 50)`.

**Why:** A function that long does several jobs, and its name can say only one. The limit is a prompt to extract, not a goal in
itself: a test suite's `describe` callback is long on purpose, so exempt it with `ignore_names`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `50` | the most lines one function may span |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `include_nested` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of an inner function count toward the outer one too |
| `include_iife` | `boolean` | `false` | measure an immediately invoked function, `(() => { … })()`, as a function of its own |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; functions named like this are exempt, e.g. "^(test\|it\|describe)" |

### How to fix

1. Find a block inside the function that does one thing (a loop body, a branch, a run of statements that build one value).
2. Extract it into a well-named function, and pass in what it reads.
3. Repeat until each piece fits `max`. If the function is long on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule js/max-lines-per-function`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  for (const item of items) sum += item;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  const rows = items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>);
  const empty = <p>none</p>;
  return rows.length ? <ul>{rows}</ul> : empty;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>)}</ul>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
function total(items: number[]): number {
  let sum = 0;
  for (const item of items) sum += item;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```ts
function total(items: number[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item, 0);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const rows = items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>);
  const empty = <p>none</p>;
  return rows.length ? <ul>{rows}</ul> : empty;
}
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li>{item}</li>)}</ul>;
}
```

## `js/max-params` — A function takes at most a maximum number of parameters

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (grouping parameters changes the function's signature and every call to it; which belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/max-params.md

### What it checks

A function takes at most `max` parameters (3 by default). A destructured object or array parameter counts as one, which
is the usual way out. A rest parameter and a TypeScript `this:` parameter are not counted unless `count_varargs` or
`count_this` is `true`, and neither is a parameter whose name matches `ignore_names` (`"^_"` by default: a
parameter named `_unused` is already said to be unused). A TypeScript `override` method, an overload signature, a
`declare` function, an abstract method and anything in a `.d.ts` file are skipped, since you do not own that
signature; set `ignore_overrides` or `ignore_declarations` to `false` to count them. A constructor that only
declares parameter properties (`constructor(private a: A, private b: B)`) can be skipped with
`ignore_constructor_injection`. The rule reports on the function's name: `createOrder takes 6 parameters (max 3)`.

**Why:** A call with many positional arguments is easy to get in the wrong order, and every added parameter is a change to every
caller. Grouping related parameters in one object names them at the call site.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `3` | the most parameters a function may take |
| `count_this` | `boolean` | `false` | TypeScript: count a `this:` parameter |
| `count_varargs` | `boolean` | `false` | count a rest parameter, `...rest` |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | `"^_"` | a regular expression; parameters named like this do not count |
| `ignore_overrides` | `boolean` | `true` | skip a TypeScript `override` method: its signature is not yours |
| `ignore_declarations` | `boolean` | `true` | skip an overload signature, a `declare` function, an abstract method and a `.d.ts` file |
| `ignore_constructor_injection` | `boolean` | `false` | TypeScript: skip a constructor whose parameters are all parameter properties (Angular, NestJS) |

### How to fix

1. Group the parameters that belong together into one options object: `createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address })`.
2. Update the callers to pass the object, and give the destructured parameter a type in TypeScript.
3. If the signature is not yours to change, exempt it: an `override`, an overload and a `declare` function already are.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function createOrder(customer, items, coupon, address) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

##### Do

```js
function createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address }) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function Card(title, body, footer, onClose) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function Card({ title, body, footer, onClose }) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function createOrder(customer: string, items: string[], coupon: string, address: string) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function createOrder({ customer, items, coupon, address }: Order) {
  return { customer, items, coupon, address };
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function Card(title: string, body: string, footer: string, onClose: () => void) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function Card({ title, body, footer, onClose }: CardProps) {
  return <div>{title}{body}{footer}{onClose}</div>;
}
```

## `js/no-async-promise-executor` — A Promise executor is not an async function

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the rewrite depends on what the executor does)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-async-promise-executor.md

### What it checks

The function passed to `new Promise(...)` is not `async`.

**Why:** An error thrown in an async executor doesn't reject the promise, and an executor that needs
`await` doesn't need the `Promise` wrapper.

### How to fix

1. If the executor only awaits and resolves, use the awaited promise directly.
2. Otherwise make the executor a plain function and handle errors with `reject`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(await load());
});
```

##### Do

```js
const data = load();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(await load());
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const data = load();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(await load());
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const data = load();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const data = new Promise(async (resolve) => {
  resolve(await load());
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const data = load();
```

## `js/no-case-declarations` — No let, const, function or class directly in a case

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (another case may rely on the shared declaration)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-case-declarations.md

### What it checks

A `let`, `const`, `function` or `class` inside a `case` sits in a block `{ … }` of its own.

**Why:** Declarations in a case are scoped to the whole `switch`, so another case can see them
uninitialised.

### How to fix

1. Wrap the case's statements in `{ … }`.
2. If another case uses the declaration, move it above the `switch`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a": {
    const n = 1;
    use(n);
    break;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-class-assign` — A class name is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the assignment was for is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-class-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to the name a class declaration binds.

**Why:** Reassigning a class name is almost always a mistake, and makes every later use mean
something else.

### How to fix

1. Assign to a new variable instead of the class name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Point {}
Point = null;
```

##### Do

```js
class Point {}
const origin = null;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Point {}
Point = null;
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Point {}
const origin = null;
```

## `js/no-compare-neg-zero` — No comparisons against -0

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether `0` or `-0` was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-compare-neg-zero.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't compare a value with `-0` using `==`, `===`, `<` or the other comparison operators.

**Why:** These operators treat `-0` and `0` as equal, so the comparison doesn't test what it says.

### How to fix

1. To test for negative zero, use `Object.is(x, -0)`.
2. To test for zero of either sign, compare with `0`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (x === -0) {
  flip();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (Object.is(x, -0)) {
  flip();
}
```

## `js/no-cond-assign` — No assignment in a condition, unless doubly parenthesised

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether a comparison or an assignment was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-cond-assign.md

### What it checks

The condition of an `if`, `while`, `do … while` or `for` is not an assignment, unless it is wrapped
in a second pair of parentheses to say it's meant.

**Why:** `if (a = b)` assigns and tests the result, which is almost always a mistyped `===`.

### How to fix

1. If a comparison was meant, use `===`.
2. If the assignment is meant, wrap it in a second pair of parentheses.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```js
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```jsx
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```ts
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (user = admin) {
  grant();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (user === admin) {
  grant();
}
```

```tsx
while ((node = node.next)) {
  visit(node);
}
```

## `js/no-console` — No console calls left in the code

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (deleting the call also drops its arguments, which may have side effects; and a call whose value is used needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-console.md

### What it checks

Code makes no calls on the global `console` (`console.log(…)`, `console["debug"](…)`), except the
methods the `allow` option names. A local variable named `console` is not the global one.

**Why:** `console` output is debugging left behind: it clutters the browser console and the server
logs, and it can leak data. A team that wants it on a laptop and not in CI sets the rule to `warn`
in `[profiles.local]` and `error` in `[profiles.ci]`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `string[]` | `[]` | console methods that may stay, e.g. ["warn", "error"] |

### How to fix

1. Delete the call (`codelaw fix --unsafe` does when the call is a whole statement).
2. If the output is wanted, report through the project's logger instead.
3. If the method should stay everywhere, add it to the rule's `allow` option.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load(items) {
  console.log(items);
  return items.length;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  console.log(items);
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function List({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load(items: string[]): number {
  console.log(items);
  return items.length;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load(items: string[]): number {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  console.log(items);
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function List({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  return <ul>{items}</ul>;
}
```

## `js/no-const-assign` — A const is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the variable should be `let` or the assignment should go is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-const-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to a `const`.

**Why:** Assigning to a `const` throws a TypeError at run time.

### How to fix

1. If the value is meant to change, declare it with `let`.
2. Otherwise assign to a new variable.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = 0;
total = 1;
```

##### Do

```js
let total = 0;
total = 1;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = 0;
total = 1;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let total = 0;
total = 1;
```

## `js/no-constant-binary-expression` — No binary expression whose result is fixed

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended grouping or comparison needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-constant-binary-expression.md

### What it checks

The left side of `??`, `||` and `&&` is not a value whose nullishness or truthiness is fixed, and
nothing is compared with a newly created object or with `null` when it can never be `null`.

**Why:** Such an expression always gives the same answer, which usually means the author misread
operator precedence.

### How to fix

1. Add the parentheses the expression was meant to have.
2. Or compare with the value that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Do

```js
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Do

```ts
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const total = price + tax ?? 0;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const total = price + (tax ?? 0);
```

## `js/no-constant-condition` — No conditions that are always true or always false

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to remove the branch or fix the condition needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-constant-condition.md

### What it checks

The condition of an `if`, `while` or `do … while` is not a literal or another value that is always
truthy or always falsy; `while (true)` is allowed.

**Why:** A constant condition is usually leftover debugging or a typo, and hides dead code.

### How to fix

1. If the branch is dead, remove it.
2. Otherwise replace the constant with the condition that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```js
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```jsx
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```ts
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (0) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (debug) {
  debugPanel();
}
```

```tsx
while (true) {
  step();
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only literal conditions are checked; ESLint also folds some expressions such as `typeof x` and `!1`.

## `js/no-control-regex` — No control characters in regular expressions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which character was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-control-regex.md

### What it checks

A regular expression literal doesn't match ASCII control characters (`\x00`–`\x1F`).

**Why:** Control characters rarely appear in text, so matching them is usually an escaping mistake.

### How to fix

1. Use the named escape (`\t`, `\n`, `\f`) if one was meant.
2. Otherwise remove the control character from the pattern.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /\x0C/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /\f/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /\x0C/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /\f/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /\x0C/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /\f/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /\x0C/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /\f/;
```

## `js/no-debugger` — No debugger statements

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-debugger.md

### What it checks

Code contains no `debugger` statements.

**Why:** `debugger` pauses execution wherever developer tools are open, which nobody wants in
shipped code.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load() {
  debugger;
  return fetchAll();
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {
  return fetchAll();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function load() {
  debugger;
  return fetchAll();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {
  return fetchAll();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load() {
  debugger;
  return fetchAll();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {
  return fetchAll();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function load() {
  debugger;
  return fetchAll();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load() {
  return fetchAll();
}
```

## `js/no-default-export` — No default exports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (every importer of the default export must change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-default-export.md

### What it checks

Modules export by name; `export default` is not used.

**Why:** A named export has one name everywhere, so it can be found, renamed and auto-imported
reliably.

### How to fix

1. Give the exported value a name and export it with `export { name }`.
2. Change every `import x from` of this module to `import { name } from`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {}
export { load };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export default function load() {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load() {}
export { load };
```

## `js/no-delete-var` — No delete on a variable

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the code meant to clear is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-delete-var.md

### What it checks

`delete` is applied to object properties, never to a variable.

**Why:** Deleting a variable does nothing in sloppy mode and is a syntax error in strict mode.

### How to fix

1. To clear the value, assign `undefined` or a fresh value.
2. To remove a property, `delete obj.key`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
let cache = {};
delete cache;
```

##### Do

```js
let cache = {};
cache = {};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
let cache = {};
delete cache;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let cache = {};
cache = {};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let cache = {};
delete cache;
```

##### Do

```ts
let cache = {};
cache = {};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let cache = {};
delete cache;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let cache = {};
cache = {};
```

## `js/no-dupe-args` — No two parameters share a name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which parameter was meant can't be known from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-args.md

### What it checks

A function's parameters, destructured ones included, all have different names.

**Why:** The later parameter silently hides the earlier one, so one argument can never be read.

### How to fix

1. Rename the duplicate parameter.
2. Update the body to read the parameter it meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function add(a, b, a) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function add(a, b, c) {
  return a + b + c;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function add(a, b, a) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function add(a, b, c) {
  return a + b + c;
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-class-members` — No two class members share a name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two members to keep is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-class-members.md

### What it checks

A class declares each method and field name once, separately for static and instance members; a
getter and a setter may share a name.

**Why:** The later declaration replaces the earlier one, so one of them is dead code.

### How to fix

1. Decide which declaration is right.
2. Remove or rename the other.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  subtotal() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  total() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cart {
  total() {
    return 1;
  }
  subtotal() {
    return 2;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-else-if` — No two conditions in an if/else-if chain are the same

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the second condition should have been is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-else-if.md

### What it checks

Each condition in an `if … else if …` chain is different from the ones before it.

**Why:** A repeated condition's branch can never run, because the earlier one already took it.

### How to fix

1. Find the repeated condition.
2. Correct it to the case it was meant to handle, or remove the dead branch.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAdmin) {
  audit();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (isAdmin) {
  grant();
} else if (isAuditor) {
  audit();
}
```

## `js/no-dupe-keys` — No two keys in an object literal are the same

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value should win can't be known from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-dupe-keys.md

### What it checks

An object literal names each key once; `a`, `'a'` and `["a"]` are the same key, as are `1` and
`0x1`.

**Why:** The later value silently replaces the earlier one.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Remove the other entry, or give it its own key.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  name: "Grace",
};
```

##### Do

```js
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  nickname: "Grace",
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  name: "Grace",
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  nickname: "Grace",
};
```

## `js/no-duplicate-case` — No two case labels in a switch are the same

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which label was meant is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-duplicate-case.md

### What it checks

Each `case` in a `switch` tests a different expression.

**Why:** A repeated case can never match: the first one always wins.

### How to fix

1. Find the label that was meant to test something else.
2. Correct it, or merge the two bodies.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 200:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 503:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 200:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 503:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 200:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 503:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 200:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (status) {
  case 200:
    ok();
    break;
  case 503:
    retry();
    break;
}
```

## `js/no-empty` — No empty blocks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to fill the block, remove it or document it needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-empty.md

### What it checks

A block or `switch` has at least one statement, or a comment saying why it is empty. Function bodies
may be empty.

**Why:** An empty block is usually unfinished code, and an empty `catch` hides errors.

### How to fix

1. If the block is unfinished, write its code.
2. If it's meant to be empty, put a comment in it saying why.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {}
```

##### Do

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  // The cache is optional: a failed load is not an error.
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {}
```

##### Do

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  // The cache is optional: a failed load is not an error.
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {}
```

##### Do

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  // The cache is optional: a failed load is not an error.
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {}
```

##### Do

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  // The cache is optional: a failed load is not an error.
}
```

## `js/no-empty-character-class` — No empty character classes in regular expressions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which characters the class should hold needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-empty-character-class.md

### What it checks

A regular expression contains no empty character class `[]`; `[^]`, which matches any character, is
fine.

**Why:** `[]` matches no character at all, so the whole pattern can never match.

### How to fix

1. Put the characters the class should match inside it.
2. If `[]` was meant literally, escape it: `\[\]`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```js
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```jsx
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```ts
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /^abc[]/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /^abc[a-z]/;
```

```tsx
const brackets = /^\s*[{[]/;
```

## `js/no-empty-pattern` — No empty destructuring patterns

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the pattern was meant to bind needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-empty-pattern.md

### What it checks

A destructuring pattern names at least one binding.

**Why:** `const {} = obj` binds nothing; it's usually a mistyped default such as `{ a = {} }`.

### How to fix

1. Name the properties to bind inside the pattern, or remove it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't


##### Do

```js
const { a = {} } = options;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const { a: {} } = options;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const { a = {} } = options;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const { a: {} } = options;
```

##### Do

```ts
const { a = {} } = options;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const { a: {} } = options;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const { a = {} } = options;
```

## `js/no-ex-assign` — A caught error is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the original error should go is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-ex-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to the parameter of a `catch` clause.

**Why:** Reassigning the caught error discards it, so nothing can report or rethrow it.

### How to fix

1. Use a new variable for the new value.
2. Keep the original error, e.g. as `{ cause: err }`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  err = new Error("failed");
  throw err;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("failed", { cause: err });
}
```

## `js/no-extra-boolean-cast` — No needless !! or Boolean() in a condition

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-extra-boolean-cast.md

### What it checks

A condition (`if`, `while`, `do … while`, `? :`) doesn't convert its value with `!!`.

**Why:** A condition is already evaluated as a boolean, so `!!` only adds noise.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (!!user) {
  greet();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (user) {
  greet();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (!!user) {
  greet();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (user) {
  greet();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (!!user) {
  greet();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (user) {
  greet();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (!!user) {
  greet();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (user) {
  greet();
}
```

### Differences from the source

`Boolean(x)` in a condition is not checked yet.

## `js/no-fallthrough` — A switch case does not fall through into the next by accident

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the fall-through is intended needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-fallthrough.md

### What it checks

A `case` with statements ends in `break`, `return`, `throw` or `continue`, or says `// falls
through` before the next case.

**Why:** Falling through is easy to do by accident and hard to see in review.

### How to fix

1. If the case should stop, end it with `break` (or `return`).
2. If it should fall through, say so with a `// falls through` comment before the next case.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

```js
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

```jsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
    break;
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

```tsx
switch (kind) {
  case "a":
    first();
  // falls through
  case "b":
    second();
    break;
}
```

## `js/no-func-assign` — A function declaration is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the assignment was for is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-func-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to the name a function declaration binds.

**Why:** Overwriting a declared function is almost always a mistake, and every later call means
something else.

### How to fix

1. Assign to a new variable instead.
2. If the function must be replaceable, declare it with `let` as a function expression.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function save() {}
save = null;
```

##### Do

```js
function save() {}
const saveHandler = null;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function save() {}
save = null;
```

##### Do

```jsx
function save() {}
const saveHandler = null;
```

## `js/no-global-assign` — No assignment to built-in globals

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended variable needs a name of its own)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-global-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign to JavaScript's built-in globals such as `Object`, `undefined` or `NaN`.

**Why:** Built-in globals are read-only or shared by every module, so assigning to one is a bug or a
hazard.

### How to fix

1. Declare a local variable with its own name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
Object = null;
```

##### Do

```js
const object = null;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
Object = null;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const object = null;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
Object = null;
```

##### Do

```ts
const object = null;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
Object = null;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const object = null;
```

## `js/no-import-assign` — An imported binding is not reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new value needs a variable of its own)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-import-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign a new value to a name bound by `import`.

**Why:** Imported bindings are read-only: assigning to one throws a TypeError.

### How to fix

1. Copy the import into a local variable and change that.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import config from "./config.js";
config = {};
```

##### Do

```js
import config from "./config.js";
const local = { ...config };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import config from "./config.js";
config = {};
```

##### Do

```jsx
import config from "./config.js";
const local = { ...config };
```

## `js/no-invalid-regexp` — RegExp() is given a valid pattern and flags

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended pattern needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-invalid-regexp.md

### What it checks

A `RegExp(...)` or `new RegExp(...)` whose pattern and flags are string literals is valid: brackets
and groups close, quantifiers follow something, and the flags are known and not repeated.

**Why:** An invalid pattern throws a SyntaxError when that line runs, not when the file loads.

### How to fix

1. Correct the pattern or the flags the message names.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = new RegExp("[a-z");
```

##### Do

```js
const re = new RegExp("[a-z]");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = new RegExp("[a-z");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = new RegExp("[a-z]");
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = new RegExp("[a-z");
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = new RegExp("[a-z]");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = new RegExp("[a-z");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = new RegExp("[a-z]");
```

### Differences from the source

Only structural problems are found: unbalanced brackets and groups, misplaced quantifiers, out-of-
order ranges, invalid group syntax and flags.

## `js/no-irregular-whitespace` — No irregular whitespace in templates, regular expressions, JSX text or comments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the escape keeps a template's cooked value but changes the raw string a tagged template such as `String.raw` sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-irregular-whitespace.md

### What it checks

Templates, regular expressions and JSX text spell a no-break space, zero-width space or other
irregular whitespace as an escape (`\u00A0`, `&#x00A0;`), and comments use ordinary spaces.

**Why:** Irregular whitespace is invisible in most editors. In a template, regular expression or JSX
text it silently becomes part of the value, so the text looks right and compares wrong.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const label = `Total: 1`;
```

##### Do

```js
const label = `Total:\u00A01`;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const label = <p>Total: 1</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const label = <p>Total:&#x00A0;1</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const label = `Total: 1`;
```

##### Do

```ts
const label = `Total:\u00A01`;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const label = <p>Total: 1</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const label = <p>Total:&#x00A0;1</p>;
```

### Differences from the source

- **Between tokens the formatter owns it.** ESLint also reports irregular whitespace between tokens;
  here that is layout, and `codelaw format` replaces it with a space (SR-FORMATTER decision 3), so
  this rule does not report it.
- **Strings are skipped**, as ESLint's `skipStrings` default does.
- **The fix escapes, it doesn't delete:** `\uXXXX` in a template or regular expression, `&#xXXXX;`
  in JSX text, so the value is unchanged; a comment gets an ordinary space.

## `js/no-loss-of-precision` — Number literals keep their value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to use a BigInt, a string or a rounder value depends on how the number is used)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-loss-of-precision.md

### What it checks

A number literal can be represented exactly as a JavaScript number.

**Why:** A literal with more precision than a double holds is silently rounded, so the code doesn't
mean what it says.

### How to fix

1. Use a BigInt (`123n`) for an exact large integer.
2. Or keep the value as a string, or write the value the code really gets.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const id = 9007199254740993;
```

##### Do

```js
const id = 9007199254740993n;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const id = 9007199254740993;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const id = 9007199254740993n;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const id = 9007199254740993;
```

##### Do

```ts
const id = 9007199254740993n;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const id = 9007199254740993;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const id = 9007199254740993n;
```

## `js/no-misleading-character-class` — No character class holding a character made of several code points

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether an alternation or a different class was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-misleading-character-class.md

### What it checks

A character class contains no character built from several code points — an emoji with a skin-tone
modifier, a flag, a letter with a combining mark — and no astral character without the `u` flag.

**Why:** A class matches one code point at a time, so `[👍🏻]` matches the thumb or the tone, never
the pair.

### How to fix

1. Use an alternation such as `(?:👍🏻|👍)` for multi-code-point characters.
2. Add the `u` flag for astral characters.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /^[❤️]$/u;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /^(?:❤️)$/u;
```

## `js/no-new-native-nonconstructor` — No new on Symbol or BigInt

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the call throws today, so removing `new` changes what the code does)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-new-native-nonconstructor.md

### What it checks

`Symbol` and `BigInt` are called as functions, never with `new`.

**Why:** `new Symbol()` and `new BigInt()` throw a TypeError.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const id = new Symbol("id");
```

##### Do

```js
const id = Symbol("id");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const id = new Symbol("id");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const id = Symbol("id");
```

## `js/no-nonoctal-decimal-escape` — No \8 or \9 escapes in strings

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the digit or a literal backslash was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-nonoctal-decimal-escape.md

### What it checks

A string contains no `\8` or `\9` escape.

**Why:** `\8` and `\9` are legacy escapes that just mean the digits, and are errors in template
literals and strict code.

### How to fix

1. Write the digit without the backslash, or `\\8` for a backslash and a digit.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const msg = "version \8";
```

##### Do

```js
const msg = "version 8";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const msg = "version \8";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const msg = "version 8";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const msg = "version \8";
```

##### Do

```ts
const msg = "version 8";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const msg = "version \8";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const msg = "version 8";
```

## `js/no-obj-calls` — No calling Math, JSON, Reflect, Atomics or Intl as functions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which method was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-obj-calls.md

### What it checks

The built-in namespace objects `Math`, `JSON`, `Reflect`, `Atomics` and `Intl` are not called or
constructed.

**Why:** They are plain objects; calling one throws a TypeError.

### How to fix

1. Call the method of the namespace that was meant, e.g. `Math.round(x)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const n = Math(2.5);
```

##### Do

```js
const n = Math.round(2.5);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const n = Math(2.5);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const n = Math.round(2.5);
```

## `js/no-octal` — No legacy octal literals

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether octal or decimal was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-octal.md

### What it checks

Number literals don't start with `0` followed by a digit.

**Why:** `071` is octal (57) in sloppy code and an error in strict code; `0o71` says what it means.

### How to fix

1. For an octal number, write `0o` and the digits.
2. For a decimal number, drop the leading zero.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const mode = 0755;
```

##### Do

```js
const mode = 0o755;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const mode = 0755;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const mode = 0o755;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const mode = 0755;
```

##### Do

```ts
const mode = 0o755;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const mode = 0755;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const mode = 0o755;
```

## `js/no-prototype-builtins` — No calling Object.prototype methods on the object itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an object whose own method is meant would change behaviour)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-prototype-builtins.md

### What it checks

`hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf` and `propertyIsEnumerable` are called through `Object.prototype`,
not on the object being tested.

**Why:** An object can shadow these methods, or have no prototype at all, and then the call breaks
or lies.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (options.hasOwnProperty("debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(options, "debug")) {
  enable();
}
```

## `js/no-redeclare` — No variable is declared twice

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to rename or to assign needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-redeclare.md

### What it checks

A name is declared once per scope: a second `var` or `function` with the same name is not allowed.

**Why:** Redeclaring silently merges two declarations, so one of them is usually a mistake.

### How to fix

1. If it's the same variable, drop the second `var` and assign.
2. If it's a different one, rename it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
var count = 1;
var count = 2;
```

##### Do

```js
var count = 1;
count = 2;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
var count = 1;
var count = 2;
```

##### Do

```jsx
var count = 1;
count = 2;
```

## `js/no-regex-spaces` — No runs of spaces in a regular expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-regex-spaces.md

### What it checks

A regular expression writes several spaces as ` {n}`, not as a run of spaces.

**Why:** A run of spaces is impossible to count by eye.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /a   b/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /a {3}b/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /a   b/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /a {3}b/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /a   b/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /a {3}b/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /a   b/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /a {3}b/;
```

## `js/no-self-assign` — No assigning a variable to itself

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (assigning a property to itself can run a setter, so removing it may change behaviour)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-self-assign.md

### What it checks

An assignment's left and right sides are not the same expression.

**Why:** `a = a` has no effect; it is usually a typo for another name.

### How to fix

1. If another value was meant, assign that.
2. Otherwise remove the assignment.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
let x = 1;
x = x;
```

##### Do

```js
let x = 1;
x = y;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
let x = 1;
x = x;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let x = 1;
x = y;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let x = 1;
x = x;
```

##### Do

```ts
let x = 1;
x = y;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let x = 1;
x = x;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let x = 1;
x = y;
```

## `js/no-setter-return` — A setter does not return a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the returned expression was meant as a side effect needs a reader)
