- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-setter-return.md

### What it checks

A setter body contains no `return <value>`; a bare `return;` to leave early is fine.

**Why:** The value a setter returns is discarded, so returning one hides a mistake.

### How to fix

1. Keep the expression's side effect as a statement.
2. Remove the value from the `return`, or the `return`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    return (this.n = n);
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    this.n = n;
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    return (this.n = n);
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const box = {
  set size(n) {
    this.n = n;
  },
};
```

## `js/no-shadow-restricted-names` — No declaring undefined, NaN, Infinity, arguments, eval or globalThis

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-shadow-restricted-names.md

### What it checks

No variable, parameter or function is named `undefined`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `arguments`, `eval` or
`globalThis`.

**Why:** Shadowing these names makes code that relies on them behave in confusing ways.

### How to fix

1. Rename the declaration and its uses.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function check(NaN) {
  return NaN;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function check(value) {
  return value;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function check(NaN) {
  return NaN;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function check(value) {
  return value;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function check(NaN) {
  return NaN;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function check(value) {
  return value;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function check(NaN) {
  return NaN;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function check(value) {
  return value;
}
```

## `js/no-sparse-arrays` — No holes in array literals

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether a value is missing or a comma is extra needs a reader)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-sparse-arrays.md

### What it checks

An array literal has no empty slots such as `[1, , 2]`.

**Why:** A hole is usually a typo, and holes behave differently from `undefined` in many array
methods.

### How to fix

1. Put the missing value in the slot, or remove the extra comma.
2. If an empty slot is really meant, write `undefined` explicitly.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const colors = ["red", , "blue"];
```

##### Do

```js
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const colors = ["red", , "blue"];
```

##### Do

```jsx
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const colors = ["red", , "blue"];
```

##### Do

```ts
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const colors = ["red", , "blue"];
```

##### Do

```tsx
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

## `js/no-this-before-super` — this is not used before super() in a derived constructor

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving statements across `super()` can change what the base class sees)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-this-before-super.md

### What it checks

In the constructor of a class that extends another, `this` and `super.x` are used only after
`super()` has been called.

**Why:** Before `super()` runs, `this` is not initialised and touching it throws a ReferenceError.

### How to fix

1. Move the `super(...)` call above the first use of `this`.
2. If the base class needs a value computed from `this`, compute it into a local first.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
    super();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    this.lives = 9;
    super();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.lives = 9;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-unassigned-vars` — A variable that is read is also assigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the value the variable should hold is the author's)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unassigned-vars.md

### What it checks

A variable declared without a value is assigned somewhere before it's read.

**Why:** A variable that is read but never assigned always holds `undefined`, which is a bug or dead
code.

### How to fix

1. Assign the value the variable should hold.
2. If it's meant to be `undefined`, use `undefined` directly.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
let status;
report(status);
```

##### Do

```js
let status = "ok";
report(status);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
let status;
report(status);
```

##### Do

```jsx
let status = "ok";
report(status);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let status;
report(status);
```

##### Do

```ts
let status = "ok";
report(status);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let status;
report(status);
```

##### Do

```tsx
let status = "ok";
report(status);
```

## `js/no-undef` — No references to undeclared names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right declaration — an import, a local, or an environment — is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-undef.md

### What it checks

Every name the code reads or writes is declared in the file, built into JavaScript, or a global of
an environment the rule's `env` option names. As in ESLint, a `/* global a, b:writable */` comment
declares names for that file (`name:off` declares nothing), and a `/* eslint-env node */` comment
adds environments.

**Why:** An undeclared name is usually a typo or a missing import, and throws a ReferenceError when
that line runs.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` | `string[]` | `["shared-node-browser"]` | environments whose globals are declared: browser, node, commonjs, worker, serviceworker, shared-node-browser, jest, mocha, vitest |
| `globals` | `string[]` | `[]` | more names to treat as declared |
| `typeof` | `boolean` | `false` | also report names used only as `typeof x` |

### How to fix

1. If it's a typo, correct the name.
2. If it comes from another module, import it.
3. If it's a global of the runtime (browser, Node), add that environment to the rule's `env` option.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```js
const prices = [1, 2];
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
const prices = [1, 2];
const total = prices.reduce(add, 0);
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

## `js/no-unexpected-multiline` — A line break doesn't silently join two lines into one expression

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the lines were meant to join can only be known from intent)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unexpected-multiline.md

### What it checks

A line that starts with `(`, `[` or a template literal does not continue the expression on the line
before it without a semicolon.

**Why:** Without semicolons, JavaScript joins such lines: `a\n(b)` is the call `a(b)`, which is
rarely what was written.

### How to fix

1. If the lines are separate statements, end the first with a semicolon.
2. If they are one expression, move the `(` or `[` onto the first line.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```js
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```ts
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const total = sum
(items).forEach(log);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const total = sum;
(items).forEach(log);
```

## `js/no-unreachable` — No code after a return, throw, break or continue

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (deleting the code is right only when it was really dead, not misplaced)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unreachable.md

### What it checks

Statements after an unconditional `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue` in the same block are
removed or moved; hoisted function declarations and uninitialised `var`s are allowed.

**Why:** Unreachable code never runs, so it misleads every reader who assumes it does.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
  log(items);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
  log(items);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function total(items) {
  return items.length;
}
```

## `js/no-unsafe-finally` — No return, throw, break or continue in finally

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what should happen to the try block's result is a decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-finally.md

### What it checks

A `finally` block doesn't end the function or loop with `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`.

**Why:** Control flow in `finally` silently replaces whatever the `try` or `catch` block returned or
threw.

### How to fix

1. Move the `return` or `throw` out of `finally` into the `try` or `catch` block.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function load() {
  try {
    return fetchAll();
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

## `js/no-unsafe-negation` — No negating the left side of in or instanceof

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (code that really meant `(!a) in b` would change)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-negation.md

### What it checks

`!` before `a in b` or `a instanceof B` wraps the whole test in parentheses.

**Why:** `!a in b` means `(!a) in b`, which tests whether `true` or `false` is a key — never what
was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (!key in cache) {
  load(key);
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (!(key in cache)) {
  load(key);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (!key in cache) {
  load(key);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (!(key in cache)) {
  load(key);
}
```

## `js/no-unsafe-optional-chaining` — No ?. chain used where undefined throws

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right fallback value depends on the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unsafe-optional-chaining.md

### What it checks

A `?.` chain, which can evaluate to `undefined`, is not called through parentheses, constructed,
spread into an array or call, destructured, iterated with `for … of`, used on the right of `in` or
`instanceof`, or extended.

**Why:** In those places `undefined` throws a TypeError, which defeats the point of `?.`.

### How to fix

1. Give the chain a fallback with `??`.
2. Or move the `?.` so that it covers the operation that can fail.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```js
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```ts
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const { name } = user?.profile;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const { name } = user?.profile ?? {};
```

## `js/no-unused-labels` — Every label is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-labels.md

### What it checks

Every statement label is the target of a `break` or `continue`.

**Why:** An unused label is leftover from a refactor and makes the reader look for a jump that isn't
there.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

##### Do

```js
for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
outer: for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
for (const row of rows) {
  draw(row);
}
```

## `js/no-unused-private-class-members` — Every private class member is read

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing a member may also remove writes that matter, so it's a reader's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-private-class-members.md

### What it checks

A private field, method or accessor (`#name`) is read somewhere in its class; only being written
doesn't count.

**Why:** A private member nothing reads is dead code, since nothing outside the class can reach it.

### How to fix

1. Check that nothing needs the member's value.
2. Remove the member and the writes to it, or read it where it was meant to be used.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```js
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  #unused = 1;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  get value() {
    return this.#count;
  }
}
```

## `js/no-unused-vars` — Every declared name is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing a declaration can drop the side effects of its initialiser)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-unused-vars.md

### What it checks

Every variable, function, class, import, parameter and caught error is read somewhere. Parameters
before the last used one are allowed (`args: after-used`).

**Why:** An unused declaration is either dead code or a sign the code doesn't do what it was meant
to.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vars` | `string` | `"all"` | all, or local to skip module-level names |
| `args` | `string` | `"after-used"` | after-used, all or none |
| `caughtErrors` | `string` | `"all"` | all or none |
| `ignoreRestSiblings` | `boolean` | `false` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `varsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression of names to skip |
| `argsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrorsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `destructuredArrayIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Check the initialiser has no side effect that matters.
2. Remove the declaration, or use it where it was meant to be used.
3. For a parameter that must stay for its position, prefix it with `_` and set `argsIgnorePattern: "^_"`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```js
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path) => readFile(path);
```

## `js/no-useless-assignment` — No value is stored that nothing reads

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the store is dead or the read is missing needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-assignment.md

### What it checks

A variable is not assigned a value that is overwritten before anything reads it, or that nothing
reads after the assignment.

**Why:** A dead store is wasted work and usually means the code reads the wrong variable.

### How to fix

1. If the value is not needed, remove the assignment.
2. If it should be read, read it where it was meant to be used.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function total(items) {
  let sum = 0;
  sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function total(items) {
  const sum = items.length;
  return sum;
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only stores a straight-line reading proves dead are reported: an overwrite in the same block, or a
last assignment outside any loop. A variable a nested function touches is skipped.

## `js/no-useless-backreference` — No backreference that can only match the empty string

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the reference was meant to repeat needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-backreference.md

### What it checks

A backreference such as `\1` or `\k<name>` appears after its group closes, in the same alternative,
and not into a negative lookaround.

**Why:** A backreference that comes first, sits inside its own group or in another alternative
always matches the empty string.

### How to fix

1. Move the backreference after the group it refers to.
2. Or remove it if it was meant to be literal text.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Do

```js
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Do

```ts
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const re = /\1(a)/;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const re = /(a)\1/;
```

## `js/no-useless-catch` — No catch that only rethrows

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing the try block changes the scope of declarations inside it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-catch.md

### What it checks

A `catch` clause does more than rethrow the error it caught.

**Why:** `catch (e) { throw e; }` does nothing but add noise and a level of nesting.

### How to fix

1. If there is no `finally`, replace the `try` statement with the statements of its block.
2. If there is a `finally`, remove only the `catch` clause.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Do

```js
load();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
load();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
load();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
load();
```

## `js/no-useless-escape` — No backslash that changes nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-useless-escape.md

### What it checks

A string or template literal escapes only characters that need it: quotes that match the delimiter,
`\\`, line breaks and the escape letters.

**Why:** A useless escape suggests the author meant something else, and makes the string harder to
read.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```js
const path = "a.b";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```jsx
const path = "a.b";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```ts
const path = "a.b";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const path = "a\.b";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const path = "a.b";
```

### Differences from the source

Escapes inside regular expressions are not checked yet. A tagged template (`String.raw`, `html`) is not checked: its tag sees the raw text, backslashes included, as in ESLint.

## `js/no-var` — let or const instead of var

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`let` is block-scoped, so a `var` used outside its block or before its declaration changes meaning)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-var.md

### What it checks

Variables are declared with `let` or `const`, never `var`.

**Why:** `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, which causes bugs `let` and `const` rule out.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```js
let total = 0;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```jsx
let total = 0;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```ts
let total = 0;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
var total = 0;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let total = 0;
```

## `js/no-with` — No with statements

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each name inside needs to be qualified by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/no-with.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't use `with`.

**Why:** `with` makes it impossible to tell which names are properties and which are variables, and
is an error in strict code.

### How to fix

1. Replace each property used inside `with` by `object.property`.
2. Remove the `with`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
with (Math) {
  area = PI * r * r;
}
```

##### Do

```js
area = Math.PI * r * r;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
with (Math) {
  area = PI * r * r;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
area = Math.PI * r * r;
```

## `js/prefer-const` — const for variables that are never reassigned

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-const.md

### What it checks

A `let` whose names all get their value in the declaration and are never reassigned is a `const`.

**Why:** `const` tells the reader the binding won't change, and the engine enforces it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
let limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

##### Do

```js
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
let limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

##### Do

```ts
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const limit = 10;
use(limit);
```

## `js/prefer-rest-params` — Rest parameters instead of arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the parameter list has to be rewritten by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-rest-params.md

### What it checks

Functions take a rest parameter `...args` instead of reading `arguments`.

**Why:** `arguments` is not a real array, isn't available in arrow functions, and hides how many
arguments a function takes.

### How to fix

1. Add a rest parameter `...args` to the function.
2. Replace each use of `arguments` with it.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```js
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function sum() {
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce(add, 0);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce(add, 0);
}
```

## `js/prefer-spread` — Spread instead of .apply()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/typescript` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/prefer-spread.md

### What it checks

A function is called with spread arguments, `f(...args)`, instead of `f.apply(null, args)`.

**Why:** Spread says the same thing more directly, and doesn't need a `this` value.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```js
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```ts
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least.apply(null, values);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const max = Math.max.apply(null, values);
const min = least(...values);
```

### Differences from the source

Only `f.apply(null, args)` and `f.apply(undefined, args)` on a plain function name are checked;
method calls are left alone.

## `js/preserve-caught-error` — A rethrown error keeps the caught one as its cause

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the new error class must accept an options argument)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/preserve-caught-error.md

### What it checks

A built-in error (`Error`, `TypeError` and the rest) thrown from a `catch` block passes the caught
error as `{ cause }`.

**Why:** Without the cause, the original error and its stack are lost.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```js
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```ts
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed");
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
try {
  load();
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Load failed", { cause: err });
}
```

## `js/require-yield` — A generator function yields

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to yield or to drop the `*` needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/require-yield.md

### What it checks

A non-empty generator function contains at least one `yield`.

**Why:** A generator without `yield` is either unfinished or should be a plain function.

### How to fix

1. Add the `yield` the generator was meant to have, or remove the `*`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
function* ids() {
  return 1;
}
```

##### Do

```js
function* ids() {
  yield 1;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
function* ids() {
  return 1;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
function* ids() {
  yield 1;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function* ids() {
  return 1;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function* ids() {
  yield 1;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function* ids() {
  return 1;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function* ids() {
  yield 1;
}
```

## `js/use-instead` — Use the project's function instead of the one it wraps

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/use-instead.md

### What it checks

A project names the function it wants called instead of another, once, and codelaw holds the code to it. The rule is inert until `replacements` is set. A key is a dotted path, matched on a call's callee or a member read, exactly or as a prefix at a `.` boundary (`process.env` matches `process.env.API_URL`), and only where its first name is a global or an import, never a local that shadows it. A file that matches the entry's `allow_in` is exempt.

```toml
[rules."js/use-instead".options.replacements]
"fetch"              = { use = "apiFetch",     from = "@acme/http",     drop_in = true, allow_in = ["src/lib/http.ts"] }
"DOMPurify.sanitize" = { use = "sanitizeHtml", from = "@acme/security", drop_in = true, allow_in = ["src/security/**"] }
"console.log"        = { use = "logger.info",  from = "@acme/log" }
```

**Why:** A wrapper is where a team puts what every call needs - an auth header, a timeout, an approved sanitizer, a logger. Code that calls the wrapped function directly skips all of it, and only a rule can notice. It complements the rules that name an approved function at one sink (`sanitizers`): this one reports the wrong function anywhere.

**Limits:** it matches by the spelling of a path and where its first name comes from; it does not follow a value through a variable (`const f = fetch; f(x)`), and a shorthand property (`{ fetch }`) is not a read it sees. The wrapper calls the thing it wraps, so name its file in `allow_in`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `replacements` | `object` | `{}` | a dotted path to { use, from, drop_in?, allow_in? }: `use` is the function or variable to call instead, `from` the module it comes from, `drop_in` lets `codelaw fix` swap it in and add the import, `allow_in` lists globs of files exempt (the wrapper itself) |

### How to fix

1. With `drop_in = true`, run `codelaw fix`: the path becomes `use` and the import is added when the file lacks it.
2. Without `drop_in`, change the call by hand: the replacement takes other arguments or returns another shape.
3. In the wrapper's own file, add the file to `allow_in` rather than the call to the baseline.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```js
fetch("/api/orders");
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```js
import { apiFetch } from "@acme/http";
apiFetch("/api/orders");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```jsx
const Orders = () => <button onClick={() => fetch("/api/orders")}>load</button>;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```jsx
import { apiFetch } from "@acme/http";
const Orders = () => <button onClick={() => apiFetch("/api/orders")}>load</button>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```ts
const load = (): Promise<Response> => fetch("/api/orders");
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```ts
import { apiFetch } from "@acme/http";
const load = (): Promise<Response> => apiFetch("/api/orders");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```tsx
const Orders = () => <button onClick={() => fetch("/api/orders")}>load</button>;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ replacements = { fetch = { use = "apiFetch", from = "@acme/http", drop_in = true } } }`

```tsx
import { apiFetch } from "@acme/http";
const Orders = () => <button onClick={() => apiFetch("/api/orders")}>load</button>;
```

## `js/use-isnan` — Test for NaN with Number.isNaN

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the comparison's operator decides whether to negate)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/use-isnan.md

### What it checks

Code tests for `NaN` with `Number.isNaN(x)`, never by comparing with `NaN`.

**Why:** `NaN` is not equal to anything, itself included, so `x === NaN` is always false.

### How to fix

1. Replace `x === NaN` or `x == NaN` with `Number.isNaN(x)`.
2. Replace `x !== NaN` or `x != NaN` with `!Number.isNaN(x)`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (price === NaN) {
  reset();
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (Number.isNaN(price)) {
  reset();
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (price === NaN) {
  reset();
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (Number.isNaN(price)) {
  reset();
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (price === NaN) {
  reset();
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (Number.isNaN(price)) {
  reset();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (price === NaN) {
  reset();
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (Number.isNaN(price)) {
  reset();
}
```

## `js/valid-typeof` — typeof is compared with a type it can return

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-js` · `codelaw-rules-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which type was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:js/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/js/valid-typeof.md

### What it checks

`typeof x` is compared only with a string it can return: `"undefined"`, `"object"`, `"boolean"`,
`"number"`, `"string"`, `"function"`, `"symbol"` or `"bigint"`.

**Why:** A misspelled type such as `"strnig"` makes the comparison always false.

### How to fix

1. Correct the string to the type that was meant.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (typeof name === "strnig") {
  greet(name);
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (typeof name === "string") {
  greet(name);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (typeof name === "strnig") {
  greet(name);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (typeof name === "string") {
  greet(name);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (typeof name === "strnig") {
  greet(name);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (typeof name === "string") {
  greet(name);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (typeof name === "strnig") {
  greet(name);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (typeof name === "string") {
  greet(name);
}
```

## `json/no-duplicate-keys` — No key twice in one JSON object

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two values was meant can't be known from the file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/no-duplicate-keys.md

### What it checks

Each key appears once in a JSON object. Keys are compared by value, so `"a"` and `"\u0061"` are the same key.

**Why:** RFC 8259 leaves duplicate keys undefined: most parsers keep the last value and silently drop the first, others keep the first or refuse the file.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Delete the other entry, or move it under a key of its own.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "name": "web-app"
}
```

##### Do

```json
{
  "name": "web-app",
  "version": "1.0.0"
}
```

## `json/package-deps-sorted` — package.json dependency lists are sorted by name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/package-json` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/package-deps-sorted.md

### What it checks

The `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies`, `optionalDependencies` and `bundleDependencies` of a `package.json` are in name order.

**Why:** npm writes these lists sorted, so a hand-added entry out of order turns into an unrelated diff the next time npm touches the file; a sorted list is also quicker to scan.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "dependencies": {
    "react": "^19.0.0",
    "@tanstack/query": "^5.0.0",
    "lodash": "^4.17.21"
  }
}
```

##### Do

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "dependencies": {
    "@tanstack/query": "^5.0.0",
    "lodash": "^4.17.21",
    "react": "^19.0.0"
  }
}
```

### Notes

Names compare by Unicode code point, so scoped packages (`@scope/…`) come first. `bundleDependencies` may be a list of names; its items are sorted the same way. A list with comments between its entries is reported without a fix: the comments would be left behind while the entries move.

## `json/package-engines` — package.json declares engines.node

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the supported Node.js range is a project decision; the fix inserts the `node` option, which may not be the right range)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/package-json` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/package-engines.md

### What it checks

A `package.json` says which Node.js versions the package runs on, in `engines.node`.

**Why:** Without it, npm and package managers can't warn someone installing on an unsupported Node.js, and the package fails later with an error that doesn't say why.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | `string` | `">=22"` | the range the fix writes into `engines.node` |

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0"
}
```

##### Do

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22"
  }
}
```

## `json/package-json-schema` — package.json matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `manual` (a value the schema rejects is wrong in a way only its author knows how to correct)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/package-json` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/package-json-schema.md

### What it checks

A `package.json` matches SchemaStore's schema for it: every field has the type and the form npm reads, and `name` and `version` are written the way the registry accepts.

**Why:** npm and the tools that read `package.json` ignore or misread a field of the wrong shape — a `bin` that is a list, a `files` that is a string, an `engines` range that is a number — so the mistake surfaces later, far from the line that caused it.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the field and the form the schema expects.
2. Rewrite the value in that form, or remove the field if it was a mistake.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "files": "dist",
  "private": "yes"
}
```

##### Do

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "files": ["dist"],
  "private": true
}
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `package.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/package.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. Fields whose schema lives in another SchemaStore file (`eslintConfig`, `prettier`, `stylelint`, `ava`, `release`, `nodemonConfig`, …) accept any value. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`, and a pattern the engine's regular expressions can't read (look-around) accepts every value.

## `json/package-scripts-sorted` — package.json scripts are sorted by name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/package-json` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/package-scripts-sorted.md

### What it checks

The `scripts` of a `package.json` are in name order. A `pre<name>` or `post<name>` script sorts next to the `<name>` script it hooks into.

**Why:** A sorted list is quicker to scan and gives smaller diffs when scripts are added; npm runs scripts by name, so their order means nothing to it.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest",
    "build": "tsc",
    "pretest": "npm run build",
    "lint": "codelaw check"
  }
}
```

##### Do

```json path=package.json
{
  "name": "app",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tsc",
    "lint": "codelaw check",
    "pretest": "npm run build",
    "test": "vitest"
  }
}
```

### Notes

Names compare by Unicode code point. A `scripts` object that uses `npm-run-all`, `run-s` or `run-p` is left alone: those runners expand patterns such as `build:*` in the order the scripts are written, so sorting would change what runs. A `scripts` object with comments in it is reported without a fix, because the comments would stay behind while the scripts move.

## `json/tsconfig-schema` — tsconfig.json matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `manual` (a misspelt or misshapen option has several possible meanings; the author picks the one they intended)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/tsconfig` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/tsconfig-schema.md

### What it checks

A `tsconfig.json` matches SchemaStore's schema for it: every compiler option is one TypeScript knows, with a value of the type it takes.

**Why:** `tsc` reports an unknown option only when it runs, and many editors and bundlers that read `tsconfig.json` skip it silently, so a misspelt `"stirct": true` leaves the project less strict than it looks.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the option and what the schema expects, and suggests the option meant when the name is misspelt.
2. Correct the name or the value; remove an option TypeScript no longer has.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "stirct": true,
    "noEmit": "true"
  }
}
```

##### Do

```json path=tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true
  }
}
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `tsconfig.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/tsconfig.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. Comments and trailing commas are allowed, as `tsc` allows them. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`.

## `json/tsconfig-strict` — tsconfig.json turns on strict mode

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** JSON
- **Fix:** `suggest` (turning on strict mode can surface type errors the code then has to fix)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/tsconfig` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/json/tsconfig-strict.md

### What it checks

A `tsconfig.json` sets `"strict": true` in `compilerOptions`. A config that `extends` another and doesn't set `strict` itself is left alone, since it may inherit it.

**Why:** Strict mode turns on the checks that catch `null` and `undefined` mistakes and implicit `any`; without it the compiler lets most of those bugs through.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json path=tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext"
  }
}
```

##### Do

```json path=tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext"
  }
}
```

## `md/commands-show-output` — No $ before shell commands that show no output

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/commands-show-output.md

### What it checks

A code block in which every line is a command starting with `$` drops the `$`. A block that also shows output keeps it, since the `$` then tells commands from output.

**Why:** Readers copy commands straight from the block, and a pasted `$` makes every one of them fail.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
```sh
$ npm install
$ npm test
```
````

##### Do

````md
```sh
npm install
npm test
```
````

## `md/descriptive-link-text` — Link text says where the link goes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (describing the target needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/descriptive-link-text.md

### What it checks

A link's text is not a generic phrase such as "click here", "here", "link" or "more".

**Why:** Screen-reader users often jump from link to link, hearing only the link text; "here" tells them nothing.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prohibited_texts` | `string[]` | `["click here", "here", "link", "more"]` | link texts that say nothing about the target, compared ignoring case and punctuation |

### How to fix

1. Say in a few words what the link leads to.
2. Make those words the link text.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
For details, click [here](docs/setup.md).
````

##### Do

````md
For details, see [the setup guide](docs/setup.md).
````

## `md/fence-language` — Fenced code blocks name their language

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which language the code is in can't always be told from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/fence-language.md

### What it checks

A fenced code block names its language after the opening fence: ` ```ts `, ` ```sh `, or ` ```text ` for plain output.

**Why:** The language drives syntax highlighting, and lets tools — codelaw's `lint_code_blocks` among them — check the code inside.

### How to fix

1. Work out what the block holds.
2. Add its language after the opening fence, or `text` when it is plain output.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
```
npm install codelaw
```
````

##### Do

````md
```sh
npm install codelaw
```
````

## `md/first-line-heading` — A document starts with its title heading

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (the title text needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/first-line-heading.md

### What it checks

The first block of a document, after any front matter and HTML comments, is a level-1 heading — Markdown, or an HTML `<h1>`. A front matter `title:` counts as the heading.

**Why:** The first heading names the document for readers, search results and tools that build navigation from it.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `level` | `integer` | `1` | the level of the title heading |
| `allow_preamble` | `boolean` | `false` | allow text before the title heading |

### How to fix

1. Write a heading that names the document.
2. Put it first, above any introduction.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
This tool formats code.

# Formatter
````

##### Do

````md
# Formatter

This tool formats code.
````

## `md/heading-increment` — Heading levels go down one at a time

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the fix raises the skipped heading and its subsections, which changes the outline readers and tools see)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/heading-increment.md

### What it checks

A heading is at most one level deeper than the heading before it: `#` can be followed by `##`, not by `###`. When the front matter has a `title:`, it counts as the level-1 heading.

**Why:** Headings are the document's outline; a skipped level leaves a section with no parent, which confuses screen readers and tables of contents.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
# Install

### From npm

Run the installer.
````

##### Do

````md
# Install

## From npm

Run the installer.
````

### Differences from the source

The fix renumbers the whole outline at once: a raised heading's subsections move up with it.

## `md/link-fragments` — In-page links point at a heading or anchor that exists

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which section the link meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/link-fragments.md

### What it checks

A link to `#fragment` in the same document matches an anchor: a heading's GitHub-style id (lower case, punctuation dropped, spaces as dashes, `-1`, `-2` … for repeats), a `{#id}` after a heading, or an HTML `id` or `name`. `#top` and GitHub line anchors such as `#L20` are always valid.

**Why:** A fragment that matches nothing scrolls nowhere; it is usually a heading that was renamed after the link was written.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignore_case` | `boolean` | `false` | compare fragments with anchors ignoring case |

### How to fix

1. Find the section the link meant.
2. Change the fragment to that heading's id, or add an anchor where the link should land.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
# Guide

## Getting started

See [the first steps](#getting-startd).
````

##### Do

````md
# Guide

## Getting started

See [the first steps](#getting-started).
````

## `md/link-image-reference-definitions` — Every reference definition is used, and defined once

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/link-image-reference-definitions.md

### What it checks

A `[label]: url` definition is referred to by some link or image, and no label is defined twice. The fix deletes the unused or repeated definition.

**Why:** A definition nothing uses is dead text that goes stale, and only the first of two definitions counts, so the second one misleads.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignored_definitions` | `string[]` | `["//"]` | labels never reported (`[//]: # (…)` is a comment idiom) |

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
Read [the spec][spec].

[spec]: https://spec.commonmark.org/
[old]: https://example.com/old
````

##### Do

````md
Read [the spec][spec].

[spec]: https://spec.commonmark.org/
````

## `md/no-alt-text` — Images have alt text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (describing the image needs a person who can see it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-alt-text.md

### What it checks

A Markdown image has alt text: `![what it shows](…)`. HTML `<img>` elements are checked by `html/img-alt` in the HTML pack.

**Why:** Screen readers read the alt text in place of the image, and it shows when the image fails to load.

### How to fix

1. Look at the image and say in a few words what it shows.
2. Put that between the brackets; for a purely decorative image, use HTML with `alt=""`.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
![](diagram.png)
````

##### Do

````md
![The request flow from client to cache](diagram.png)
````

### Differences from the source

markdownlint also checks HTML `<img>`; here that is the HTML pack's `html/img-alt`, which lints HTML embedded in Markdown.

## `md/no-bare-urls` — URLs are links, not bare text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-bare-urls.md

### What it checks

A URL in running text is wrapped in angle brackets, `<https://…>`, or written as a link. URLs in code spans, links, autolinks and HTML are left alone.

**Why:** CommonMark only links a URL in angle brackets; a bare one is plain text in many renderers.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
The docs are at https://example.com/docs.
````

##### Do

````md
The docs are at <https://example.com/docs>.
````

### Differences from the source

Bare e-mail addresses are not reported.

## `md/no-duplicate-heading` — No two sibling headings with the same text

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which heading to rename, and to what, needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-duplicate-heading.md

### What it checks

Headings under the same parent heading have different text.

**Why:** Readers and tables of contents tell sections apart by their headings, and repeated headings get anchors (`#setup`, `#setup-1`) that are easy to link to the wrong one.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `siblings_only` | `boolean` | `true` | only compare headings under the same parent; `false` compares every heading in the document |

### How to fix

1. Decide whether the two sections are one topic; if so, merge them.
2. Otherwise rename one heading to say how it differs.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
# Tools

## Setup

Install the CLI.

## Setup

Configure it.
````

##### Do

````md
# Tools

## Setup

Install the CLI.

## Configuration

Configure it.
````

### Differences from the source

`siblings_only` defaults to `true` here (markdownlint defaults it to `false`), so a changelog's repeated `### Fixed` under each version is not reported.

## `md/no-emphasis-as-heading` — Headings are headings, not bold lines

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which heading level the line should become depends on the outline)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-emphasis-as-heading.md

### What it checks

A paragraph that is a single line of bold or italic text, standing alone, is a heading. Lines ending in punctuation are sentences and are not reported.

**Why:** Emphasis only looks like a heading: it doesn't appear in the outline, gets no anchor and isn't announced as a heading by screen readers.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `punctuation` | `string` | `".,;:!?。，；：！？"` | a line ending in one of these is a sentence, not a heading |

### How to fix

1. Pick the level the section belongs at.
2. Replace the emphasis with a heading of that level.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
# Guide

**Installation**

Run the installer.
````

##### Do

````md
# Guide

## Installation

Run the installer.
````

## `md/no-empty-links` — Links have a destination

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the link should go needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-empty-links.md

### What it checks

A link has a destination: not `()`, `(<>)` or a bare `(#)`.

**Why:** An empty link looks clickable but goes nowhere, usually because a URL was never filled in.

### How to fix

1. Find where the link should point.
2. Write that destination, or remove the link and keep its text.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
See [the changelog]().
````

##### Don't

````md
See [the changelog](#).
````

##### Do

````md
See [the changelog](CHANGELOG.md).
````

## `md/no-inline-html` — No raw HTML in Markdown

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (the Markdown equivalent, if there is one, needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-inline-html.md

### What it checks

A Markdown document doesn't use raw HTML elements, except those listed in `allowed_elements`. HTML comments are not reported.

**Why:** Raw HTML ties the document to renderers that pass it through; many (GitHub among them) strip some of it, and it hides the structure Markdown tools read.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allowed_elements` | `string[]` | `[]` | element names that may be used, such as `details` or `kbd` |

### How to fix

1. Rewrite the element in Markdown where an equivalent exists.
2. Where none does, add the element to `allowed_elements`.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
<b>Note:</b> back up first.
````

##### Do

````md
**Note:** back up first.
````

### Notes

This rule is in `data/conventions`, not `md/recommended`: most READMEs rely on HTML for layout (centred logos, `<details>`), so it is a house style rather than a correctness check.

## `md/no-reversed-links` — Links are written [text](url), not (text)[url]

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/no-reversed-links.md

### What it checks

Text written as `(text)[url]` is a link with its brackets swapped. Footnote references such as `(note)[^1]` are not reported.

**Why:** The reversed form doesn't render as a link: readers see the brackets and the raw URL.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
Read (the guide)[https://example.com/guide].
````

##### Do

````md
Read [the guide](https://example.com/guide).
````

## `md/reference-links-images` — Reference links use a label that is defined

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the reference should point needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/reference-links-images.md

### What it checks

A reference link or image — `[text][label]`, `[label][]`, `![alt][label]` — uses a label that a `[label]: url` definition in the document defines. Labels match ignoring case and spacing.

**Why:** A reference to an undefined label isn't a link at all: it renders as the literal brackets.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ignored_labels` | `string[]` | `["x"]` | labels never reported (`x` is a task-list checkbox) |
| `shortcut_syntax` | `boolean` | `false` | also check `[label]` shortcuts, which plain bracketed text looks like |

### How to fix

1. Check the label for a typo against the definitions.
2. Fix the label, or add the missing `[label]: url` definition.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
Read [the spec][spec].
````

##### Do

````md
Read [the spec][spec].

[spec]: https://spec.commonmark.org/
````

## `md/relative-links` — Relative links point at a file that exists

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the file moved, was renamed or was never written needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/relative-links.md

### What it checks

A link or image whose destination is a path, not a URL, names a file or folder of the project. The path is read from the linking file's folder (from the project root when it starts with `/`), without its `#fragment` or `?query`. Links with a scheme (`https:`, `mailto:`), in-page `#fragments`, template syntax and paths that leave the project are not checked.

**Why:** A relative link breaks silently when the file it names is moved or renamed; the reader gets a 404 where the documentation should be.

### How to fix

1. Find where the file went: `git log --follow --stat -- <path>` shows a rename.
2. Point the link at the file's new path, or remove the link if the file is gone.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
<!-- docs/guide.md -->
Start with [the setup](./setup.md), then read the [FAQ](../FAQ.md).
<!-- docs/setup.md -->
# Setup
````

##### Do

````md
<!-- docs/guide.md -->
Start with [the setup](./setup.md), then read the [FAQ](../FAQ.md).
<!-- docs/setup.md -->
# Setup
<!-- FAQ.md -->
# FAQ
````

## `md/single-h1` — One level-1 heading per document

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which heading is the title, and what level the others become, needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/single-h1.md

### What it checks

A document has one top-level heading, its title. Every later level-1 heading is reported; when the front matter has a `title:`, every level-1 heading is.

**Why:** The level-1 heading names the document; a second one splits the outline in two and gives the page two titles.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `level` | `integer` | `1` | the level of the title heading |

### How to fix

1. Keep the heading that names the document at level 1.
2. Make the others level 2 and shift their subsections down to match.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
# Guide

Intro.

# Usage

Steps.
````

##### Do

````md
# Guide

Intro.

## Usage

Steps.
````

### Differences from the source

markdownlint applies the rule only when the first line of the file is the level-1 heading; here the first level-1 heading anywhere is the title, so a README that starts with badges is checked too.

## `md/table-column-count` — Table rows have as many cells as the header

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** Markdown
- **Fix:** `manual` (which cell is missing or extra needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:md/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/md/table-column-count.md

### What it checks

Every row of a pipe table has the same number of cells as its header row.

**Why:** Renderers drop extra cells and leave missing ones empty, so a misplaced pipe silently loses or shifts data.

### How to fix

1. Compare the row with the header.
2. Add the missing cells or remove the extra ones, or add a header column if the data needs it.

### Examples

#### Markdown

##### Don't

````md
| Name | Type |
| ---- | ---- |
| id | number | required |
````

##### Do

````md
| Name | Type | Note |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| id | number | required |
````

## `node/hashbang` — Commands start with a Node.js hashbang, and nothing else has one

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing the hashbang of a script someone runs directly (`./tool.js`) stops it running)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/hashbang.md

### What it checks

A file the nearest `package.json` names in `bin` starts with `#!/usr/bin/env node`; a file it doesn't name has no hashbang. Without a `package.json` above the file, nothing is checked.

**Why:** npm links a `bin` entry as an executable, which the shell runs through its hashbang: without one the command fails, or runs under the wrong interpreter. A hashbang on a library file is noise that suggests it is a command.

### How to fix

1. On a command `bin` names, make the first line `#!/usr/bin/env node`.
2. On any other file, remove the hashbang, or add the file to `bin` if it is a command.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// package.json
{ "name": "tool", "bin": { "tool": "./bin/tool.js" } }
// bin/tool.js
console.log("hello");
```

##### Do

```js
// package.json
{ "name": "tool", "bin": { "tool": "./bin/tool.js" } }
// bin/tool.js
#!/usr/bin/env node
console.log("hello");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
// package.json
{ "name": "tool", "bin": "./cli.jsx" }
// lib/view.jsx
#!/usr/bin/env node
export const View = () => <p>hello</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
// package.json
{ "name": "tool", "bin": "./cli.jsx" }
// lib/view.jsx
export const View = () => <p>hello</p>;
```

### Differences from the source

TypeScript sources are not checked: eslint-plugin-n maps them to their built JavaScript through `convertPath`, which this rule has no option for yet. The source's checks for a byte-order mark and CRLF line endings in a command are not ported, and there is no `additionalExecutables` or `executableMap` option.

## `node/no-deprecated-api` — No deprecated Node.js APIs

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each deprecated API has its own replacement)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-deprecated-api.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't use Node.js APIs the documentation deprecates — `new Buffer()`, `fs.exists`,
`url.parse`, `util.isArray`, the `domain` module and the rest — whether reached by `import`,
`require()` or a global.

**Why:** Deprecated APIs are unsafe, slow or due for removal, and each has a documented replacement.

### How to fix

1. Replace the call with the API the message names.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { isArray } from "node:util";
export const ok = isArray([]);
```

##### Do

```js
export const ok = Array.isArray([]);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { isArray } from "node:util";
export const ok = isArray([]);
```

##### Do

```jsx
export const ok = Array.isArray([]);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { isArray } from "node:util";
export const ok = isArray([]);
```

##### Do

```ts
export const ok = Array.isArray([]);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { isArray } from "node:util";
export const ok = isArray([]);
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const ok = Array.isArray([]);
```

### Differences from the source

The pack's `node/deprecated-api` data table lists the APIs; the Node.js version a project supports
is not read.

## `node/no-exports-assign` — No assigning to exports

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether `module.exports` or a property was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-exports-assign.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't assign to the CommonJS `exports` variable; `exports = module.exports = …` is allowed.

**Why:** Assigning to `exports` only rebinds a local variable, so nothing is exported.

### How to fix

1. Assign to `module.exports`, or set properties on `exports` (`exports.name = …`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
exports = { start };
```

##### Do

```js
module.exports = { start };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
exports = { start };
```

##### Do

```jsx
module.exports = { start };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
exports = { start };
```

##### Do

```ts
module.exports = { start };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
exports = { start };
```

##### Do

```tsx
module.exports = { start };
```

## `node/no-extraneous-import` — Imported packages must be declared

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which dependency field and version to add is the package owner's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-extraneous-import.md

### What it checks

Every package an `import`, `export … from` or `import()` names is declared in the nearest `package.json`: `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies` or `optionalDependencies`.

**Why:** an undeclared package works only while something else happens to install it — a hoisted monorepo dependency or a transitive one — and breaks for every user who doesn't have it.

### How to fix

1. Add the package to the nearest `package.json` (`dependencies` if the shipped code needs it, `devDependencies` if only tests and tooling do), with your package manager's `add` command.
2. A type-only import is satisfied by its `@types/` package.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.js
import lodash from "lodash";
console.log(lodash);
```

##### Do

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.js
import lodash from "lodash";
console.log(lodash);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.jsx
import lodash from "lodash";
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.jsx
import lodash from "lodash";
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.ts
import lodash from "lodash";
console.log(lodash);
```

##### Do

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.ts
import lodash from "lodash";
console.log(lodash);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.tsx
import lodash from "lodash";
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.tsx
import lodash from "lodash";
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

## `node/no-extraneous-require` — Required packages must be declared

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which dependency field and version to add is the package owner's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-extraneous-require.md

### What it checks

Every package a `require()` names is declared in the nearest `package.json`: `dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies` or `optionalDependencies`.

**Why:** an undeclared package works only while something else happens to install it, and breaks for every user who doesn't have it.

### How to fix

1. Add the package to the nearest `package.json` (`dependencies` if the shipped code needs it, `devDependencies` if only tests and tooling do), with your package manager's `add` command.

### Examples

```js files
// package.json

const lodash = require("lodash");
```

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.js
const lodash = require("lodash");
console.log(lodash);
```

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
```
