```jsx files
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.jsx
const lodash = require("lodash");
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.ts
const lodash = require("lodash");
console.log(lodash);
```

##### Do

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.ts
const lodash = require("lodash");
console.log(lodash);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/app.tsx
const lodash = require("lodash");
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "app", "dependencies": { "react": "19.0.0", "lodash": "4.17.21" } }
// src/app.tsx
const lodash = require("lodash");
export const App = () => <p>{String(lodash)}</p>;
```

## `node/no-missing-import` — Imported project paths must exist

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right path depends on where the module went)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-missing-import.md

### What it checks

An `import`, `export … from` or `import()` path of the project — relative, absolute or a tsconfig `paths` alias — names a file that exists.

**Why:** a path that names no file fails at build or load time, and only on the code path that reaches it.

### How to fix

1. Point the specifier at the file that exists (check the extension and the folder), or restore the missing file.
2. A path to a generated file the repo doesn't hold is reported too: generate it before `codelaw check`, or suppress the line with a reason.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js files
// src/app.js
import { helper } from "./helpers";
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.js
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```js files
// src/app.js
import { helper } from "./helper";
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.js
export const helper = 1;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx files
// src/app.jsx
import { helper } from "./helpers";
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.jsx
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```jsx files
// src/app.jsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.jsx
export const helper = 1;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts files
// src/app.ts
import { helper } from "./helpers";
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.ts
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```ts files
// src/app.ts
import { helper } from "./helper";
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.ts
export const helper = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx files
// src/app.tsx
import { helper } from "./helpers";
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.tsx
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```tsx files
// src/app.tsx
import { helper } from "./helper";
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.tsx
export const helper = 1;
```

## `node/no-missing-require` — Required project paths must exist

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right path depends on where the module went)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-missing-require.md

### What it checks

A `require()` path of the project — relative, absolute or a tsconfig `paths` alias — names a file that exists.

**Why:** a path that names no file throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and only when that line runs.

### How to fix

1. Point the specifier at the file that exists (check the extension and the folder), or restore the missing file.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js files
// src/app.js
const { helper } = require("./helpers");
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.js
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```js files
// src/app.js
const { helper } = require("./helper");
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.js
export const helper = 1;
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx files
// src/app.jsx
const { helper } = require("./helpers");
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.jsx
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```jsx files
// src/app.jsx
const { helper } = require("./helper");
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.jsx
export const helper = 1;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts files
// src/app.ts
const { helper } = require("./helpers");
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.ts
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```ts files
// src/app.ts
const { helper } = require("./helper");
console.log(helper);
// src/helper.ts
export const helper = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx files
// src/app.tsx
const { helper } = require("./helpers");
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.tsx
export const helper = 1;
```

##### Do

```tsx files
// src/app.tsx
const { helper } = require("./helper");
export const App = () => <p>{String(helper)}</p>;
// src/helper.tsx
export const helper = 1;
```

## `node/no-process-exit` — No process.exit()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (how to end the program cleanly depends on what is still running)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-process-exit.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't call `process.exit()`.

**Why:** `process.exit()` ends the process at once, dropping pending writes and skipping cleanup;
libraries that call it take that choice away from the program.

### How to fix

1. Set `process.exitCode` and let the program finish, or throw an error the caller handles.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
if (failed) {
  process.exit(1);
}
```

##### Do

```js
if (failed) {
  process.exitCode = 1;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
if (failed) {
  process.exit(1);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
if (failed) {
  process.exitCode = 1;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
if (failed) {
  process.exit(1);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
if (failed) {
  process.exitCode = 1;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
if (failed) {
  process.exit(1);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
if (failed) {
  process.exitCode = 1;
}
```

## `node/no-unpublished-import` — Published files import only what is published

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to publish the file, move the dependency or move the code is the package owner's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-unpublished-import.md

### What it checks

In a package that is not `private` and lists `files`, a file `npm publish` packs imports neither a project file it doesn't pack nor a package that is only a `devDependency`.

**Why:** the published package then fails to load for its users: the file isn't in the tarball, or the devDependency isn't installed.

### How to fix

1. Add the imported file to `files` in the nearest `package.json`, move the package from `devDependencies` to `dependencies`, or move the import out of the published code.
2. A type-only import is not reported: it is erased from the published JavaScript.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.js", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.js
import { fixtures } from "../test/fixtures";
console.log(fixtures);
// test/fixtures.js
export const fixtures = [];
```

##### Do

```js files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.js", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.js
import { fixtures } from "./fixtures";
console.log(fixtures);
// lib/fixtures.js
export const fixtures = [];
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.jsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.jsx
import { fixtures } from "../test/fixtures";
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// test/fixtures.jsx
export const fixtures = [];
```

##### Do

```jsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.jsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.jsx
import { fixtures } from "./fixtures";
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// lib/fixtures.jsx
export const fixtures = [];
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.ts", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.ts
import { fixtures } from "../test/fixtures";
console.log(fixtures);
// test/fixtures.ts
export const fixtures = [];
```

##### Do

```ts files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.ts", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.ts
import { fixtures } from "./fixtures";
console.log(fixtures);
// lib/fixtures.ts
export const fixtures = [];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.tsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.tsx
import { fixtures } from "../test/fixtures";
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// test/fixtures.tsx
export const fixtures = [];
```

##### Do

```tsx files
// package.json
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.tsx", "files": ["lib"] }
// lib/index.tsx
import { fixtures } from "./fixtures";
export const App = () => <p>{String(fixtures)}</p>;
// lib/fixtures.tsx
export const fixtures = [];
```

## `node/no-unpublished-require` — Published files require only what is published

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-node` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to publish the file, move the dependency or move the code is the package owner's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:node/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/node/no-unpublished-require.md

### What it checks

**Why:** the published package then fails to load for its users: the file isn't in the tarball, or the devDependency isn't installed.

```jsx files
{ "name": "lib", "main": "lib/index.jsx", "files": ["lib"] }
```

## `py/abstract-base-class-without-abstract-method` — An abstract base class has an abstract method

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which methods subclasses must provide is a design decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/abstract-base-class-without-abstract-method.md

### What it checks

A class that inherits only from `ABC` (or uses `ABCMeta`) declares at least one `@abstractmethod`.

**Why:** Without one, nothing stops the base class being instantiated, and readers can't tell what subclasses must provide.

### How to fix

1. Mark the methods subclasses must override with `@abstractmethod`, or
2. drop `ABC` if the class isn't meant to be abstract.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from abc import ABC

class Shape(ABC):
    def area(self):
        return 0
```

##### Do

```py
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        return 0
```

## `py/all-sorted` — `__all__` is sorted

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/all-sorted.md

### What it checks

A module's `__all__` lists its names in isort's order: CONSTANTS, then Classes, then other names, each group in natural order.

**Why:** A sorted `__all__` is easy to scan and to keep in sync with the module.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
__all__ = ["save", "Loader", "load", "VERSION"]
```

##### Do

```py
__all__ = ["VERSION", "Loader", "load", "save"]
```

## `py/ambiguous-class-name` — No classes named `l`, `O` or `I`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice, and other modules may use the old one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/ambiguous-class-name.md

### What it checks

Classes aren't named `l`, `O` or `I`.

**Why:** In many fonts they are indistinguishable from `1` and `0`.

### How to fix

1. Rename the class.
2. Update its uses, here and in modules that import it.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
class I:
    pass
```

##### Do

```py
class Item:
    pass
```

## `py/ambiguous-function-name` — No functions named `l`, `O` or `I`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice, and other modules may use the old one)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/ambiguous-function-name.md

### What it checks

Functions aren't named `l`, `O` or `I`.

**Why:** In many fonts they are indistinguishable from `1` and `0`.

### How to fix

1. Rename the function.
2. Update its callers, here and in modules that import it.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def O():
    return 0
```

##### Do

```py
def origin():
    return 0
```

## `py/ambiguous-variable-name` — No variables named `l`, `O` or `I`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/ambiguous-variable-name.md

### What it checks

Variables, parameters and import aliases aren't named `l`, `O` or `I`.

**Why:** In many fonts they are indistinguishable from `1` and `0`.

### How to fix

1. Rename the variable to a descriptive name.
2. Update its uses.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
l = len(items)
```

##### Do

```py
length = len(items)
```

## `py/assert-false` — Don't `assert False`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the check now also runs under `python -O`, where the assert was skipped)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/assert-false.md

### What it checks

Code that must never be reached raises `AssertionError` instead of using `assert False`.

**Why:** `python -O` removes asserts, so the check silently disappears.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
assert False, "unreachable"
```

##### Do

```py
raise AssertionError("unreachable")
```

## `py/assert-raises-exception` — Tests don't expect a bare `Exception`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the exception the test expects has to be named by its author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/assert-raises-exception.md

### What it checks

`assertRaises(Exception)` and `pytest.raises(Exception)` (without `match=`) aren't used as context managers.

**Why:** They pass for any error at all, including a typo in the code under test.

### How to fix

1. Name the specific exception the code should raise.
2. With `pytest.raises`, add `match=` if the class can't be narrowed.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import unittest

class TestParse(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_bad_input(self):
        with self.assertRaises(Exception):
            parse("x")
```

##### Do

```py
import unittest

class TestParse(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_bad_input(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            parse("x")
```

## `py/assert-tuple` — `assert` doesn't test a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing the parentheses turns a no-op into a check that can now fail)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/assert-tuple.md

### What it checks

An `assert` tests a condition, not a parenthesised `(condition, message)` tuple.

**Why:** A non-empty tuple is always true, so the assert can never fail.

### How to fix

1. Remove the parentheses so the message becomes the assert's second operand.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
assert (count > 0, "count must be positive")
```

##### Do

```py
assert count > 0, "count must be positive"
```

## `py/assignment-to-os-environ` — Don't assign to `os.environ`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to clear the environment first or only update it needs a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/assignment-to-os-environ.md

### What it checks

Code changes the environment through `os.environ`'s items, never by assigning a new object to `os.environ`.

**Why:** Assigning replaces Python's mapping but not the process environment, so child processes don't see the change.

### How to fix

1. Update `os.environ` item by item (`os.environ[key] = value`), clearing it first if that was meant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os

os.environ = {"PATH": "/bin"}
```

##### Do

```py
import os

os.environ.clear()
os.environ["PATH"] = "/bin"
```

## `py/batched-without-explicit-strict` — `itertools.batched()` says `strict=`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`strict=` exists only from Python 3.13, and codelaw cannot tell which Python the code runs on: on an older one the added keyword raises `TypeError`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/batched-without-explicit-strict.md

### What it checks

`itertools.batched()` is called with `strict=True` or `strict=False`.

**Why:** Without it, a short last batch passes silently. The keyword exists from Python 3.13.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target_version` | `string` | *none* | the oldest Python the code supports; below 3.13 the rule is off |

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import itertools

batches = itertools.batched(items, 2)
```

##### Do

```py
import itertools

batches = itertools.batched(items, 2, strict=True)
```

##### Fixed

```py
import itertools

batches = itertools.batched(items, 2, strict=False)
```

### Differences from the source

Ruff reports this without a fix; codelaw suggests `strict=False`, which keeps today's behaviour. The fix is `suggest` (`codelaw fix --unsafe`), not `auto`: the `target_version` option may be unset, and on Python before 3.13 the keyword raises `TypeError`.

## `py/break-outside-loop` — `break` only inside a loop

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (what should happen instead (return, raise) is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/break-outside-loop.md

### What it checks

`break` appears only inside the body of a `for` or `while` loop in the same function.

**Why:** Outside a loop it is a `SyntaxError`.

### How to fix

1. Use `return` to leave a function, or move the `break` into the loop.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def stop():
    break
```

##### Do

```py
def stop(items):
    for item in items:
        break
```

## `py/cached-instance-method` — No `lru_cache` on methods

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the cache should live is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/cached-instance-method.md

### What it checks

`functools.lru_cache` and `functools.cache` decorate functions and static methods, not instance methods.

**Why:** The cache keeps a reference to every `self` it sees, so instances are never freed.

### How to fix

1. Move the cached work into a module-level function or a `staticmethod`.
2. Or keep a per-instance cache in an attribute.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import functools

class Store:
    @functools.lru_cache
    def get(self, key):
        return key.upper()
```

##### Do

```py
import functools

@functools.lru_cache
def normalise(key):
    return key.upper()

class Store:
    def get(self, key):
        return normalise(key)
```

## `py/continue-outside-loop` — `continue` only inside a loop

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (what should happen instead is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/continue-outside-loop.md

### What it checks

`continue` appears only inside the body of a `for` or `while` loop in the same function.

**Why:** Outside a loop it is a `SyntaxError`.

### How to fix

1. Move the `continue` into the loop, or restructure the code.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def skip():
    continue
```

##### Do

```py
def skip(items):
    for item in items:
        continue
```

## `py/default-except-not-last` — A bare `except:` is the last handler

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (reordering handlers changes which one runs)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/default-except-not-last.md

### What it checks

In a `try` statement, a bare `except:` comes after every other handler.

**Why:** Handlers after a bare `except:` can never run, and Python rejects it as a `SyntaxError`.

### How to fix

1. Move the bare `except:` to the end.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except:
    log()
except ValueError:
    retry()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except ValueError:
    retry()
except:
    log()
```

## `py/duplicate-dict-key` — A dict literal doesn't repeat a literal key

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value should win can't be known from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/duplicate-dict-key.md

### What it checks

A dict literal names each literal key (`"a"`, `1`, `True`) once.

**Why:** Only the last value is kept, so the earlier one is silently lost.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Remove the other entry, or give it its own key.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
colors = {"red": 1, "red": 2}
```

##### Do

```py
colors = {"red": 1, "blue": 2}
```

## `py/duplicate-dict-key-variable` — A dict literal doesn't repeat a variable key

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value should win can't be known from the code)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/duplicate-dict-key-variable.md

### What it checks

A dict literal uses the same variable as a key at most once.

**Why:** Both entries have the same key at run time, so only the last value is kept.

### How to fix

1. Decide which entry is meant.
2. Remove the other one, or use a different key.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
scores = {player: 1, player: 2}
```

##### Do

```py
scores = {player: 1, rival: 2}
```

## `py/duplicate-handler-exception` — No exception listed twice in one handler

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/duplicate-handler-exception.md

### What it checks

An `except` tuple names each exception once.

**Why:** A repeated exception is redundant and often a typo for a different one.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except (ValueError, ValueError, TypeError):
    retry()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    retry()
```

### Differences from the source

Exceptions are compared by name as written; aliases such as `IOError` and `OSError` are not merged.

## `py/duplicate-set-value` — No duplicate items in a set literal

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/duplicate-set-value.md

### What it checks

A set literal lists each literal value once.

**Why:** A repeated item is dropped silently and is often a typo for another value.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
colors = {"red", "green", "red"}
```

##### Do

```py
colors = {"red", "green"}
```

## `py/duplicate-try-block-exception` — An exception is caught by one handler only

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which handler's code is meant to run needs a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/duplicate-try-block-exception.md

### What it checks

Within one `try` statement, each exception class appears in only one `except` clause.

**Why:** Only the first matching handler runs, so the later one is dead code.

### How to fix

1. Merge the handlers' code into the first one, or remove the dead one.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except ValueError:
    retry()
except ValueError:
    log()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except ValueError:
    retry()
    log()
```

## `py/empty-method-without-abstract-decorator` — Empty methods in an abstract base class are abstract

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the method is a required hook or an optional no-op is a design decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/empty-method-without-abstract-decorator.md

### What it checks

In a class that inherits from `ABC`, a method whose body is empty is marked `@abstractmethod`.

**Why:** An empty, unmarked method lets subclasses forget to implement it.

### How to fix

1. Add `@abstractmethod` if subclasses must implement it.
2. Otherwise give it a docstring saying it is an optional hook.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...

    def draw(self):
        pass
```

##### Do

```py
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self): ...

    @abstractmethod
    def draw(self): ...
```

## `py/except-with-empty-tuple` — No `except ():`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the exceptions to catch are the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/except-with-empty-tuple.md

### What it checks

An `except` clause doesn't name an empty tuple.

**Why:** `except ():` catches nothing, so the handler never runs.

### How to fix

1. Name the exceptions to catch, or remove the handler.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except ():
    log()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except ValueError:
    log()
```

## `py/except-with-non-exception-classes` — `except` names exception classes

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the exception class to catch is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/except-with-non-exception-classes.md

### What it checks

An `except` clause names exception classes (or tuples of them), not literals or other values.

**Why:** Catching anything else raises `TypeError` the moment an exception reaches the handler.

### How to fix

1. Replace the value with the exception class you meant to catch.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except "error":
    log()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except RuntimeError:
    log()
```

## `py/f-string-docstring` — Docstrings aren't f-strings

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the docstring's wording has to change to drop the placeholder)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/f-string-docstring.md

### What it checks

The first statement of a module, class or function isn't an f-string meant as its docstring.

**Why:** Python treats an f-string there as an expression, so `__doc__` stays empty.

### How to fix

1. Remove the `f` prefix and write the text without placeholders.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def greet():
    f"""Say hello to {NAME}."""
```

##### Do

```py
def greet():
    """Say hello to the configured name."""
```

## `py/f-string-missing-placeholders` — An f-string has a placeholder

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/f-string-missing-placeholders.md

### What it checks

A string with the `f` prefix contains at least one `{…}` placeholder.

**Why:** Without one, the prefix does nothing and often means a placeholder was forgotten.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
print(f"hello")
```

##### Do

```py
print("hello")
```

## `py/format-invalid` — A `.format` string is well formed

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the brace is a field or literal text has to be decided)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/format-invalid.md

### What it checks

A string literal passed through `.format()` has balanced braces; literal braces are written `{{` and `}}`.

**Why:** A stray brace raises `ValueError` when the string is formatted.

### How to fix

1. Close the field, or double a literal brace (`{{`, `}}`).

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "{".format(1)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "{}".format(1)
```

## `py/format-missing-argument` — Every `.format` field has an argument

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the missing value has to be supplied)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/format-missing-argument.md

### What it checks

A `.format()` call passes an argument for every `{}`, `{0}` and `{name}` field.

**Why:** A missing argument raises `IndexError` or `KeyError` when the string is formatted.

### How to fix

1. Pass the missing argument, or remove the field.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "{} is {}".format("Ada")
```

##### Do

```py
message = "{} is {}".format("Ada", 36)
```

## `py/format-mixed-numbering` — A `.format` string doesn't mix `{}` and `{0}`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which numbering the author wants has to be chosen)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/format-mixed-numbering.md

### What it checks

A `.format()` string numbers its fields automatically (`{}`) or explicitly (`{0}`), not both.

**Why:** Python raises `ValueError: cannot switch from manual field specification to automatic field numbering`.

### How to fix

1. Number every field, or none of them.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "{0} is {}".format("Ada", 36)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "{0} is {1}".format("Ada", 36)
```

## `py/format-unused-named-argument` — Every keyword passed to `.format` is used

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/format-unused-named-argument.md

### What it checks

A `.format()` call has no keyword arguments the string never names.

**Why:** An unused keyword is usually a misspelled field name.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "{name}".format(name="Ada", age=36)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "{name}".format(name="Ada")
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is offered only when the removed values are plain names or literals.

## `py/format-unused-positional-argument` — Every positional argument to `.format` is used

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/format-unused-positional-argument.md

### What it checks

A `.format()` call has no positional arguments the string never refers to.

**Why:** An extra argument is usually a missing `{}` field.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "{}".format("Ada", 36)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "{}".format("Ada")
```

### Differences from the source

The fix removes unused arguments only from the end of the list, and only plain names or literals.

## `py/forward-annotation-syntax-error` — A string annotation is valid Python

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended type can't be inferred from broken text)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/forward-annotation-syntax-error.md

### What it checks

A type annotation written as a string parses as a Python expression.

**Why:** Type checkers and `typing.get_type_hints()` fail on an annotation they can't parse.

### How to fix

1. Correct the annotation so it parses.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def total(values: "list[int") -> int:
    return sum(values)
```

##### Do

```py
def total(values: "list[int]") -> int:
    return sum(values)
```

### Differences from the source

Strings inside `Literal[...]` and `Annotated[...]` are not treated as annotations.

## `py/function-call-in-default-argument` — No function calls in default arguments

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the value should be computed per call or once at import needs a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/function-call-in-default-argument.md

### What it checks

A parameter's default isn't computed by a function call, except calls known to return immutable values (`tuple()`, `frozenset()`, `int()`, `re.compile()`, `datetime.timedelta()`, …).

**Why:** The call runs once, when the function is defined, so every call shares the same result — a stale timestamp, or one shared object.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `extend_immutable_calls` | `string[]` | `[]` | more calls whose results are immutable, by qualified name |

### How to fix

1. Default to `None` and compute the value in the body, or
2. compute it once into a module-level constant and use that as the default.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import time

def log(message, when=time.time()):
    print(when, message)
```

##### Do

```py
import time

def log(message, when=None):
    if when is None:
        when = time.time()
    print(when, message)
```

## `py/function-uses-loop-variable` — Closures don't capture a loop variable by name

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (binding the value now (a default argument, `functools.partial`) changes the function's signature)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/function-uses-loop-variable.md

### What it checks

A function or lambda defined in a loop doesn't read a variable the loop rebinds, unless it is called or consumed straight away.

**Why:** Python closures look names up when they run, so every closure sees the loop's last value.

### How to fix

1. Bind the current value with a default argument (`lambda name=name: …`) or `functools.partial`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
callbacks = []
for name in ["a", "b"]:
    callbacks.append(lambda: print(name))
```

##### Do

```py
callbacks = []
for name in ["a", "b"]:
    callbacks.append(lambda name=name: print(name))
```

## `py/getattr-with-constant` — No `getattr` with a constant name

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/getattr-with-constant.md

### What it checks

`getattr(obj, "name")` with a constant, valid attribute name is written `obj.name`.

**Why:** `getattr` with a constant name is no safer than attribute access, only harder to read.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
name = getattr(user, "name")
```

##### Do

```py
name = user.name
```

## `py/if-tuple` — `if` doesn't test a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended condition can't be inferred from the tuple)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/if-tuple.md

### What it checks

An `if` or `elif` condition isn't a non-empty tuple.

**Why:** A non-empty tuple is always true, so the branch always runs.

### How to fix

1. Write the condition you meant, usually the tuple's first element.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if (ready, "waiting"):
    start()
```

##### Do

```py
if ready:
    start()
```

## `py/import-shadowed-by-loop-var` — A loop variable doesn't reuse an imported name

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new loop variable name is a choice the author has to make)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/import-shadowed-by-loop-var.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop's target doesn't rebind a name that an import in the same scope bound.

**Why:** After the loop the name no longer refers to the module, so later uses break in ways that are hard to trace.

### How to fix

1. Rename the loop variable.
2. Update its uses inside the loop body.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import path

for path in ["a.txt", "b.txt"]:
    print(path)
```

##### Do

```py
import path

for name in ["a.txt", "b.txt"]:
    print(path.join(name))
```

## `py/invalid-print-syntax` — No Python 2 `print >>`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the rewrite depends on how the Python 2 arguments were meant)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/invalid-print-syntax.md

### What it checks

`print` is called as a function; the Python 2 form `print >> stream, value` isn't used.

**Why:** In Python 3 it shifts the `print` function right, raising `TypeError`.

### How to fix

1. Rewrite as `print(value, file=stream)`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import sys

print >> sys.stderr, "error"
```

##### Do

```py
import sys

print("error", file=sys.stderr)
```

## `py/is-literal` — Literals are compared with `==`, not `is`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`==` calls the object's `__eq__`, which can behave differently from identity)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/is-literal.md

### What it checks

`is` and `is not` aren't used to compare with a string, bytes or number literal.

**Why:** Whether two equal literals are the same object is an implementation detail; Python warns about it with `SyntaxWarning`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if name is "admin":
    grant()
```

##### Do

```py
if name == "admin":
    grant()
```

## `py/jump-statement-in-finally` — No `return`, `break` or `continue` in `finally`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (how errors should propagate has to be decided)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/jump-statement-in-finally.md

### What it checks

A `finally` block doesn't leave through `return`, `break` or `continue`.

**Why:** Leaving `finally` that way silently discards any exception in flight.

### How to fix

1. Move the `return`, `break` or `continue` out of the `finally` block.
2. Handle the exception explicitly with `except` if it should be swallowed.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def read(path):
    try:
        return load(path)
    finally:
        return None
```

##### Do

```py
def read(path):
    try:
        return load(path)
    finally:
        close(path)
```

## `py/lambda-assignment` — Define functions with `def`, not a lambda

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an annotation on the assigned name is dropped by the rewrite)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/lambda-assignment.md

### What it checks

A name is bound to a function with `def`, not by assigning a `lambda`.

**Why:** A `def` has a real name in tracebacks, can have a docstring, and reads as a definition.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
double = lambda x: x * 2
```

##### Do

```py
def double(x):
    return x * 2
```

## `py/late-future-import` — `from __future__` imports come first

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving statements above it can change the order the module runs in)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/late-future-import.md

### What it checks

`from __future__ import …` statements come before any other statement except the module docstring.

**Why:** Python rejects a late `__future__` import with a `SyntaxError`.

### How to fix

1. Move the `from __future__` import to the top, after the docstring.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os
from __future__ import annotations
```

##### Do

```py
from __future__ import annotations
import os
```

## `py/loop-variable-overrides-iterator` — A loop variable doesn't replace what it iterates

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the new name is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/loop-variable-overrides-iterator.md

### What it checks

A `for` loop's target doesn't reuse a name read in the iterable expression.

**Why:** After the loop the name holds the last item, not the collection, which breaks later uses.

### How to fix

1. Give the loop variable its own name.
2. Update its uses in the loop body.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
for items in items:
    print(items)
```

##### Do

```py
for item in items:
    print(item)
```

## `py/map-without-explicit-strict` — `map()` over several iterables says `strict=`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`strict=` exists only from Python 3.14, and codelaw cannot tell which Python the code runs on: on an older one the added keyword raises `TypeError`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/map-without-explicit-strict.md

### What it checks

`map()` with two or more iterables is called with `strict=True` or `strict=False`.

**Why:** Without it, `map` silently stops at the shortest input. The keyword exists from Python 3.14.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target_version` | `string` | *none* | the oldest Python the code supports; below 3.14 the rule is off |

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys)
```

##### Do

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys, strict=True)
```

##### Fixed

```py
sums = map(add, xs, ys, strict=False)
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is `suggest` (`codelaw fix --unsafe`), not `auto`: the `target_version` option may be unset, and on Python before 3.14 the keyword raises `TypeError`.

## `py/max-lines` — A module stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (splitting a module changes its structure; which names belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-lines.md

### What it checks

A module has at most `max` lines (1000 by default, as Pylint's `too-many-lines`). Blank lines and lines that hold
only a comment are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines` or `skip_comments` is `false`; a line that holds code and a
comment counts as code. `skip_docstrings` leaves out the lines of module, class and function docstrings, and
`skip_imports` the top-level import block. The rule reports once, on the first line over the limit, with the measured
count: `1204 lines (max 1000; blank lines and comments not counted)`.

**Why:** A module that long is usually several modules: it is slow to review, and every import of it pays for all of it. The
limit is a prompt to split, not a goal in itself: raise `max` for a module that is long on purpose, or leave generated
code to `[files] lint_generated = false`. Only the host file is measured, never a code block in Markdown.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `1000` | the most lines a module may have |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_docstrings` | `boolean` | `false` | the lines of docstrings do not count |
| `skip_imports` | `boolean` | `false` | the import block does not count |

### How to fix

1. Find a cohesive group of names (one class and its helpers, one feature's functions) and move it to a new module in the same package.
2. Import it back in the old module, or re-export it from the package's `__init__.py`, so callers do not change.
3. If the module is long on purpose, raise `max` for it in an `[[overrides]]` entry, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule py/max-lines`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
a = 1
b = 2
c = 3
d = 4
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
from more import d

a = 1
b = 2
```

## `py/max-lines-per-function` — A function stays under a maximum number of lines

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (extracting part of a function changes its structure; where to cut and what to call the piece is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-lines-per-function.md

### What it checks

A function (`def` or `async def`, a method included) spans at most `max` lines (50 by default), from its `def` line to
its last. Blank lines, comment-only lines and docstring lines are not counted unless `skip_blank_lines`,
`skip_comments` or `skip_docstrings` is `false`. With `include_nested` (the default) an inner function's lines count
toward the outer function as well; with `include_nested = false` they do not, from the inner `def` to its last
line. `ignore_names` is a regular expression for names to exempt, such as `"^test_"`. The rule reports on the
function's name: `render_orders is 84 lines (max 50)`. A `lambda` is an expression, not a function here.

**Why:** A function that long does several jobs, and its name can say only one. The limit is a prompt to extract, not a goal in
itself: a long table of test data is long on purpose, so exempt it with `ignore_names`.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `50` | the most lines one function may span |
| `skip_blank_lines` | `boolean` | `true` | blank lines do not count |
| `skip_comments` | `boolean` | `true` | lines that hold only a comment do not count |
| `skip_docstrings` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of the function's docstring (and of a nested one's) do not count |
| `include_nested` | `boolean` | `true` | the lines of an inner function count toward the outer one too |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | *none* | a regular expression; functions named like this are exempt, e.g. "^test_" |

### How to fix

1. Find a block inside the function that does one thing (a loop body, a branch, a run of statements that build one value).
2. Extract it into a well-named function, and pass in what it reads.
3. Repeat until each piece fits `max`. If the function is long on purpose, name it in `ignore_names`, or freeze it with `codelaw baseline add --rule py/max-lines-per-function`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
def total(items):
    result = 0
    for item in items:
        result += item
    return result
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ max = 3 }`

```py
def total(items):
    return sum(items)
```

## `py/max-params` — A function takes at most a maximum number of parameters

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (grouping parameters changes the function's signature and every call to it; which belong together is the author's call)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/size` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/max-params.md

### What it checks

A function (`def` or `async def`, a method included) takes at most `max` parameters (5 by default, as Pylint and
Ruff). `self` and `cls` are not counted, nor are `*args` and `**kwargs` unless `count_varargs` is `true`, nor a
parameter whose name matches `ignore_names` (`"^_"` by default). A keyword-only parameter counts. `max_positional`
adds a second cap on the parameters a caller can pass by position, those before `*` or `*args`. A method decorated
`@override` and an `@overload` stub are skipped, since you do not own that signature; set `ignore_overrides` or
`ignore_declarations` to `false` to count them. The rule reports on the function's name:
`create_order takes 6 parameters (max 5)`.

**Why:** A call with many positional arguments is easy to get in the wrong order, and every added parameter is a change to every
caller. Grouping related parameters in one object, or making them keyword-only, names them at the call site.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | `integer` | `5` | the most parameters a function may take |
| `max_positional` | `integer` | *none* | a separate cap on positional parameters, those before `*` or `*args` (Ruff PLR0917); none by default |
| `count_varargs` | `boolean` | `false` | count `*args` and `**kwargs` |
| `ignore_self_cls` | `boolean` | `true` | `self` and `cls`, the first parameter of a method, do not count |
| `ignore_names` | `string` | `"^_"` | a regular expression; parameters named like this do not count |
| `ignore_overrides` | `boolean` | `true` | skip a method decorated `@override` or `@typing.override`: its signature is not yours |
| `ignore_declarations` | `boolean` | `true` | skip an `@overload` stub |

### How to fix

1. Group the parameters that belong together into a dataclass or a `TypedDict`: `create_order(Order(customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift))`.
2. Or make the rarely used ones keyword-only with a bare `*`, and set `max_positional` to cap how many a caller passes by position.
3. If the signature is not yours to change, exempt it: an `@override` and an `@overload` stub already are.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def create_order(customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift):
    return (customer, items, coupon, address, note, gift)
```

##### Do

```py
def create_order(order):
    return order
```

## `py/module-import-not-at-top` — Module-level imports come first

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving an import above other code changes the order the module runs in)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/module-import-not-at-top.md

### What it checks

Module-level imports come before other code. A docstring, `__future__` imports, dunder assignments (`__all__`, `__version__`), `if`/`try`/`with` blocks and changes to `sys.path` or `os.environ` may come before them.

**Why:** Imports scattered through a module hide its dependencies, and code that runs before them can change what they load.

### How to fix

1. Move the import up to the module's import section.
2. If it must run after the code above it, keep it and suppress the finding with a comment saying why.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os

print(os.name)

import sys
```

##### Do

```py
import os
import sys

print(os.name)
```

## `py/multiple-imports-on-one-line` — One module per `import` statement

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-imports-on-one-line.md

### What it checks

Each `import` statement imports one module; `import os, sys` is split into one line per module.

**Why:** One import per line keeps diffs and merges clean and lets import sorting work line by line.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import os, sys
```

##### Do

```py
import os
import sys
```

### Differences from the source

`from module import a, b` is not affected; it imports from one module.

## `py/multiple-starred-expressions` — One starred target per assignment

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which target should collect the rest has to be chosen)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/multiple-starred-expressions.md

### What it checks

An unpacking assignment has at most one starred target.

**Why:** Two starred targets are ambiguous and a `SyntaxError`.

### How to fix

1. Keep the star on one target only.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
*head, *tail = values
```

##### Do

```py
head, *tail = values
```

## `py/mutable-contextvar-default` — No mutable `ContextVar` defaults

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to use an immutable value or set a fresh one per context is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/mutable-contextvar-default.md

### What it checks

A `ContextVar`'s `default=` isn't a list, dict, set or the result of a call.

**Why:** The default is one object shared by every context, so mutating it leaks state between them.

### How to fix

1. Use an immutable default, or no default and set a fresh value in each context.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from contextvars import ContextVar

items = ContextVar("items", default=[])
```

##### Do

```py
from contextvars import ContextVar

items = ContextVar("items", default=())
```

## `py/nested-star-import` — `import *` only at module level

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the names to import must be chosen by reading the function)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/nested-star-import.md

### What it checks

`from module import *` appears only at the top level of a module.

**Why:** Inside a function or class a star import is a `SyntaxError` in Python 3.

### How to fix

1. Replace the star with the names the function uses.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def paths():
    from os.path import *
    return join("a", "b")
```

##### Do

```py
def paths():
    from os.path import join
    return join("a", "b")
```

## `py/no-bare-except` — No bare `except:`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`except Exception:` no longer catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-bare-except.md

### What it checks

Every `except` clause names the exceptions it handles.

**Why:** A bare `except:` also catches `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, so Ctrl-C and `sys.exit()` stop working inside it.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    run()
except:
    log()
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    run()
except Exception:
    log()
```

### Differences from the source

As in Ruff, a handler whose body re-raises with a bare `raise` is allowed: it doesn't swallow anything.

## `py/no-explicit-stacklevel` — `warnings.warn` sets `stacklevel`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`stacklevel=2` is right for a warning about the caller; deeper helpers need a higher value)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-explicit-stacklevel.md

### What it checks

`warnings.warn()` is called with `stacklevel=` (or `skip_file_prefixes=`).

**Why:** The default `stacklevel=1` points the warning at the line inside your library, not at the caller who needs to change.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import warnings

warnings.warn("old API")
```

##### Do

```py
import warnings

warnings.warn("old API", stacklevel=2)
```

## `py/no-mutable-default` — No mutable default arguments

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (callers that relied on the shared object, or passed `None` on purpose, behave differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-mutable-default.md

### What it checks

A parameter's default isn't a list, dict or set (literal, comprehension or constructor call).

**Why:** The default is created once, when the function is defined, and every call shares and mutates the same object.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def append(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items
```

##### Do

```py
def append(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is offered only for unannotated parameters whose default doesn't read the parameter's own name; Ruff also rewrites an annotation to `T | None`.

## `py/no-print` — No `print()` in library code

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the log level, and whether the output was meant for the user, need a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-print.md

### What it checks

Code under `src/` reports through `logging`, not `print()`.

**Why:** `print` writes to standard output whether or not the caller wants it; a logger can be filtered, redirected and silenced.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py path=src/app.py
import logging

def run():
    print("started")
```

##### Do

```py path=src/app.py
import logging

def run():
    logging.getLogger(__name__).info("%s", "started")
```

## `py/no-star-import` — No `from module import *`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which names the module needs can only be found by reading its uses)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-star-import.md

### What it checks

Modules import the names they use explicitly instead of `from module import *`.

**Why:** A star import hides where names come from, can silently replace local names, and stops a linter from finding undefined names.

### How to fix

1. List the names the module uses from the star-imported module.
2. Replace the star with those names.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
from os.path import *

print(join("a", "b"))
```

##### Do

```py
from os.path import join

print(join("a", "b"))
```

### Differences from the source

Relative star imports (`from .sub import *`) are not reported: that is how a package re-exports its submodules' API, and Ruff leaves them alone in `__init__.py`.

## `py/no-tunable-literals` — No hard-coded timeouts, limits or thresholds

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which configuration key holds the value is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/no-tunable-literals.md

### What it checks

A number passed as, defaulted to or assigned to a setting whose name says it is tunable (`timeout`, `retries`, `max_*`, `limit`, `threshold`, `interval`, `delay`, `ttl`, `backoff`, `deadline`, …) comes from configuration, not a literal in the code. `0` and `1` are allowed, and so are module-level `UPPER_CASE` constants, the one place such a value may be written down.

**Why:** Tunable values buried in code can't be changed per environment without a release, and the same number drifts apart in several places.

### How to fix

1. Pick or add a configuration key for the value.
2. Read the value from configuration where it is used.
3. For a fixed protocol constant, name it as a module-level `UPPER_CASE` constant instead.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def fetch(url):
    return get(url, timeout=30)
```

##### Do

```py
from config import settings

def fetch(url):
    return get(url, timeout=settings.http_timeout)
```

## `py/none-comparison` — Compare with `None` using `is`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (an object whose `__eq__` treats itself as equal to `None` would compare differently)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/none-comparison.md

### What it checks

Comparisons with `None` use `is` / `is not`, not `==` / `!=`.

**Why:** `None` is a singleton; `==` calls the other object's `__eq__`, which may not return what you expect.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if user == None:
    login()
```

##### Do

```py
if user is None:
    login()
```

## `py/not-in-test` — Write `x not in y`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/not-in-test.md

### What it checks

A membership test is negated as `x not in y`, not `not x in y`.

**Why:** `not x in y` reads as `(not x) in y`; `not in` says what is meant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if not item in seen:
    keep(item)
```

##### Do

```py
if item not in seen:
    keep(item)
```

## `py/not-is-test` — Write `x is not y`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/not-is-test.md

### What it checks

An identity test is negated as `x is not y`, not `not x is y`.

**Why:** `not x is y` reads as `(not x) is y`; `is not` says what is meant.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
if not value is None:
    use(value)
```

##### Do

```py
if value is not None:
    use(value)
```

## `py/percent-format-count-mismatch` — A `%` format string gets one value per placeholder

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value is missing, or extra, can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-count-mismatch.md

### What it checks

The tuple (or single literal) formatted into a `%` string has as many values as the string has positional placeholders.

**Why:** Too few values raise `TypeError: not enough arguments`; too many raise `TypeError: not all arguments converted`.

### How to fix

1. Add or remove values, or placeholders, until they match.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%s is %s" % ("Ada",)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s is %s" % ("Ada", 36)
```

## `py/percent-format-expected-mapping` — Named `%` placeholders get a mapping

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the key each value belongs to isn't written anywhere)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-expected-mapping.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string with named placeholders (`%(name)s`) is applied to a mapping, not a tuple.

**Why:** Python raises `TypeError: format requires a mapping`.

### How to fix

1. Pass a dict whose keys are the placeholder names.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s" % ("Ada",)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

## `py/percent-format-expected-sequence` — Positional `%` placeholders get a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the order of the values isn't written anywhere)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-expected-sequence.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string with two or more positional placeholders is applied to a tuple, not a dict.

**Why:** A dict is a single value, so Python raises `TypeError: not enough arguments`.

### How to fix

1. Pass a tuple with one value per placeholder, or switch to named placeholders.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%s and %s" % {"a": 1, "b": 2}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s and %s" % (1, 2)
```

## `py/percent-format-invalid` — A `%` format string is complete

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended placeholder can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-invalid.md

### What it checks

A string formatted with `%` has no unfinished placeholder such as `%(name` or a trailing `%`.

**Why:** Python raises `ValueError` when the string is formatted.

### How to fix

1. Finish the placeholder (`%(name)s`) or escape a literal percent as `%%`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

## `py/percent-format-missing-argument` — Every named `%` placeholder has a value

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the value for the missing key has to be supplied)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-missing-argument.md

### What it checks

A dict literal formatted into a `%` string has a key for every named placeholder.

**Why:** A missing key raises `KeyError` when the string is formatted.

### How to fix

1. Add the missing key to the dict, or remove the placeholder.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s is %(age)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s is %(age)s" % {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
```

## `py/percent-format-mixed-placeholders` — A `%` format string doesn't mix positional and named placeholders

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which style the string should use is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-mixed-placeholders.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string uses either positional placeholders (`%s`) or named ones (`%(name)s`), not both.

**Why:** Python can't fill both from one right-hand side and raises `TypeError`.

### How to fix

1. Name every placeholder, or make every placeholder positional.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s is %s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s is %(age)s" % {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
```

## `py/percent-format-star-requires-sequence` — A `*` width in a `%` format takes a tuple

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the order of the values has to be decided)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-star-requires-sequence.md

### What it checks

A `%` format string using `*` for a width or precision is applied to a tuple.

**Why:** The `*` takes its value from the next positional argument, which a mapping doesn't have.

### How to fix

1. Pass a tuple with the width before the value.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%*d" % {"width": 5, "value": 1}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%*d" % (5, 1)
```

## `py/percent-format-unsupported-character` — A `%` format uses known conversions

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended conversion can't be inferred)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-unsupported-character.md

### What it checks

Each `%` placeholder ends with a conversion Python knows (`s`, `r`, `a`, `d`, `f`, `x`, …).

**Why:** An unknown conversion raises `ValueError: unsupported format character`.

### How to fix

1. Use the conversion you meant, or escape a literal percent as `%%`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%y" % (1,)
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%s" % (1,)
```

## `py/percent-format-unused-named-argument` — Every key given to `%` is used

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/percent-format-unused-named-argument.md

### What it checks

A dict literal formatted into a `%` string has no keys the string never names.

**Why:** An unused key is usually a misspelled placeholder.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
```

##### Do

```py
message = "%(name)s" % {"name": "Ada"}
```

### Differences from the source

The fix is offered only when the removed values are plain names or literals, so no call is dropped.

## `py/raise-literal` — Raise exceptions, not literals

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (the exception class to raise is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/raise-literal.md

### What it checks

`raise` is given an exception, not a string or number literal.

**Why:** Raising a literal is a `TypeError` in Python 3.

### How to fix

1. Raise an exception class with the literal as its message.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
raise "failed"
```

##### Do

```py
raise RuntimeError("failed")
```

## `py/raise-not-implemented` — Raise `NotImplementedError`, not `NotImplemented`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (callers catching the `TypeError` the broken code raised would now see a different exception)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/raise-not-implemented.md

### What it checks

`raise` uses `NotImplementedError`, not the `NotImplemented` constant.

**Why:** `NotImplemented` is a value for binary operators; raising it is a `TypeError`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
class Shape:
    def area(self):
        raise NotImplemented
```

##### Do

```py
class Shape:
    def area(self):
        raise NotImplementedError
```

## `py/raise-without-from-inside-except` — Raising in `except` says `from`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to chain the original error or hide it is the author's choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/raise-without-from-inside-except.md

### What it checks

A `raise` inside an `except` block that raises a new exception says `from err` or `from None`.

**Why:** Without it, the traceback reads as if a second error happened while handling the first.

### How to fix

1. Bind the caught exception (`except E as err:`).
2. Raise with `from err`, or `from None` to hide the original deliberately.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError:
    raise TypeError("not a number")
```

##### Do

```py
try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError as err:
    raise TypeError("not a number") from err
```

## `py/re-sub-positional-args` — `re.sub` count and flags by keyword

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which parameter the value was meant for needs a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/re-sub-positional-args.md

### What it checks

`re.sub()`, `re.subn()` and `re.split()` receive `count`, `maxsplit` and `flags` as keyword arguments.

**Why:** Their positions are easy to confuse: `re.sub(p, r, s, re.IGNORECASE)` passes the flag as `count`.

### How to fix

1. Pass `count=`, `maxsplit=` and `flags=` by name.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import re

text = re.sub("a", "b", text, 1)
```

##### Do

```py
import re

text = re.sub("a", "b", text, count=1)
```

## `py/redefined-while-unused` — A definition isn't replaced before it is used

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `manual` (which definition is meant, and whether to rename or remove the other, needs a person)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:py/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/py/redefined-while-unused.md

### What it checks

A function, class or import isn't redefined (by another `def`, `class`, import or assignment) before anything reads it.

**Why:** The first definition is dead: usually a copy-paste mistake, or a name clash with an import.

### How to fix

1. Decide which definition is meant.
2. Rename or remove the other one.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
def load():
    return 1

def load():
    return 2
```

##### Do

```py
def load():
    return 1

def reload():
    return 2
```

### Differences from the source

A read anywhere between the two definitions counts as a use, including inside a function body Python only runs later.

## `py/redundant-tuple-in-exception-handler` — No one-element tuple in `except`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
