```tsx
  $sceProvider.enabled(false);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.config(function ($sceProvider) {
  $sceProvider.enabled(true);
});
```

## `sec-js/cookie-flags` — A cookie sets httpOnly, secure and sameSite

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a cookie a script must read, or one used cross-site, needs different flags)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/cookie-flags.md

### What it checks

`res.cookie`, `reply.setCookie` and `ctx.cookies.set` pass an options object with `httpOnly`, `secure` and `sameSite`.

**Why:** Without `httpOnly` a script reads the cookie, without `secure` it travels over plain HTTP, and without `sameSite` the browser sends it on cross-site requests (CWE-614, CWE-1004, CWE-352).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
res.cookie("sid", sid);
```

##### Do

```js
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

##### Fixed

```js
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
res.cookie("sid", sid);
```

##### Do

```jsx
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
res.cookie("sid", sid);
```

##### Do

```ts
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

##### Fixed

```ts
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
res.cookie("sid", sid);
```

##### Do

```tsx
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
res.cookie("sid", sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: "lax" });
```

## `sec-js/express-hardening` — An Express app turns off x-powered-by or uses helmet

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`app.use(helmet())` is the better fix and needs an import; the inserted line only hides the framework)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `warn` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/express-hardening.md

### What it checks

A file that creates an Express app also calls `helmet()` or disables `x-powered-by`.

**Why:** The default `X-Powered-By: Express` header names the framework for every scanner, and without `helmet` the app sends none of the headers that limit framing, sniffing and mixed content (CWE-200).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const app = express();
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Do

```js
const app = express();
app.use(helmet());
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Fixed

```js
const app = express();
app.disable("x-powered-by");
app.get("/", handler);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const app = express();
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const app = express();
app.use(helmet());
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const app = express();
app.disable("x-powered-by");
app.get("/", handler);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const app = express();
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Do

```ts
const app = express();
app.use(helmet());
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const app = express();
app.disable("x-powered-by");
app.get("/", handler);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const app = express();
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const app = express();
app.use(helmet());
app.get("/", handler);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const app = express();
app.disable("x-powered-by");
app.get("/", handler);
```

## `sec-js/express-session-secret` — express-session has a secret from the environment and a secure cookie

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the secret comes from is a deployment decision)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/express-session-secret.md

### What it checks

`express-session`, `cookie-session` and `session()` are not given a literal `secret`, and their cookie does not set `secure: false`.

**Why:** A secret in the source is in every clone and every build; anyone who has it forges a session cookie, and `secure: false` lets the cookie travel over plain HTTP (CWE-798, CWE-614).

### How to fix

1. Read the secret from the environment or a secret store, and rotate it if it was ever committed.
2. Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: "lax" }` in production (behind a proxy, set `trust proxy`).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.use(session({ secret: "keyboard cat", resave: false }));
```

##### Do

```js
app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false }));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(session({ secret: "keyboard cat", resave: false }));
```

##### Do

```jsx
app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false }));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(session({ secret: "keyboard cat", resave: false }));
```

##### Do

```ts
app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(session({ secret: "keyboard cat", resave: false }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false }));
```

## `sec-js/graphql-hardening` — A GraphQL server limits query depth and cost, and hides introspection

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the limits that fit the schema are a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `warn` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/graphql-hardening.md

### What it checks

An Apollo, Yoga or express-graphql server names a depth or cost limit in its options, and does not set `introspection: true`.

**Why:** A query can nest or fan out without bound and exhaust the server, and introspection hands an attacker the whole schema (CWE-770, CWE-200).

### How to fix

1. Add a depth limit (`graphql-depth-limit`) and a cost or complexity limit to `validationRules`, and cap the page size of list fields.
2. Turn introspection off in production, and use persisted queries where the clients are your own.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
```

##### Do

```js
const server = new ApolloServer({
  typeDefs,
  resolvers,
  validationRules: [depthLimit(8)],
  introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
```

##### Do

```jsx
const server = new ApolloServer({
  typeDefs,
  resolvers,
  validationRules: [depthLimit(8)],
  introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
```

##### Do

```ts
const server = new ApolloServer({
  typeDefs,
  resolvers,
  validationRules: [depthLimit(8)],
  introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const server = new ApolloServer({ typeDefs, resolvers });
```

##### Do

```tsx
const server = new ApolloServer({
  typeDefs,
  resolvers,
  validationRules: [depthLimit(8)],
  introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
});
```

## `sec-js/helmet-config` — helmet is not given false for a header it sets

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the header's directives should be is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/helmet-config.md

### What it checks

`helmet({ … })` does not set `contentSecurityPolicy`, `frameguard`, `hsts`, `noSniff`, `xssFilter` or the cross-origin policies to `false`.

**Why:** Each of these headers closes one class of attack (injected scripts, clickjacking, downgrade to HTTP, MIME sniffing); turning one off opens it again (CWE-693).

### How to fix

1. Keep the header on and tune it: give `contentSecurityPolicy` the directives the app needs.
2. If a header must go for one route, set it off for that route only, with a comment that says why.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```js
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } } }));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```jsx
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } } }));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```ts
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } } }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: false }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } } }));
```

## `sec-js/jwt-verify` — A JWT is verified with a named algorithm, never `none`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the algorithm to name is the one the issuer signs with)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/jwt-verify.md

### What it checks

`jwt.verify` is given an `algorithms` list, no algorithm is `none`, and `jwt.decode` is not the whole check.

**Why:** Without `algorithms` a token can pick its own: `none` carries no signature, and an RSA public key used as an HMAC secret lets anyone mint tokens (CWE-347). `decode` reads a token without checking it.

### How to fix

1. Pass `{ algorithms: ["RS256"] }` (or the one algorithm you issue with) to `jwt.verify`.
2. Never put `none` in the list, and never use a public key as an HMAC secret.
3. Use `jwt.decode` only to read a token that `jwt.verify` has already accepted.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey);
```

##### Do

```js
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ["RS256"] });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ["RS256"] });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey);
```

##### Do

```ts
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ["RS256"] });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ["RS256"] });
```

## `sec-js/missing-rate-limit` — A login or reset route has a rate limit

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the limits that fit the route are a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `warn` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/missing-rate-limit.md

### What it checks

A route that signs in, resets a password or checks a one-time code is registered with middleware, and the file mentions a rate limiter.

**Why:** Without a limit an attacker tries passwords, codes and reset tokens as fast as the server answers (CWE-307, CWE-770).

### How to fix

1. Add `express-rate-limit` (or the framework's equivalent) to the route: a few attempts per minute per address and per account.
2. Add a lock-out or a growing delay after repeated failures, and log them.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.post("/login", (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

##### Do

```js
const loginLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 60000, max: 10 });
app.post("/login", loginLimiter, (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.post("/login", (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
const loginLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 60000, max: 10 });
app.post("/login", loginLimiter, (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.post("/login", (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
const loginLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 60000, max: 10 });
app.post("/login", loginLimiter, (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.post("/login", (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
const loginLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 60000, max: 10 });
app.post("/login", loginLimiter, (req, res) => {
  signIn(req, res);
});
```

## `sec-js/no-archive-slip` — No archive entry name written to disk unchecked

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what to do with an entry that leaves the folder (skip, stop, report) is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-archive-slip.md

### What it checks

A file written while unpacking an archive is not named by the entry's own path or name without a check that it stays inside the target folder.

**Why:** An entry named `../../etc/cron.d/x` or an absolute path writes outside the folder the code meant: the zip-slip bug (CWE-22).

### How to fix

1. Resolve the entry's path against the target folder and reject the entry when the result does not start with `target + path.sep`.
2. Skip symbolic links and absolute entry names; set a limit on the number and total size of entries (a zip bomb).

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(path.join(dest, entry.path)));
```

##### Do

```js
const target = path.resolve(dest, entry.path);
if (!target.startsWith(dest + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error("archive entry leaves the folder");
}
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(target));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(path.join(dest, entry.path)));
```

##### Do

```jsx
const target = path.resolve(dest, entry.path);
if (!target.startsWith(dest + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error("archive entry leaves the folder");
}
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(target));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(path.join(dest, entry.path)));
```

##### Do

```ts
const target = path.resolve(dest, entry.path);
if (!target.startsWith(dest + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error("archive entry leaves the folder");
}
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(target));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(path.join(dest, entry.path)));
```

##### Do

```tsx
const target = path.resolve(dest, entry.path);
if (!target.startsWith(dest + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error("archive entry leaves the folder");
}
entry.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(target));
```

## `sec-js/no-bad-tag-filter` — No regular expression that filters HTML tags

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which tags and attributes may stay is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-bad-tag-filter.md

### What it checks

A regular expression is not used to strip or test HTML tags (`/<script>/`, `/<[^>]*>/`); a sanitizer is.

**Why:** HTML is not regular: `<script >`, `<SCRIPT>`, `<scr<script>ipt>` and a tag split across lines slip past a pattern, and what is left still runs (CWE-116, CWE-185).

### How to fix

1. Sanitize with a library built for it: `DOMPurify.sanitize(html)` in the browser, `sanitize-html` on the server.
2. To show markup as text, escape it (`&lt;`) instead of removing it, or write it with `textContent`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const clean = input.replace(/<script>/gi, "");
```

##### Do

```js
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(input);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const clean = input.replace(/<script>/gi, "");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(input);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const clean = input.replace(/<script>/gi, "");
```

##### Do

```ts
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(input);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const clean = input.replace(/<script>/gi, "");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(input);
```

## `sec-js/no-biased-random` — No byte taken modulo a number that does not divide 256

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`crypto.randomInt` needs Node 14.10 or later, and a range that starts above zero needs the bounds written)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-biased-random.md

### What it checks

A random byte or integer from `crypto.randomBytes` is not reduced with `%`; `crypto.randomInt(max)` does it without bias.

**Why:** `byte % 6` makes some results more likely than others (256 is not a multiple of 6), which weakens a token, a die or a shuffle (CWE-327).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const roll = crypto.randomBytes(1)[0] % 6;
```

##### Do

```js
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

##### Fixed

```js
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const roll = crypto.randomBytes(1)[0] % 6;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const roll = crypto.randomBytes(1)[0] % 6;
```

##### Do

```ts
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const roll = crypto.randomBytes(1)[0] % 6;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const roll = crypto.randomInt(6);
```

## `sec-js/no-bidi-characters` — No hidden bidirectional control characters in code

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a comment is removed whole, since its hidden text cannot be told from the rest; a string or regular expression with such a character has no mechanical fix)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-bidi-characters.md

### What it checks

Source code, comments, strings and regular expressions hold no bidirectional control characters (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069).

**Why:** These characters reorder how an editor and a review tool show the code, so what a reviewer reads is not what the compiler runs: the Trojan Source attack (CVE-2021-42574).

### How to fix

1. Delete the character: show hidden characters in the editor (or run `git diff --word-diff-regex=.`) and remove each one.
2. If a string needs right-to-left text, write the characters as escapes (`\u202E`) so the source does not hide them.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const level = readLevel();
// check the access level ‮ ⁦ admin
```

##### Do

```js
const level = readLevel();
```

##### Fixed

```js
const level = readLevel();
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const level = readLevel();
// check the access level ‮ ⁦ admin
```

##### Do

```jsx
const level = readLevel();
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const level = readLevel();
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const level = readLevel();
// check the access level ‮ ⁦ admin
```

##### Do

```ts
const level = readLevel();
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const level = readLevel();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const level = readLevel();
// check the access level ‮ ⁦ admin
```

##### Do

```tsx
const level = readLevel();
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const level = readLevel();
```

## `sec-js/no-child-process-shell` — No shell command built from a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the program and its arguments have to be separated by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-child-process-shell.md

### What it checks

`exec` and `execSync` (from `child_process`) are called with a literal command only, and `spawn`-style calls do not set `shell: true`.

**Why:** A command string is parsed by a shell, so a value spliced into it can add commands with `;`, `&&` or `$(…)` (CWE-78).

### How to fix

1. Call `execFile` or `spawn` with the program name first and the values as an array: no shell parses them.
2. Leave `shell` at its default (`false`); if a shell feature (a pipe, a glob) is needed, do it in the program, not in a command string.
3. A value that must reach a command is checked against an allow-list first.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const { exec } = require("child_process");
exec("convert " + name + " out.png");
```

##### Do

```js
const { execFile } = require("child_process");
execFile("convert", [name, "out.png"]);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const { exec } = require("child_process");
exec("convert " + name + " out.png");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const { execFile } = require("child_process");
execFile("convert", [name, "out.png"]);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const { exec } = require("child_process");
exec("convert " + name + " out.png");
```

##### Do

```ts
const { execFile } = require("child_process");
execFile("convert", [name, "out.png"]);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const { exec } = require("child_process");
exec("convert " + name + " out.png");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const { execFile } = require("child_process");
execFile("convert", [name, "out.png"]);
```

## `sec-js/no-cleartext-http` — No request made over http://

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the server must answer on HTTPS before the scheme is switched, and the text of a URL cannot be rewritten by an edit primitive)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-cleartext-http.md

### What it checks

`fetch`, `axios`, `http.get`, `got` and similar are not given a literal `http://` URL, other than for localhost.

**Why:** A request over plain HTTP can be read and rewritten by anyone on the network path, including the credentials and tokens in it (CWE-319).

### How to fix

1. Change `http://` to `https://` in the URL, and check the server answers on it.
2. Where the host has no certificate, get one (Let's Encrypt) rather than falling back to HTTP.
3. A URL that is only ever local (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`) may stay; those are not flagged.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const response = await fetch("http://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

##### Do

```js
const response = await fetch("https://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const response = await fetch("http://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

##### Do

```jsx
const response = await fetch("https://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const response = await fetch("http://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

##### Do

```ts
const response = await fetch("https://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const response = await fetch("http://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

##### Do

```tsx
const response = await fetch("https://api.example-bank.com/accounts");
```

## `sec-js/no-cors-wildcard-credentials` — No CORS that allows every origin together with credentials

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which origins may call the API is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-cors-wildcard-credentials.md

### What it checks

`cors()` is not given `origin: "*"` or `origin: true` together with `credentials: true`.

**Why:** `origin: true` reflects whatever origin asks, so any website can send the visitor's cookies to your API and read the answer (CWE-942).

### How to fix

1. List the origins that may call the API: `origin: ["https://app.example.com"]`, or a function that checks a list.
2. Drop `credentials: true` if the API does not use cookies; then `origin: "*"` is acceptable for public data.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }));
```

##### Do

```js
app.use(cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true }));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }));
```

##### Do

```jsx
app.use(cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true }));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }));
```

##### Do

```ts
app.use(cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }));
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.use(cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true }));
```

## `sec-js/no-csrf-before-method-override` — No method-override before the CSRF check

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (moving a middleware changes the order every route in the file runs them in)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-csrf-before-method-override.md

### What it checks

`methodOverride` is registered after the CSRF middleware, not before it.

**Why:** The CSRF middleware decides by the request's method: a `POST` rewritten to `DELETE` after the check was never checked as one that changes state (CWE-352).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
app.use(csurf());
```

##### Do

```js
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

##### Fixed

```js
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
app.use(csurf());
```

##### Do

```jsx
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
app.use(csurf());
```

##### Do

```ts
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

##### Fixed

```ts
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
app.use(csurf());
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
app.use(csurf());
app.use(methodOverride("_method"));
```

## `sec-js/no-dangerously-set-inner-html` — No dangerouslySetInnerHTML from a value that is not sanitized

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the value needs markup at all is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-dangerously-set-inner-html.md

### What it checks

React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is given a literal, or a value that went through a sanitizer such as `DOMPurify.sanitize`.

**Your sanitizer:** a value passes when it is a call to one of the `sanitizers`: the built-in list (DOMPurify, sanitize-html, xss, escape-html, lodash and he `escape`, Trusted Types `createHTML`) plus your own, each matched by name and by the module it is imported from, so a local `function sanitize(x) { return x }` does not pass. `sanitizers_mode = "replace"` makes yours the only ones that count. It does not follow a value through a variable: `const c = clean(x)` then `c` at the sink is not a call. Add a project function with `sanitizers = [{ name = "sanitizeHtml", module = "@acme/security" }]`.

**Why:** The name is the warning: the value becomes the element's HTML, so markup an attacker supplies runs in the page (CWE-79).

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sanitizers` | `call[]` | 10 entries (below) | functions whose result may reach the sink: a callee path (global) or { name, module }; `sanitizers_mode: replace` makes them the only ones that count |
| `sanitizers_mode` | `string` | `"extend"` | `extend` adds your `sanitizers` to the default list; `replace` uses only yours |

### How to fix

1. Render the value as text (`{comment.body}`) wherever it need not carry markup.
2. Where it must, pass it through a sanitizer first: `DOMPurify.sanitize(html)`, and keep the allowed tags narrow.
3. Sanitize once, at the edge, and keep the sanitized string in its own variable so the call is next to the use.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: comment.body } };
```

##### Do

```js
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) } };
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: comment.body } };
```

##### Do

```jsx
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) } };
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: comment.body } };
```

##### Do

```ts
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) } };
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: comment.body } };
```

##### Do

```tsx
const props = { dangerouslySetInnerHTML: { __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) } };
```

## `sec-js/no-document-cookie-token` — No token or session written to document.cookie

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the cookie has to be set by the server, which is a change to the response)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-document-cookie-token.md

### What it checks

A token, a session id or a password is not written to `document.cookie`; the server sets it with `Set-Cookie`.

**Why:** A cookie script can write is a cookie script can read, so it has no `HttpOnly` flag, and any XSS reads it (CWE-1004).

### How to fix

1. Return the credential in the response and let the server send `Set-Cookie: token=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.
2. Keep the cookie out of script's reach: the page calls the API and the browser attaches the cookie.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
document.cookie = "token=" + token + "; path=/";
```

##### Do

```js
document.cookie = "theme=dark; path=/";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
document.cookie = "token=" + token + "; path=/";
```

##### Do

```jsx
document.cookie = "theme=dark; path=/";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
document.cookie = "token=" + token + "; path=/";
```

##### Do

```ts
document.cookie = "theme=dark; path=/";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
document.cookie = "token=" + token + "; path=/";
```

##### Do

```tsx
document.cookie = "theme=dark; path=/";
```

## `sec-js/no-dynamic-script-src` — No script or frame source taken from a value that is not a literal

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which sources the page may load is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-dynamic-script-src.md

### What it checks

The `src` of a `<script>`, `<iframe>`, `<frame>` or `<embed>` element is not set from a value that is not a literal.

**Why:** A script source the page computes is code it loads and runs; a value an attacker influences loads code of their choosing (CWE-829).

### How to fix

1. Use a literal URL, or pick one from a table of literal URLs by a key the code controls.
2. If the URL must come from configuration, check its origin against an allow-list and add `integrity` (Subresource Integrity) to the element.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = scriptUrl;
```

##### Do

```js
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = "https://cdn.example.com/lib.js";
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = scriptUrl;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = "https://cdn.example.com/lib.js";
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = scriptUrl;
```

##### Do

```ts
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = "https://cdn.example.com/lib.js";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = scriptUrl;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const script = document.createElement("script");
script.src = "https://cdn.example.com/lib.js";
```

## `sec-js/no-electron-insecure` — No insecure Electron window setting

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the window's preload and renderer code may rely on the setting; a setting set to `true` (such as `nodeIntegration`) has no mechanical fix and is reported as manual)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-electron-insecure.md

### What it checks

`webSecurity`, `contextIsolation` and `sandbox` are not `false`, and `nodeIntegration`, `nodeIntegrationInWorker`, `allowRunningInsecureContent` and `enableRemoteModule` are not `true`.

**Why:** Each switch removes a wall between web content and the machine: with Node integration on or context isolation off, one XSS bug in a window is code execution on the user's computer (CWE-79, CWE-829).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const win = new BrowserWindow({ webPreferences: { contextIsolation: false } });
```

##### Do

```js
const win = new BrowserWindow({ webPreferences: { contextIsolation: true } });
```

```js
const win = new BrowserWindow({ webPreferences: { contextIsolation: true } });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const win = new BrowserWindow({ webPreferences: { contextIsolation: false } });
```

##### Do

```jsx

```

##### Fixed

```jsx
const win = new BrowserWindow({ webPreferences: { contextIsolation: true } });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts

```

##### Do


##### Fixed

##### Don't

```tsx

```

##### Fixed

```tsx

```

## `sec-js/no-eval` — No eval, new Function or string timers

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the string stood for (a function, a table of operations, a parser) is a design choice)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-eval.md

### What it checks

Code is not built from a string at run time: no `eval`, `new Function`, `Function(…)`, and no `setTimeout` or `setInterval` given a string.

**Why:** Whatever reaches the string runs with the program's full privileges, so a single untrusted byte in it is remote code execution (CWE-94).

### How to fix

1. Pass a function, not a string, to `setTimeout` and `setInterval`.
2. Parse data with `JSON.parse`; for an expression language use a lookup table of allowed operations or a real parser instead of `eval`.
3. Replace `new Function(…)` with a named function that takes its inputs as parameters.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const result = eval(expression);
setTimeout("tick()", 100);
```

##### Do

```js
const result = JSON.parse(payload);
setTimeout(() => tick(), 100);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const result = eval(expression);
setTimeout("tick()", 100);
```

##### Do

```jsx
const result = JSON.parse(payload);
setTimeout(() => tick(), 100);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const result = eval(expression);
setTimeout("tick()", 100);
```

##### Do

```ts
const result = JSON.parse(payload);
setTimeout(() => tick(), 100);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const result = eval(expression);
setTimeout("tick()", 100);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const result = JSON.parse(payload);
setTimeout(() => tick(), 100);
```

## `sec-js/no-format-string` — No request data as a format string

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-js` · `codelaw-rules-security-js` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (it changes what is printed when the value has `%` in it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-js/strict` at `warn` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-js/no-format-string.md

### What it checks

`util.format` and the `console` methods are not given request data as their only argument, where it is read as a format string.

**Why:** A value with `%s`, `%d` or `%o` in it is a format string, so it can print values the author did not mean to log, and a formatter given too few arguments drops text (CWE-134).

### How to fix

### Examples


##### Do

```js
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

##### Fixed

```js
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
console.log(req.query.msg);
```

##### Do

```jsx
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

##### Fixed

```jsx
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
console.log(req.query.msg);
```

##### Do

```ts
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

##### Fixed

```ts
console.log("%s", req.query.msg);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

