```py
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
```

## `sec-py/yaml-safe-load` — `yaml.safe_load` instead of `yaml.load`

- **Pack:** `codelaw-rules-security-python` · **Languages:** Python
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`safe_load` rejects the Python-specific tags (`!!python/object`) a document may rely on)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-py/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-py/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-py/yaml-safe-load.md

### What it checks

YAML is read with `yaml.safe_load`, or with `yaml.load` and `SafeLoader`.

**Why:** The default and full loaders build arbitrary Python objects, so a crafted document runs code (CWE-502).

### How to fix

1. Replace `yaml.load(stream)` with `yaml.safe_load(stream)`.
2. If you pass a `Loader`, pass `yaml.SafeLoader`.

### Examples

#### Python

##### Don't

```py
import yaml

data = yaml.load(stream)
```

##### Do

```py
import yaml

data = yaml.safe_load(stream)
```

## `sec-ts/angular-bypass-security-trust` — No bypassSecurityTrust call on a value that is not a literal

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the value needs to be trusted at all is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/angular-bypass-security-trust.md

### What it checks

`DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, `…Script`, `…Style`, `…Url` and `…ResourceUrl` are not given a value that is not a literal.

**Why:** Angular sanitizes what it binds; these calls tell it to stop, so markup, a script or a `javascript:` URL in the value runs in the page (CWE-79).

### How to fix

1. Bind the value (`[innerHTML]="body"`) and let Angular sanitize it: it keeps safe tags and drops scripts.
2. If an element must be trusted (a fixed SVG), pass a literal, or sanitize the value with a library first (`DOMPurify`) and add a comment that says why trust is needed.
3. Never trust a value that came from a request, a URL or a user.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Post {
  safe = this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(this.body);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Post {
  safe = this.body;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Post {
  safe = this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(this.body);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Post {
  safe = this.body;
}
```

## `sec-ts/angular-native-element-html` — No HTML written to a native element or through Renderer2

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the value is text or markup is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/angular-native-element-html.md

### What it checks

`ElementRef.nativeElement.innerHTML`, `outerHTML` and `insertAdjacentHTML`, and `Renderer2.setProperty(el, "innerHTML", value)`, are not given a value that is not a literal.

**Your sanitizer:** a value passes when it is a call to one of the `sanitizers`: the built-in list (DOMPurify, sanitize-html, xss, escape-html, lodash and he `escape`, Trusted Types `createHTML`) plus your own, each matched by name and by the module it is imported from, so a local `function sanitize(x) { return x }` does not pass. `sanitizers_mode = "replace"` makes yours the only ones that count. It does not follow a value through a variable: `const c = clean(x)` then `c` at the sink is not a call. Add a project function with `sanitizers = [{ name = "sanitizeHtml", module = "@acme/security" }]`.

**Why:** These write the value as markup without Angular's sanitizer, so a `<script>` or an `onerror=` in it runs in the page (CWE-79).

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sanitizers` | `call[]` | 10 entries (below) | functions whose result may reach the sink: a callee path (global) or { name, module }; `sanitizers_mode: replace` makes them the only ones that count |
| `sanitizers_mode` | `string` | `"extend"` | `extend` adds your `sanitizers` to the default list; `replace` uses only yours |

### How to fix

1. Bind the value in the template: `[innerText]="text"` for text, `[innerHTML]="html"` for markup that Angular sanitizes.
2. With `Renderer2`, use `setProperty(el, "textContent", value)` or `createText` and `appendChild`.
3. If markup is needed and trusted, sanitize it first (`DomSanitizer.sanitize(SecurityContext.HTML, value)`).

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
class Box {
  show(html: string) {
    this.el.nativeElement.innerHTML = html;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
class Box {
  show(html: string) {
    this.text = html;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
class Box {
  show(html: string) {
    this.el.nativeElement.innerHTML = html;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
class Box {
  show(html: string) {
    this.text = html;
  }
}
```

## `sec-ts/nest-cors` — NestJS CORS names its origins

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which origins may call the API is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/nest-cors.md

### What it checks

`app.enableCors()` is given options with an origin list, not no options, and not `origin: true` together with `credentials: true`; `NestFactory.create(…, { cors: true })` is not used.

**Why:** `enableCors()` allows every origin, and `origin: true` reflects the caller's; with credentials any website can use the visitor's session on your API (CWE-942).

### How to fix

1. Pass the origins that may call the API: `app.enableCors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"] })`.
2. Keep `credentials: true` only with an explicit origin list.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableCors();
```

##### Do

```ts
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableCors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableCors();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
app.enableCors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true });
```

## `sec-ts/nest-missing-guard` — A NestJS controller has a guard

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which guard protects the route is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/nest-missing-guard.md

### What it checks

A class decorated `@Controller` carries `@UseGuards`, or the file registers a global guard.

**Why:** A route with no guard answers anyone; one forgotten controller is an open door (CWE-862). This reads one file: a guard registered in another file (`APP_GUARD` in a module) is not seen, so it warns.

### How to fix

1. Add `@UseGuards(AuthGuard)` to the controller (or register `APP_GUARD` once for the app and mark public routes `@Public()`).
2. Add role checks (`@Roles("admin")` with a `RolesGuard`) where the route is not for every signed-in user.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Controller("users")
export class UsersController {
  @Get()
  list() {
    return [];
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Controller("users")
@UseGuards(AuthGuard)
export class UsersController {
  @Get()
  list() {
    return [];
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Controller("users")
export class UsersController {
  @Get()
  list() {
    return [];
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Controller("users")
@UseGuards(AuthGuard)
export class UsersController {
  @Get()
  list() {
    return [];
  }
}
```

## `sec-ts/nest-throttler` — A NestJS sign-in controller is rate limited

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the limits that fit the route are a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/nest-throttler.md

### What it checks

A controller with a login, register, reset or one-time-code route carries `@Throttle` or `ThrottlerGuard`.

**Why:** Without a limit an attacker tries passwords, codes and reset tokens as fast as the server answers (CWE-307, CWE-770).

### How to fix

1. Install `@nestjs/throttler`, add `ThrottlerGuard` to the controller (or globally) and `@Throttle({ default: { limit: 5, ttl: 60000 } })` to the route.
2. Add a lock-out or a growing delay after repeated failures for one account, and log them.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Controller("auth")
export class AuthController {
  @Post("login")
  login() {
    return signIn();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Controller("auth")
@UseGuards(ThrottlerGuard)
export class AuthController {
  @Post("login")
  login() {
    return signIn();
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Controller("auth")
export class AuthController {
  @Post("login")
  login() {
    return signIn();
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Controller("auth")
@UseGuards(ThrottlerGuard)
export class AuthController {
  @Post("login")
  login() {
    return signIn();
  }
}
```

## `sec-ts/nest-validation-whitelist` — ValidationPipe has whitelist on

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a client that sends fields no DTO names starts getting them stripped, which can change what an endpoint does)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/nest-validation-whitelist.md

### What it checks

`new ValidationPipe(…)` is given `whitelist: true`, so a property no DTO decorator names is stripped.

**Why:** Without it a request can carry extra fields (`isAdmin`, `role`) that the DTO never declared and the code copies into a model: mass assignment (CWE-915).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe());
```

##### Do

```ts
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }));
```

##### Fixed

```ts
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe());
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }));
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }));
```

## `sec-ts/next-server-action-validation` — A Next.js server action validates its input

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the schema and the authorisation check are written by the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/next-server-action-validation.md

### What it checks

An exported function in a `"use server"` file that takes arguments calls a validator (`schema.parse`, `safeParse`, `validate`) on them.

**Your validator:** the function passes when it calls one of the `validators` anywhere in its body, or in a function around it: the built-in list (zod and valibot imports and a `*Schema.parse`, any `.safeParse`, `.parseAsync`, `.validate` or `.assert`, yup, joi, class-validator, class-transformer's `plainToInstance`, superstruct, typia) plus your own, each matched by name and by the module it is imported from, so a local `function validate(x) { return x }` does not count. `validators_mode = "replace"` makes yours the only ones that count. Add a project function with `validators = [{ name = "checkInput", module = "@acme/validation" }]`. A validator that a helper calls for you is not seen: name the helper.

**Why:** A server action is a public HTTP endpoint: its arguments come from the client whatever the form looks like, so an unchecked one writes what an attacker sends (CWE-20, CWE-862). Whether the function also checks who is calling is not decided from the syntax.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validators` | `call[]` | 25 entries (below) | calls that check input, any one of which in the function counts: a callee path or { name, module }; `validators_mode: replace` makes yours the only ones that count |
| `validators_mode` | `string` | `"extend"` | `extend` adds your `validators` to the default list; `replace` uses only yours |

### How to fix

1. Parse the arguments with a schema (`zod`, `valibot`) at the top of the action and use the parsed value only.
2. Check the caller next: read the session and refuse when the user may not do this (`const session = await auth(); if (!session) throw …`).
3. Return a small, typed result; never return a database row whole.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
"use server";
export async function createPost(input: FormData) {
  await db.insert(posts).values({ title: String(input.get("title")) });
}
```

##### Do

```ts
"use server";
export async function createPost(input: FormData) {
  const data = postSchema.parse({ title: input.get("title") });
  await db.insert(posts).values(data);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
"use server";
export async function createPost(input: FormData) {
  await db.insert(posts).values({ title: String(input.get("title")) });
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
"use server";
export async function createPost(input: FormData) {
  const data = postSchema.parse({ title: input.get("title") });
  await db.insert(posts).values(data);
}
```

## `sec-ts/no-any-request-handler` — No request typed any

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the real shape of the request is known only to the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-any-request-handler.md

### What it checks

A route handler's request parameter or `@Body()`, `@Query()`, `@Param()` and `@Headers()` argument is not typed `any`.

**Why:** `any` turns the type checker off for everything that came from the client, so a wrong shape is not caught where it enters (CWE-20). This reads the written type only; without type information it cannot see an `any` that is inferred.

### How to fix

1. Type the request: `Request<Params, ResBody, ReqBody, Query>` in Express, a DTO class in NestJS.
2. Validate the body at run time as well (see `sec-ts/no-unchecked-cast-of-input`): a type only describes what the code expects.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
app.post("/users", (req: any, res: Response) => {
  save(req.body);
});
```

##### Do

```ts
app.post("/users", (req: Request<{}, {}, CreateUser>, res: Response) => {
  save(req.body);
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
app.post("/users", (req: any, res: Response) => {
  save(req.body);
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
app.post("/users", (req: Request<{}, {}, CreateUser>, res: Response) => {
  save(req.body);
});
```

## `sec-ts/no-permissive-schema` — No request schema that lets anything through

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a client that sends extra keys starts getting an error instead of having them kept; `z.any()` and class-validator's `validate` have no mechanical fix)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-permissive-schema.md

### What it checks

A request schema does not use `z.any()` or `.passthrough()`, and class-validator's `validate` and `validateSync` are given `forbidUnknownValues`.

**Why:** A schema that accepts any value, or keeps unknown keys, lets a client send fields the code never meant to read, which then reach a model or a query (CWE-915, CWE-20).

### How to fix

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).passthrough();
```

##### Do

```ts
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).strict();
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).strict();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).passthrough();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).strict();
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() }).strict();
```

## `sec-ts/no-prisma-raw-unsafe` — No $queryRawUnsafe or $executeRawUnsafe with a value that is not a literal

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a `${…}` in the template becomes a bound parameter, which a statement that used it for a table or column name cannot do; only `$queryRawUnsafe` with one template is rewritten)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-prisma-raw-unsafe.md

### What it checks

Prisma's `$queryRawUnsafe` and `$executeRawUnsafe` are not given a SQL string that is built or not a literal; the tagged `$queryRaw` and `$executeRaw` are used.

**Why:** The `Unsafe` calls take a plain string, so a value spliced into it changes the statement (CWE-89); the tagged templates send each `${…}` as a parameter.

### How to fix

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const rows = await prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`);
```

##### Do

```ts
const rows = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`;
```

##### Fixed

```ts
const rows = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const rows = await prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const rows = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`;
```

##### Fixed

```tsx
const rows = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM "User" WHERE id = ${id}`;
```

## `sec-ts/no-query-builder-raw` — No raw SQL fragment from a value in Drizzle, Kysely or MikroORM

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the statement and its values have to be separated by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-query-builder-raw.md

### What it checks

`sql.raw(x)`, `sql.lit(x)` and `em.execute(x)` are not given a value that is not a literal; the `sql` template tag sends each `${…}` as a parameter.

**Why:** These calls put the string into the statement as it is, so a value in it changes the statement (CWE-89).

### How to fix

1. Use the `sql` tagged template: each `${value}` becomes a parameter. `sql.raw` is for a fixed fragment you wrote, as a literal.
2. A table or column name that must vary is picked from an allow-list in code, then written with `sql.identifier(name)` (Drizzle) or `sql.id(name)` (Kysely).

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
await db.execute(sql.raw(query));
```

##### Do

```ts
await db.execute(sql`select * from users where id = ${id}`);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
await db.execute(sql.raw(query));
```

##### Do

```tsx
await db.execute(sql`select * from users where id = ${id}`);
```

## `sec-ts/no-ts-ignore-on-sink` — No type error silenced on a line that holds a security sink

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the right type is depends on the value)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-ts-ignore-on-sink.md

### What it checks

A `@ts-ignore`, a `@ts-expect-error` or an `as any` is not placed on a line that calls a dangerous API (`eval`, `exec`, `innerHTML`, a raw query, a redirect …).

**Why:** The type error is often the compiler saying the value is not what the sink needs; silencing it on the sink line removes the one check that was running (CWE-20).

### How to fix

1. Fix the type instead: narrow the value, or convert it with a function that returns the type the sink wants.
2. If the sink really needs a value of another type, write a small typed helper for it and keep the cast inside the helper, with a comment that says why it is safe.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
// @ts-ignore
element.innerHTML = html;
```

##### Do

```ts
element.textContent = html;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
// @ts-ignore
element.innerHTML = html;
```

##### Do

```tsx
element.textContent = html;
```

## `sec-ts/no-typeorm-string-query` — No TypeORM query built from a template or concatenation

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the condition and its values have to be separated by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-typeorm-string-query.md

### What it checks

TypeORM's `.query(…)` and the query builder's `.where`, `.andWhere`, `.orWhere` and `.having` are not given a template literal with `${…}` or a concatenation; named parameters are used.

**Why:** A value spliced into the string changes the statement (CWE-89); `:name` placeholders with a parameters object are sent apart from it.

### How to fix

1. Write the condition with a named parameter (`"u.id = :id"`) and pass the values as the second argument: `.where("u.id = :id", { id })`.
2. For `repo.query`, use the driver's placeholders (`$1`, `?`) and an array of values.
3. A column or table name cannot be a parameter: take it from an allow-list in code.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const user = await repo.createQueryBuilder("u").where(`u.id = ${id}`).getOne();
```

##### Do

```ts
const user = await repo.createQueryBuilder("u").where("u.id = :id", { id }).getOne();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const user = await repo.createQueryBuilder("u").where(`u.id = ${id}`).getOne();
```

##### Do

```tsx
const user = await repo.createQueryBuilder("u").where("u.id = :id", { id }).getOne();
```

## `sec-ts/no-unchecked-cast-of-input` — No type assertion on input that nothing has checked

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the schema that describes the input is written by the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/no-unchecked-cast-of-input.md

### What it checks

`JSON.parse(x) as T`, `req.body as T` and `(await res.json()) as T` are not used where the function has no runtime validator (zod, valibot, class-validator, ajv).

**Your validator:** the function passes when it calls one of the `validators` anywhere in its body, or in a function around it: the built-in list (zod and valibot imports and a `*Schema.parse`, any `.safeParse`, `.parseAsync`, `.validate` or `.assert`, yup, joi, class-validator, class-transformer's `plainToInstance`, superstruct, typia) plus your own, each matched by name and by the module it is imported from, so a local `function validate(x) { return x }` does not count. `validators_mode = "replace"` makes yours the only ones that count. Add a project function with `validators = [{ name = "checkInput", module = "@acme/validation" }]`. A validator that a helper calls for you is not seen: name the helper.

**Why:** A type assertion is a promise to the compiler, not a check: the data can be anything the client sent, and the rest of the code trusts the type (CWE-20). This reads one function's syntax; without types it cannot see a validator that runs elsewhere.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validators` | `call[]` | 25 entries (below) | calls that check input, any one of which in the function counts: a callee path or { name, module }; `validators_mode: replace` makes yours the only ones that count |
| `validators_mode` | `string` | `"extend"` | `extend` adds your `validators` to the default list; `replace` uses only yours |

### How to fix

1. Parse the value with a schema (`zod`, `valibot`, `ajv`) and use the parsed result, whose type is inferred from the schema.
2. In NestJS, take a DTO class with `class-validator` decorators and a `ValidationPipe`, not a cast.
3. For `JSON.parse`, check the shape of the result before it is used as `T`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function create(req: Request) {
  const dto = req.body as CreateUserDto;
  return save(dto);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function create(req: Request) {
  const dto = createUserSchema.parse(req.body);
  return save(dto);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function create(req: Request) {
  const dto = req.body as CreateUserDto;
  return save(dto);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function create(req: Request) {
  const dto = createUserSchema.parse(req.body);
  return save(dto);
}
```

## `sec-ts/trpc-public-mutation` — A tRPC mutation is not public

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which procedure carries the auth middleware is named by the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/trpc-public-mutation.md

### What it checks

`publicProcedure` is not used for a `.mutation(…)`; `protectedProcedure` (a procedure with an auth middleware) is.

**Why:** A mutation changes data; a public one lets anyone who finds the route change it (CWE-862).

### How to fix

1. Use `protectedProcedure` (one that runs the session check as middleware) for every mutation, and `.use(isAdmin)` where a role is needed.
2. If a mutation really is public (a contact form), leave `publicProcedure` and suppress this finding with a reason that says why, and rate-limit it.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const create = publicProcedure.input(schema).mutation(({ input }) => save(input));
```

##### Do

```ts
export const create = protectedProcedure.input(schema).mutation(({ input }) => save(input));
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const create = publicProcedure.input(schema).mutation(({ input }) => save(input));
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const create = protectedProcedure.input(schema).mutation(({ input }) => save(input));
```

## `sec-ts/typeorm-synchronize` — TypeORM does not synchronize the schema on start

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-security-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (how the schema is changed instead (migrations) is a decision for the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:sec-ts/recommended` at `error` · `codelaw:sec-ts/strict` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/sec-ts/typeorm-synchronize.md

### What it checks

A DataSource or `TypeOrmModule` configuration does not set `synchronize: true`.

**Why:** `synchronize` rewrites the database to match the entities on every start: a renamed field drops a column and its data, and it runs against whatever database the app is pointed at (CWE-1188).

### How to fix

1. Set `synchronize: false` (the default) and write migrations: `typeorm migration:generate`, then `migration:run` at deploy.
2. If it is only for a local database, set it from an environment variable that is never true in production.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const db = new DataSource({ type: "postgres", url, synchronize: true });
```

##### Do

```ts
export const db = new DataSource({ type: "postgres", url, migrations: ["dist/migrations/*.js"] });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const db = new DataSource({ type: "postgres", url, synchronize: true });
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const db = new DataSource({ type: "postgres", url, migrations: ["dist/migrations/*.js"] });
```

## `spell/known-typo` — No known typos in comments, docs and prose

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX, Python, JSON, YAML, TOML, Markdown, CSS, SCSS, HTML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:spell/recommended` at `warn` · `codelaw:spell/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/known-typo.md

### What it checks

A word in a comment, a docstring, a prose string, Markdown text, HTML text or an HTML `alt`, `title`, `aria-label` or `placeholder`, or a string value of JSON, YAML or TOML is on the pack's list of known typos (`recieve`, `lenght`, `occured`). The fix writes the one correction the list gives, in the word's case.

**Why:** a typo in a message, a doc or a comment reads as carelessness and hides from search (`grep receive` misses `recieve`). The list holds only words that are no English word and come from exactly one common word, so the fix is safe to run unattended.

A string is read only when it holds whitespace and no interpolation; keys are names, not prose. URLs, email addresses, paths, dotted names, hashes, UUIDs, base64, code and identifiers (`snake_case`, `camelCase`, letters and digits mixed) are skipped, as is any word shorter than four letters.

### How to fix

1. Run `codelaw fix`: each typo becomes its correction.
2. For a word that is right where it stands (a product name, a quoted misspelling), excuse the line: `// codelaw-ignore spell/known-typo: <reason>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// Retry until we recieve a response.
throw new Error("Unexpected lenght of the header");
```

##### Do

```js
// Retry until we receive a response.
throw new Error("Unexpected length of the header");
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p title="Wrong lenght">Retry untill it works</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p title="Wrong length">Retry until it works</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
// The adress is checked first.
const message: string = "No adress given";
```

##### Do

```ts
// The address is checked first.
const message: string = "No address given";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const Empty = (): JSX.Element => <p>Nothing recieved yet</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const Empty = (): JSX.Element => <p>Nothing received yet</p>;
```

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def parse(data):
    """Return the adress of the first record."""
```

##### Do

```python
def parse(data):
    """Return the address of the first record."""
```

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json
{ "description": "Checks the lenght of a name" }
```

##### Do

```json
{ "description": "Checks the length of a name" }
```

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
# Runs untill the queue is empty.
summary: Clears the cache untill the next run
```

##### Do

```yaml
# Runs until the queue is empty.
summary: Clears the cache until the next run
```

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
# The adress of the server.
description = "Checks the lenght of a name"
```

##### Do

```toml
# The address of the server.
description = "Checks the length of a name"
```

#### Markdown

##### Don't

```md
The cache is cleared untill the next run.
```

##### Do

```md
The cache is cleared until the next run.
```

#### CSS

##### Don't

```css
/* Keeps the lenght of a line short. */
.prose { max-width: 70ch; }
```

##### Do

```css
/* Keeps the length of a line short. */
.prose { max-width: 70ch; }
```

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
// Keeps the lenght of a line short.
.prose { max-width: 70ch; }
```

##### Do

```scss
// Keeps the length of a line short.
.prose { max-width: 70ch; }
```

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<img src="map.png" alt="The adress on a map">
```

##### Do

```html
<img src="map.png" alt="The address on a map">
```

## `spell/known-typo-identifier` — No known typos in the names a file declares

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX, Python
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:spell/recommended` at `warn` · `codelaw:spell/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/known-typo-identifier.md

### What it checks

A name declared in the file — a variable, a function, a class, a parameter, a type, an interface, a class member — holds a word on the pack's list of known typos (`recieveAll`, `lenght`, `AdressBook`). The name is split at case changes, `_`, `-`, `.` and digits, and each part of four letters or more is looked up. It is reported once, where it is declared, never at each use.

**Why:** a misspelled name spreads: every caller copies it, and `grep receive` never finds `recieveAll`. Fixing it is cheapest where it is declared, before it has callers in other files.

The fix renames the declaration and every use in the file, and only when that is safe from this file alone: the name is not exported, not a module-level name of a script or a Python module, not a Python parameter (a caller may pass it by keyword), not a class attribute or member (read through `.`), not a shorthand property (`{ recieve }` is a key too), the new name is not already taken, and every place the name is written in the file is a use the semantic model resolved to it. Otherwise the finding has no edit, and the steps below apply. Imported names are another module's and are not reported.

### How to fix

1. Run `codelaw fix`: a file-local name is renamed at its declaration and every use.
2. For an exported name, a module-level name or a member, rename it with your editor's rename across the project, and keep the old name as a deprecated alias if other packages import it.
3. For a name that is right as it stands (a product name, a field another system defines), excuse the line: `// codelaw-ignore spell/known-typo-identifier: <reason>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
export function total(items) {
  let lenght = 0;
  for (const item of items) lenght += item.size;
  return lenght;
}
```

##### Do

```js
export function total(items) {
  let length = 0;
  for (const item of items) length += item.size;
  return length;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

const AdressLine = ({ text }) => <span>{text}</span>;

export const Card = () => <AdressLine text={useState("")[0]}></AdressLine>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";

const AddressLine = ({ text }) => <span>{text}</span>;

export const Card = () => <AddressLine text={useState("")[0]}></AddressLine>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
type AdressBook = Record<string, string>;

export function lookUp(book: unknown, key: string): string | undefined {
  return (book as AdressBook)[key];
}
```

##### Do

```ts
type AddressBook = Record<string, string>;

export function lookUp(book: unknown, key: string): string | undefined {
  return (book as AddressBook)[key];
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const List = ({ rows }: { rows: string[] }) => {
  const recievedRows = rows.filter(Boolean);
  return <ul>{recievedRows.map((r) => <li key={r}>{r}</li>)}</ul>;
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const List = ({ rows }: { rows: string[] }) => {
  const receivedRows = rows.filter(Boolean);
  return <ul>{receivedRows.map((r) => <li key={r}>{r}</li>)}</ul>;
};
```

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def total(items):
    lenght = 0
    for item in items:
        lenght += item.size
    return lenght
```

##### Do

```python
def total(items):
    length = 0
    for item in items:
        length += item.size
    return length
```

## `spell/known-typo-key` — No known typos in keys, classes and ids

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** JSON, YAML, TOML, CSS, SCSS, HTML
- **Fix:** `manual` (other files read the name — the code that reads a key, the markup that uses a class, the link to an id — so renaming it here alone breaks them)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:spell/recommended` at `warn` · `codelaw:spell/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/known-typo-key.md

### What it checks

A name other files read holds a word on the pack's list of known typos: a JSON, YAML or TOML key, a CSS or SCSS class, id, custom property, `$variable`, mixin or function, or an HTML `id`. The name is split at case changes, `_`, `-`, `.` and digits, and each part of four letters or more is looked up. Each distinct name is reported once per file, where it is first declared.

**Why:** a misspelled key or class is copied into every file that reads it, and `grep receive` never finds it. It is cheapest to fix before it has readers, and it is never safe to fix in one file alone.

### How to fix

1. Find every reader of the name: search the project for it (`git grep -n recieve_all`), including code that builds it from parts.
2. Rename it here and in every reader in one change; for a key or class published to other projects, accept both names for a release before removing the old one.
3. For a name that is right as it stands (a field another system defines), excuse the line: `# codelaw-ignore spell/known-typo-key: <reason>`.

### Examples

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json
{ "recieveTimeout": 30 }
```

##### Do

```json
{ "receiveTimeout": 30 }
```

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
recieve_timeout: 30
```

##### Do

```yaml
receive_timeout: 30
```

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
[server]
recieve_timeout = 30
```

##### Do

```toml
[server]
receive_timeout = 30
```

#### CSS

##### Don't

```css
.adress-card { padding: 1rem; }
```

##### Do

```css
.address-card { padding: 1rem; }
```

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
$line-lenght: 70ch;
```

##### Do

```scss
$line-length: 70ch;
```

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<section id="adress-form"></section>
```

##### Do

```html
<section id="address-form"></section>
```

## `spell/locale-variant` — Prose is spelled in the project's locale

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX, Python, JSON, YAML, TOML, Markdown, CSS, SCSS, HTML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** no preset
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/locale-variant.md

### What it checks

With `[spell] locale` set, a word of prose (as `spell/known-typo` reads it) is the other locale's spelling: `colour`, `behaviour` or `analyse` under `en-US`; `color` or `center` under `en-GB`. The pairs are VarCon's one-to-one US and British spellings. A pair is left out when either spelling is right in the other locale under some meaning (`check` and `cheque`, `program` and `programme`, `license` and `licence`), and under `en-GB` the Oxford `-ize` spellings are never reported. The rule is in neither preset: turn it on with `"spell/locale-variant" = "warn"` and set the locale.

**Why:** one locale reads as one voice, and a search for `color` finds every place the word is used.

The fix writes the locale's spelling, in the word's case.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `locale` | `string` | `""` | `en-US` or `en-GB`: the locale whose spellings are right; read from `[spell] locale`, and the rule reports nothing while it is unset |

### How to fix

1. Run `codelaw fix`: each word becomes the locale's spelling.
2. For a quotation or a proper name (`Colour Science Ltd`), excuse the line: `// codelaw-ignore spell/locale-variant: <reason>`, or add the word to `[spell] words`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```js
// Retry colour until it works.
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```js
// Retry color until it works.
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p>Retry colour until it works</p>;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p>Retry color until it works</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```ts
// Retry colour until it works.
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```ts
// Retry color until it works.
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```tsx
const Hint = (): JSX.Element => <p>Retry colour until it works</p>;
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```tsx
const Hint = (): JSX.Element => <p>Retry color until it works</p>;
```

#### Python

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```python

    """Retry colour until it works."""
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```python

    """Retry color until it works."""
```

#### JSON

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```json
{ "description": "Retry colour until it works" }
```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```json
{ "description": "Retry color until it works" }
```

#### YAML

##### Don't

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`

```yaml

```

##### Do

*With these options:* `{ locale = "en-US" }`






## `spell/suspicious-word` — No accepted word hides a typo

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `manual` (only the team knows whether an accepted word is a real name or a misspelling it waved through)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:spell/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/suspicious-word.md

### What it checks

An entry of `[spell] words` in the root `codelaw.toml` is itself on the known-typo list (`recieve`), or is no dictionary word yet one edit from a common one (`lenth`, one letter from `length`). Every `spell/*` rule accepts the words in that list, so a misspelling there is accepted everywhere it appears.

**Why:** a word list grows by people pasting in whatever the checker flagged; one typo in it silences the check for the whole project.

### How to fix

1. Search the project for the word (`git grep -n -i recieve`).
2. If it is a misspelling, fix it where it appears and take it out of `[spell] words`.
3. If it is right (a name that looks like a typo), keep it and excuse the line: `# codelaw-ignore spell/suspicious-word: <reason>`.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path="codelaw.toml"
[spell]
words = ["recieve", "kubectl"]
```

##### Do

```toml path="codelaw.toml"
[spell]
words = ["kubectl"]
```

## `spell/unknown-word` — Every word of prose is in a word list

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-spell` · `codelaw-rules-spell` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX, Python, JSON, YAML, TOML, Markdown, CSS, SCSS, HTML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a word no list holds is often a real name, a product or a term of the trade; the nearest dictionary word is a guess the author confirms)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:spell/strict` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/spell/unknown-word.md

### What it checks

A word in a comment, a docstring, a prose string, Markdown text, HTML text or an HTML `alt`, `title`, `aria-label` or `placeholder`, or a string value of JSON, YAML or TOML is in no word list: not in the pack's dictionary (SCOWL's US and British English up to size 60, with every form written out, plus the software terms), not on the known-typo list (`spell/known-typo` reports those) and not in `[spell] words`. A word in capitals is an acronym and is not checked; so are words shorter than four letters and every token `spell/known-typo` skips (URLs, paths, identifiers, hashes).

**Why:** the known-typo list catches the misspellings codelaw can predict; the dictionary catches the rest (`seperately`, `responce`). It is in `spell/strict`, not `spell/recommended`, because code is full of real words no dictionary holds.

The fix replaces the word with the nearest dictionary word: fewest edits (Damerau-Levenshtein, at most two, the first letter kept), then the commoner word, then alphabetical order. The message names up to three.

### How to fix

1. If the word is misspelled, run `codelaw fix --unsafe` to take the first suggestion, or write the word the message names that you meant.
2. If the word is right (a name, a product, a term of your trade), add it to the root `codelaw.toml`: `[spell]` `words = ["kubectl"]`. `spell/suspicious-word` checks the list.
3. For a one-off, excuse the line: `// codelaw-ignore spell/unknown-word: <reason>`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
// Retry seperately until it works.
```

##### Do

```js
// Retry separately until it works.
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p>Retry seperately until it works</p>;
```

##### Do

```jsx
const Hint = () => <p>Retry separately until it works</p>;
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
// Retry seperately until it works.
```

##### Do

```ts
// Retry separately until it works.
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const Hint = (): JSX.Element => <p>Retry seperately until it works</p>;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const Hint = (): JSX.Element => <p>Retry separately until it works</p>;
```

#### Python

##### Don't

```python
def run():
    """Retry seperately until it works."""
```

##### Do

```python
def run():
    """Retry separately until it works."""
```

#### JSON

##### Don't

```json
{ "description": "Retry seperately until it works" }
```

##### Do

```json
{ "description": "Retry separately until it works" }
```

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
# Retry seperately until it works.
summary: Retry seperately until it works
```

##### Do

```yaml
# Retry separately until it works.
summary: Retry separately until it works
```

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
# Retry seperately until it works.
```

##### Do

```toml
# Retry separately until it works.
```

#### Markdown

##### Don't

```md

```

##### Do

```md

```

#### CSS

##### Don't

```css
/* Retry seperately until it works. */
.box { color: red; }
```

##### Do

```css

```

#### SCSS

##### Don't

```scss
// Retry seperately until it works.

```

##### Do

```scss

```

#### HTML

##### Don't

```html
<p title="Retry seperately">Retry until it works</p>
```

##### Do

```html

```

## `stencil/ban-default-true` — A boolean @Prop defaults to false

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (inverting the prop renames it for every user)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/ban-default-true.md

### What it checks

A `@Prop()` of a Stencil component doesn't default to `true`.

**Why:** An HTML boolean attribute can only switch something on; a prop that starts `true` can't be
turned off from markup.

### How to fix

1. Invert the prop's meaning so it defaults to `false` (e.g. `closable` → `hideClose`).
2. Update the component's markup users.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Shows the close button. */
  @Prop() readonly closable = true;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Hides the close button. */
  @Prop() readonly hideClose = false;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Shows the close button. */
  @Prop() readonly closable = true;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Hides the close button. */
  @Prop() readonly hideClose = false;
}
```

## `stencil/ban-exported-const-enums` — No exported const enums

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/ban-exported-const-enums.md

### What it checks

An exported enum is a plain `enum`, not a `const enum`.

**Why:** A `const enum` is erased at compile time, so code that imports it from the built bundle
finds nothing.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export const enum Size {
  Small,
  Large,
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export enum Size {
  Small,
  Large,
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export const enum Size {
  Small,
  Large,
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export enum Size {
  Small,
  Large,
}
```

## `stencil/ban-prefix` — A component tag doesn't use a reserved prefix

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming a tag changes every page that uses it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/ban-prefix.md

### What it checks

A component's `tag` doesn't start with a prefix Stencil reserves (`stencil-`, `stnl-`, `st-` by
default; the `prefixes` option changes the list).

**Why:** Reserved prefixes may clash with Stencil's own elements.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefixes` | `string[]` | `["stencil", "stnl", "st"]` | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Choose a prefix of your own and rename the tag.
2. Update every usage of the element.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'stencil-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'acme-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'stencil-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'acme-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

## `stencil/ban-side-effects` — No calls at a module's top level

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (where the call should run instead — a function, a lifecycle method — needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/ban-side-effects.md

### What it checks

A module makes no calls at its top level: every call sits inside a function, a method or a class, or
in an `export` declaration. Test files (a name with `spec.`, `e2e.` or `test.` in it) are not
checked, and `describe`, `test`, `bind` and `createStore` may be called anywhere (the `allow` option
changes that list).

**Why:** Stencil's compiler loads modules to analyse them and bundles them lazily, so a call that runs
on import runs at a time no one chose, and may not run at all when a bundle is split.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `string[]` | `["describe", "test", "bind", "createStore"]` | functions that may be called at the top level; setting it replaces the default list |

### How to fix

1. Move the call into the function, method or lifecycle hook (`componentWillLoad`, `connectedCallback`)
   that needs its effect.
2. If the call builds a value, export a function that builds it, or keep it in an `export const`.
3. If the call must run at load time, add the function's name to the `allow` option.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { setupConfig } from './config';

setupConfig({ mode: 'md' });
```

##### Do

```ts
import { setupConfig } from './config';

export function init() {
  setupConfig({ mode: 'md' });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { setupConfig } from './config';

setupConfig({ mode: 'md' });
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { setupConfig } from './config';

export function init() {
  setupConfig({ mode: 'md' });
}
```

### Differences from the source

- Every function is a boundary: the source treats arrow functions and function declarations as
  boundaries but reports calls inside a function expression or an object method, which run only
  when called.
- The option is named `allow`, not the source's unnamed list.
- A tagged template and a dynamic `import()` are not calls here, as in the source.

## `stencil/decorators-context` — Stencil decorators only inside @Component classes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the class should be a component needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/decorators-context.md

### What it checks

`@Prop`, `@State`, `@Element`, `@Method`, `@Watch`, `@Listen`, `@Event` and `@AttachInternals`
appear only in a class decorated with `@Component`.

**Why:** Outside a component Stencil ignores them, so the code silently does nothing.

### How to fix

1. Make the class a `@Component`, or remove the Stencil decorators.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
export class Store {
  @State() count = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export class Store {
  count = 0;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
export class Store {
  @State() count = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export class Store {
  count = 0;
}
```

## `stencil/enforce-slot-jsdoc` — Every slot a component renders has a @slot tag, and every @slot tag a slot

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the slot's description, or whether it should exist, needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/enforce-slot-jsdoc.md

### What it checks

A `@Component` class's JSDoc has a `@slot` tag for each `<slot>` it renders — `@slot name - what it
holds` for a named slot, `@slot - what it holds` for the default one — and no `@slot` tag for a slot
it doesn't render.

**Why:** Stencil builds the component's documentation and editor hints from these tags, so a missing
tag hides a slot from its users, and a stale one promises a slot that isn't there.

### How to fix

1. For a slot reported as rendered without a tag, add `@slot <name> - <what it holds>` (or
   `@slot - <what it holds>` for the default slot) to the JSDoc above `@Component`.
2. For a tag reported as never rendered, remove the tag, or render the `<slot>` it describes.

### Examples

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/**
 * A card.
 */
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return <slot name="header" />;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
/**
 * A card.
 * @slot header - The card's title row.
 */
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return <slot name="header" />;
  }
}
```

### Differences from the source

- A `<slot>` whose `name` is an expression (`name={this.slot}`) is left out; the source records it as
  a slot named `undefined`.
- A `@slot` tag's text stops at the end of its line; the source lets a bare `@slot` take its
  description from the next line.
- TSX only: a `.ts` file has no `<slot>` elements to check.

## `stencil/host-data-deprecated` — No hostData()

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the attributes move into `render()` by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/host-data-deprecated.md

### What it checks

A component doesn't define `hostData()`.

**Why:** `hostData()` is deprecated; the host element's attributes are set by rendering `<Host>`.

### How to fix

1. Render a `<Host>` element in `render()` with the attributes `hostData()` returned.
2. Remove `hostData()`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  hostData() {
    return { class: 'card' };
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  hostData() {
    return { class: 'card' };
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

## `stencil/methods-must-be-public` — @Method() members are public

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the method is public API needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/methods-must-be-public.md

### What it checks

A `@Method()` isn't marked `private` or `protected`.

**Why:** A `@Method()` is part of the element's public API; hiding it in TypeScript contradicts
that.

### How to fix

1. Remove `private`/`protected`, or remove `@Method()` if it isn't public API.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Opens the card. */
  @Method() private async open() {}
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Opens the card. */
  @Method() async open() {}
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Opens the card. */
  @Method() private async open() {}
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** Opens the card. */
  @Method() async open() {}
}
```

## `stencil/no-unused-watch` — @Watch watches a @Prop or @State

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which member was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/no-unused-watch.md

### What it checks

`@Watch('name')` names a `@Prop` or `@State` of the same component.

**Why:** Watching anything else never fires, so the handler is dead code.

### How to fix

1. Correct the name to the @Prop or @State it should watch, or remove the watcher.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @State() open = false;
  @Watch('opened') onOpen() {}
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @State() open = false;
  @Watch('open') onOpen() {}
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @State() open = false;
  @Watch('opened') onOpen() {}
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @State() open = false;
  @Watch('open') onOpen() {}
}
```

## `stencil/own-methods-must-be-private` — A component's own methods are private

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/own-methods-must-be-private.md

### What it checks

A method of a component that isn't a `@Method()`, a lifecycle method or `render()` is `private`.

**Why:** Only `@Method()` members reach users of the element; a public own method suggests an API
that isn't there.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  helper() {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  private helper() {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  helper() {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  private helper() {
    return 1;
  }
}
```

A class field of a component without a Stencil decorator is `private`.

isn't there.

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
```

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {

  private cache = new Map();
```

## `stencil/prefer-vdom-listener` — DOM events are handled in render(), not with @Listen

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the handler moves into the rendered markup by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/prefer-vdom-listener.md

### What it checks

A component handles DOM events on itself (`click`, `keydown`, …) with an `on…` handler in
`render()`, not `@Listen`; `@Listen` with a `target` is fine.

**Why:** Handlers in `render()` are scoped to the element they're on and cheaper than a host-wide
listener.

### How to fix

1. Attach the handler in `render()` (e.g. `onClick={…}` on `<Host>`).
2. Remove the `@Listen`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Listen('click') onClick() {}
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Listen('resize', { target: 'window' }) onResize() {}
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Listen('click') onClick() {}
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Listen('resize', { target: 'window' }) onResize() {}
}
```

## `stencil/prop-readonly` — @Prop() members are readonly unless mutable

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/prop-readonly.md

### What it checks

A `@Prop()` is `readonly`, unless its options say `mutable: true`.

**Why:** Props are set from outside; a component that writes one by accident fights its parent.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading. */
  @Prop() heading: string;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading. */
  @Prop() heading: string;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX

##### Do

## `stencil/required-jsdoc` — Public members have JSDoc

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the documentation text needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/required-jsdoc.md

### What it checks

Every `@Prop()`, `@Method()` and `@Event()` has a `/** … */` comment.

**Why:** Stencil turns these comments into the component's documentation and editor hints.

### How to fix

1. Write a `/** … */` comment above the member saying what it is for.

#### TypeScript

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading shown at the top. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The heading shown at the top. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

## `stencil/reserved-member-names` — Public members don't reuse HTML element names

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming a public member changes every user)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/reserved-member-names.md

### What it checks

A `@Prop()` or `@Method()` isn't named after an HTML global attribute or an `HTMLElement` member
(`title`, `hidden`, `id`, `click`, …).

**Why:** The element already has a member of that name, so the component's version clashes with it.

### How to fix

1. Rename the member.
2. Update its users.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The card's title. */
  @Prop() readonly title: string;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The card's heading. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The card's title. */
  @Prop() readonly title: string;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The card's heading. */
  @Prop() readonly heading: string;
}
```

## `stencil/strict-mutable` — mutable: true only on props the component changes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the component should change the prop needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/strict-mutable.md

### What it checks

A `@Prop({ mutable: true })` is assigned somewhere in the component.

**Why:** `mutable: true` says the component changes the prop; if it never does, the flag only hides
that the prop should be `readonly`.

### How to fix

1. Remove `mutable: true` and make the prop `readonly`, or assign it where the component means to.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The count. */
  @Prop({ mutable: true }) count = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The count. */
  @Prop({ mutable: true }) count = 0;
  private inc() {
    this.count++;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The count. */
  @Prop({ mutable: true }) count = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'my-card' })
export class Card {
  /** The count. */
  @Prop({ mutable: true }) count = 0;
  private inc() {
    this.count++;
  }
}
```

## `stencil/tag-prefix` — Component tags start with the project's prefix

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-stencil` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (renaming a tag changes every page that uses it)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:stencil/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/stencil/tag-prefix.md

### What it checks

Every component's `tag` starts with the project's prefix (the `prefix` option); with no prefix set,
a tag still needs one.

**Why:** One prefix keeps a project's elements apart from other libraries'.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | `string` | `""` | the prefix every tag must start with |

### How to fix

1. Rename the tag to start with the project's prefix.
2. Update every usage of the element.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```ts
@Component({ tag: 'acme-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
@Component({ tag: 'acme-card' })
export class Card {
  render() {
    return null;
  }
}
```

## `tanstack-query/array-query-key` — A query key is an array

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (wrapping the key in an array changes its hash, so a key matched elsewhere in its old form stops matching)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/array-query-key.md

### What it checks

The `queryKey` of a query's options or of query filters is an array, not a string, a number or an
object written in its place.

**Why:** TanStack Query hashes and matches keys as arrays, and its types require one. *Query Keys: "Query keys
have to be an Array at the top level".*

### How to fix

1. Wrap the key in an array: `queryKey: ['todos']`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: 'todos', queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: 'todos', queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: 'todos', queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: 'todos', queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's Query Keys guide, not a lint rule. Only a key written in place as a
string, template string, number, boolean or object literal is reported; a key passed by name is not
followed. The object must be one TanStack Query reads: next to a `queryFn`, an argument of a function
imported from a `@tanstack/*-query` package or of a QueryClient method, or an entry of `queries`.

## `tanstack-query/exhaustive-deps` — A query key names every value its query function reads

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a new key entry changes which cache entry the query reads and writes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/exhaustive-deps.md

### What it checks

An object with a `queryKey` and a `queryFn` lists in its key every prop, state value and local of the
component that the query function reads.

**Why:** TanStack Query caches by key. A value the function reads but the key leaves out makes two different
queries share one cache entry, so a change to it shows stale data and refetches nothing.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allowlist` | `object` | `{}` | `{ variables: [<name>…], types: [<type name>…] }`: values to leave out of the key, by name or by their declared type |

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo'], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo', id], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo'], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo', id], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo'], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo', id], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo'], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodo(id) {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['todo', id], queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id) });
}
```

### Differences from the source

A value counts when it is declared in the outermost function around the options object, outside the
query function; upstream counts only that function's own top-level names. A member path stops at the
first subscript (`a[i].b` needs `a`). A key held in a `const` is followed to its array, and the
suggested edit lands there. `allowlist.types` matches the type names written in the value's own
annotation; codelaw has no type checker to resolve an inferred type.

## `tanstack-query/infinite-query-property-order` — An infinite query's `queryFn` comes before its page-param callbacks

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/infinite-query-property-order.md

### What it checks

In the options of `useInfiniteQuery`, `useSuspenseInfiniteQuery` and `infiniteQueryOptions`,
`queryFn` is written before `getPreviousPageParam` and `getNextPageParam`.

**Why:** TypeScript infers the page type from the options in the order they are written: written first, the
page-param callbacks get `unknown` pages instead of `queryFn`'s result.

### How to fix

1. Move `queryFn` above `getPreviousPageParam` and `getNextPageParam`. The fix is offered only when
   every moved option is a function or a name, so the order nothing else runs in is kept.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

##### Do

```js
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

##### Do

```ts
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects'],
  queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchProjects(pageParam),
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.next,
  initialPageParam: 0,
});
```

### Differences from the source

Upstream always offers the reordering. codelaw offers it only when every moved option's value is a
function, a method or a name, since moving an expression changes when it runs; otherwise the finding
has no edit.

## `tanstack-query/mutation-property-order` — A mutation's `onMutate` comes before `onError` and `onSettled`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/mutation-property-order.md

### What it checks

In the options of `useMutation`, `onMutate` is written before `onError` and `onSettled`.

**Why:** TypeScript infers the context `onMutate` returns from the order the options are written: written
after them, `onError` and `onSettled` get an `unknown` context.

### How to fix

1. Move `onMutate` above `onError` and `onSettled`. The fix is offered only when every moved option is
   a function or a name.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
});
```

##### Do

```js
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
});
```

##### Do

```ts
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
useMutation({
  mutationFn: addTodo,
  onMutate: (todo) => snapshot(todo),
  onError: (error, todo, context) => rollback(context),
});
```

### Differences from the source
