As `tanstack-query/infinite-query-property-order`: the reordering is offered only when every moved
option's value is a function, a method or a name.

## `tanstack-query/no-mutating-set-query-data` — A `setQueryData` updater does not change the cached data in place

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the update has to be rewritten to build a new value)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-mutating-set-query-data.md

### What it checks

The updater function passed to `setQueryData` or `setQueriesData` does not assign to, `delete` from,
increment, `Object.assign` onto or call an in-place array method (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, …) on its
argument, the data in the cache.

**Why:** The cache and every component reading it still hold the same object, so nothing re-renders and the
data a later update starts from is already changed. *Updates from Mutation Responses: "Updates via
`setQueryData` must be performed in an immutable way. **DO NOT** attempt to write directly to the
cache by mutating data (that you retrieved from the cache) in place."*

### How to fix

1. Return a new value built from the old one: `{ ...old, title }`, `[...old, item]`,
   `old.filter(…)`, `old.map(…)`.
2. For deep updates, build the copy with Immer's `produce(old, (draft) => { … })`, which is
   where an in-place change is correct.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) => {
  if (oldData) {
    oldData.title = 'my new post title';
  }
  return oldData;
});
```

##### Do

```js
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) =>
  oldData ? { ...oldData, title: 'my new post title' } : oldData,
);
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) => {
  if (oldData) {
    oldData.title = 'my new post title';
  }
  return oldData;
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) =>
  oldData ? { ...oldData, title: 'my new post title' } : oldData,
);
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) => {
  if (oldData) {
    oldData.title = 'my new post title';
  }
  return oldData;
});
```

##### Do

```ts
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) =>
  oldData ? { ...oldData, title: 'my new post title' } : oldData,
);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) => {
  if (oldData) {
    oldData.title = 'my new post title';
  }
  return oldData;
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
queryClient.setQueryData(['posts', { id }], (oldData) =>
  oldData ? { ...oldData, title: 'my new post title' } : oldData,
);
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's Updates from Mutation Responses guide, not a lint rule. codelaw reads
an updater written in place and the changes made through its parameter's own name: a value taken out of
it first (`const page = old.pages[0]`), or an item a callback receives (`old.map((p) => { p.seen = true })`),
is not followed. An updater that reassigns its parameter (`old = { ...old }`) is not checked. The method
is recognised by its name, on any object.

## `tanstack-query/no-removed-v4-options` — A query takes no option TanStack Query v5 removed

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (each removed option is replaced by different code: an effect, `placeholderData`, `structuralSharing` or a hook argument)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-removed-v4-options.md

### What it checks

A query's options — in a query hook, `queryOptions`, a QueryClient query method or
`defaultOptions.queries` — do not include `onSuccess`, `onError`, `onSettled`, `keepPreviousData`,
`isDataEqual` or `context`. Mutations keep their callbacks.

**Why:** v5 removed these options and ignores them, so the code they hold never runs. *Migrating to TanStack
Query v5: "`onSuccess`, `onError` and `onSettled` have been removed from Queries. They haven't been
touched for Mutations"; "Removed `keepPreviousData` in favor of `placeholderData` identity function";
"The `isDataEqual` option has been removed"; "Removed custom `context` prop in favor of custom
`queryClient` instance".*

### How to fix

1. `onSuccess` / `onError` / `onSettled`: react to `data` or `error` where the query is rendered, move the
   work into the `queryFn`, or use the `QueryCache`'s global callbacks.
2. `keepPreviousData: true`: write `placeholderData: keepPreviousData`, importing `keepPreviousData`
   from TanStack Query, and read `isPlaceholderData` instead of `isPreviousData`.
3. `isDataEqual`: pass `structuralSharing: (old, next) => (equal(old, next) ? old : replaceEqualDeep(old, next))`.
4. `context`: pass the `QueryClient` as the hook's second argument.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    keepPreviousData: true,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery, keepPreviousData } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    keepPreviousData: true,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery, keepPreviousData } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    keepPreviousData: true,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery, keepPreviousData } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    keepPreviousData: true,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery, keepPreviousData } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Projects({ page }) {
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['projects', page],
    queryFn: () => fetchProjects(page),
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
  });
  return data;
}
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's migration guide, not a lint rule. Only option objects written in place
are read, and a hook is recognised only when it is imported from a `@tanstack/*-query` package. The
other v4 removals the guide lists — `refetchPage`, the custom logger, the `remove` method on a result,
`dehydrateMutations` — are not options of the objects this rule reads, and are not checked. The guide
also says the `suspense: boolean` flag was removed, but v5's `@tanstack/query-core` still declares
`suspense` on a query observer's options and `useBaseQuery` still reads it (the suspense hooks set it), so
the option is not ignored and is not reported.

## `tanstack-query/no-renamed-v4-options` — An option uses its TanStack Query v5 name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-renamed-v4-options.md

### What it checks

The options of a query or a mutation — in a hook, a `queryOptions` / `mutationOptions` helper, a
QueryClient method or `new QueryClient({ defaultOptions })` — use v5's names: `gcTime`, not `cacheTime`,
and `throwOnError`, not `useErrorBoundary`.

**Why:** v5 reads only the new names, so an option under its v4 name does nothing. *Migrating to TanStack
Query v5: "Rename `cacheTime` to `gcTime`" and "The `useErrorBoundary` option has been renamed to
`throwOnError`".*

### How to fix

1. Rename the key. The fix is not offered when the object already has the new name too.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  cacheTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  useErrorBoundary: true,
});
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  gcTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  throwOnError: true,
});
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  cacheTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  useErrorBoundary: true,
});
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  gcTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  throwOnError: true,
});
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  cacheTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  useErrorBoundary: true,
});
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  gcTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  throwOnError: true,
});
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  cacheTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  useErrorBoundary: true,
});
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: fetchTodos,
  gcTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,
  throwOnError: true,
});
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's migration guide, not a lint rule. codelaw reads option objects written
in place: an options object built elsewhere and passed by name is not checked. A hook or helper is
recognised only when it is imported from a `@tanstack/*-query` package; a QueryClient method
(`prefetchQuery`, `fetchQuery`, `ensureQueryData`, the infinite variants, `setQueryDefaults`,
`setMutationDefaults`) by its name alone.

## `tanstack-query/no-rest-destructuring` — No rest destructuring of a query result

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which fields the component needs is a choice only its author can make)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-rest-destructuring.md

### What it checks

The result of `useQuery`, `useInfiniteQuery`, `useSuspenseQuery` and their `useQueries` forms is not
rest-destructured (`const { data, ...rest } = useQuery(…)`) or spread (`{ ...query }`).

**Why:** A query result tracks which fields are read and re-renders only when one of them changes. A rest
element or a spread reads every field, so the component re-renders on every change to the query.

### How to fix

1. Destructure the fields the component uses by name: `const { data, isPending } = useQuery(…)`.
2. Or keep the result whole (`const query = useQuery(…)`) and read `query.data` where it is used.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, ...rest } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, rest];
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, isPending];
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, ...rest } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, rest];
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, isPending];
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, ...rest } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, rest];
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, isPending];
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, ...rest } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, rest];
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useTodos() {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos });
  return [data, isPending];
}
```

### Differences from the source

Only direct calls of the hooks, imported from a `@tanstack/*-query` package, are followed. Upstream
also finds a query result by its type when typed linting is on; codelaw has no type checker.

## `tanstack-query/no-unstable-deps` — A query hook's result is not a React hook dependency

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the fields to list depend on what the effect, callback or memo reads)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-unstable-deps.md

### What it checks

The whole result of `useQuery`, `useMutation` and the other query hooks — or of a custom hook in the
same file that returns one — is not listed in the dependency array of `useEffect`, `useCallback` or
`useMemo`.

**Why:** The result object is new on every render, so a dependency on it makes the effect run, and the
callback or memo change, on every render.

### How to fix

1. Destructure the fields the hook reads: `const { mutate } = useMutation(…)`.
2. List those fields in the dependency array instead of the whole result.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const mutation = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutation.mutate(), [mutation]);
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const { mutate } = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutate(), [mutate]);
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const mutation = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutation.mutate(), [mutation]);
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const { mutate } = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutate(), [mutate]);
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const mutation = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutation.mutate(), [mutation]);
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const { mutate } = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutate(), [mutate]);
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const mutation = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutation.mutate(), [mutation]);
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useCallback } from 'react';

function useSave() {
  const { mutate } = useMutation({ mutationFn: save });
  return useCallback(() => mutate(), [mutate]);
}
```

### Differences from the source

A custom hook is followed one level, as upstream does: a hook in the same file whose body is, or
returns, one direct query hook call.

## `tanstack-query/no-unsupported-suspense-options` — A suspense query takes no `enabled`, `placeholderData` or `throwOnError`

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing `enabled` makes the query always run, and removing `placeholderData` shows the fallback during an update)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-unsupported-suspense-options.md

### What it checks

`useSuspenseQuery`, `useSuspenseInfiniteQuery` and the entries of `useSuspenseQueries` are not given
`enabled`, `placeholderData` or `throwOnError`.

**Why:** The suspense hooks don't read them: the query always runs, always suspends, and throws when it has no
data. *Suspense: "you therefore can't conditionally enable / disable the Query"; "`placeholderData`
also doesn't exist for this Query"; "you can't change `throwOnError`".*

### How to fix

1. `enabled`: render the component only when the query should run, or use `useQuery`.
2. `placeholderData`: wrap the update that changes the query key in `startTransition`.
3. `throwOnError`: throw `error` yourself when `!isFetching`, to send every error to the boundary.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
    enabled: !!id,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
    enabled: !!id,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
    enabled: !!id,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
  });
  return data;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
    enabled: !!id,
  });
  return data;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function Todo({ id }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({
    queryKey: ['todo', id],
    queryFn: () => fetchTodo(id),
  });
  return data;
}
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's Suspense guide, not a lint rule; TypeScript reports these options too,
because v5's types leave them out of the suspense hooks' options. codelaw reports them in JavaScript as
well. Only option objects written in place are read, and the hook must be imported from a
`@tanstack/*-query` package.

## `tanstack-query/no-void-query-fn` — A query function returns its data

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (what the query should return is the data the function fetches, which the author knows)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/no-void-query-fn.md

### What it checks

A `queryFn` returns a value. A function whose body has no `return <value>` and no `throw`, or that
returns `undefined` or `void`, hands TanStack Query nothing to cache.

**Why:** TanStack Query stores what the query function returns, and treats `undefined` as an error: the query
fails, or every consumer reads `undefined`.

### How to fix

1. Return the fetched data: `return res.json()`, or `return response.data`.
2. If the function only triggers work, it is a mutation: move it to `useMutation`'s `mutationFn`.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    await fetch('/todos');
  },
};
```

##### Do

```js
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    const res = await fetch('/todos');
    return res.json();
  },
};
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    await fetch('/todos');
  },
};
```

##### Do

```jsx
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    const res = await fetch('/todos');
    return res.json();
  },
};
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    await fetch('/todos');
  },
};
```

##### Do

```ts
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    const res = await fetch('/todos');
    return res.json();
  },
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    await fetch('/todos');
  },
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
const todosQuery = {
  queryKey: ['todos'],
  queryFn: async () => {
    const res = await fetch('/todos');
    return res.json();
  },
};
```

### Differences from the source

Upstream asks the TypeScript type checker for the function's return type. codelaw reads the function
itself: it reports only a `queryFn` written in place whose body cannot return a value. A function
passed by name, or one that returns a value typed as possibly `undefined`, is not checked.

## `tanstack-query/object-syntax` — A TanStack Query call takes one options object

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the positional arguments are moved into a new object, which changes the call's shape)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/object-syntax.md

### What it checks

`useQuery`, `useInfiniteQuery`, `useMutation`, `useIsFetching`, `useIsMutating` and the QueryClient
methods that take a query key or filters (`invalidateQueries`, `refetchQueries`, `fetchQuery`,
`prefetchQuery`, …) are called with one options object, not with v4's positional `(key, fn, options)`.

**Why:** v5 removed the positional overloads: it reads the first argument as the options object, so a key passed
there is not a query. *Migrating to TanStack Query v5: "Supports a single signature, one object … now we
only support the object format."*

### How to fix

1. Move the arguments into one object: `useQuery(key, fn, options)` becomes
   `useQuery({ queryKey: key, queryFn: fn, ...options })`. The fix is offered when the arguments' roles
   can be read off the call: an options object written in place, or a function written in place.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos, { staleTime: 5000 });
```

##### Do

```js
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos, staleTime: 5000 });
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos, { staleTime: 5000 });
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos, staleTime: 5000 });
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos, { staleTime: 5000 });
```

##### Do

```ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos, staleTime: 5000 });
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos, { staleTime: 5000 });
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos, staleTime: 5000 });
```

### Differences from the source

The source is TanStack Query v5's migration guide, and the guide's codemod (`remove-overloads`) does the
same rewrite. codelaw reports a call whose first argument is a key written in place (an array or a
string; a string is wrapped in an array) or, for `useMutation`, a function; a key passed by name is not
checked, since v5's options object can be passed by name too. `queryCache.find` and `findAll` are left
out: their names are too common to read as TanStack Query's. The v4 plugin's
`prefer-query-object-syntax` asked for the same object form while v4 still allowed both.

## `tanstack-query/stable-query-client` — The QueryClient is made once, not on every render

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-tanstack-query` · **Languages:** JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the fix calls `React.useState` (or the imported `useState`), which must be in scope)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:tanstack-query/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/tanstack-query/stable-query-client.md

### What it checks

`new QueryClient()` from `@tanstack/react-query` is not assigned inside a component or hook; it is made
at module level, or once in `useState`.

**Why:** A client made during render is a new, empty cache on every render: every query refetches and nothing
is shared. An async Server Component runs once per request and may make one.

### Examples

#### JavaScript

##### Don't

```js
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient();
  return queryClient;
}
```

##### Do

```js
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const [queryClient] = React.useState(() => new QueryClient());
  return queryClient;
}
```

#### JSX

##### Don't

```jsx
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient();
  return queryClient;
}
```

##### Do

```jsx
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const [queryClient] = React.useState(() => new QueryClient());
  return queryClient;
}
```

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient();
  return queryClient;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const [queryClient] = React.useState(() => new QueryClient());
  return queryClient;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient();
  return queryClient;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function useClient() {
  const [queryClient] = React.useState(() => new QueryClient());
  return queryClient;
}
```

### Differences from the source

A component or hook is recognised by its own name or by the variable it initialises
(`const App = () => …`); upstream reads only a function's own name. The fix uses `useState` when the
file imports it from `react`, else `React.useState`, as upstream does.

## `toml/deps-sorted` — pyproject.toml dependencies are sorted by name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/deps-sorted.md

### What it checks

The requirement lists in `[project].dependencies` and in each `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra are sorted by package name. Names compare the way pip compares them: case, `-`, `_` and `.` don't matter.

**Why:** A sorted list is quicker to scan, shows a duplicate at once and gives smaller diffs; installers don't depend on the order.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.31",
    "click>=8",
    "attrs",
]
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
dependencies = [
    "attrs",
    "click>=8",
    "requests>=2.31",
]
```

### Notes

A list with comments in it is reported without a fix, because the comments would stay on their lines while the requirements move.

## `toml/no-duplicate-keys` — No key or table defined twice in TOML

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two definitions was meant can't be known from the file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/no-duplicate-keys.md

### What it checks

A key is defined once in its table, and a `[table]` header appears once. That covers dotted keys (`a.b = 1` and then `a = 2`), a table defined both by a header and by dotted keys, and keys inside inline tables.

**Why:** TOML forbids defining a key or table twice and conforming parsers refuse the file, so the mistake breaks every tool that reads it.

### How to fix

1. Decide which definition is right.
2. Delete the other one, or merge the two tables into one.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml
[tool.pytest]
addopts = "-q"
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-ra"
```

##### Do

```toml
[tool.pytest]
addopts = "-ra"
testpaths = ["tests"]
```

## `toml/pyproject-requires-python` — pyproject.toml declares requires-python

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (the supported Python range is a project decision; the fix inserts the `python` option, which may not be the right range)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/pyproject-requires-python.md

### What it checks

A `pyproject.toml` with a `[project]` table says which Python versions the package supports, in `requires-python`, unless it lists the field in `dynamic`.

**Why:** pip uses `requires-python` to pick a release that works on the running interpreter; without it, users on an old Python install a version that then fails at import.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python` | `string` | `">=3.11"` | the range the fix writes into `requires-python` |

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0.0"
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
```

## `toml/pyproject-schema` — pyproject.toml matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** TOML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a value the schema rejects is wrong in a way only its author knows how to correct)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/pyproject` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/toml/pyproject-schema.md

### What it checks

A `pyproject.toml` matches SchemaStore's schema for it: `[build-system]` and `[project]` hold the keys PEP 517, PEP 518 and PEP 621 define, each in the form they define.

**Why:** Build backends reject or ignore a `[project]` key of the wrong shape — `authors` as a string, `dependencies` as a table — and the error appears only when someone builds the package.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and the form the schema expects.
2. Rewrite the value in that form, or move a tool's setting under `[tool.<name>]`.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### TOML

##### Don't

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0"
authors = "Ada Lovelace"
dependencies = { requests = ">=2" }
```

##### Do

```toml path=pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "app"
version = "1.0"
authors = [{ name = "Ada Lovelace" }]
dependencies = ["requests>=2"]
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `pyproject.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/pyproject.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. The `[tool.*]` tables whose schemas live in other SchemaStore files (ruff, black, mypy, poetry, setuptools, uv, …) accept any value. TOML dates and times are read as strings.

## `ts/ban-ts-comment` — No @ts-ignore or @ts-nocheck; @ts-expect-error says why

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the reason the error is expected has to come from the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/ban-ts-comment.md

### What it checks

Type-checking is never switched off with `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck`, and a `@ts-expect-error`
says why the error is expected.

**Why:** `@ts-ignore` hides an error for good, even after the code it excused changes; `@ts-expect-
error` fails as soon as the error is gone.

### How to fix

1. Fix the type error if you can.
2. Otherwise replace the comment with `// @ts-expect-error: <why>`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
// @ts-ignore
const n: number = "1";
```

##### Do

```ts
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the compiler's message
const n: number = "1";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
// @ts-ignore
const n: number = "1";
```

##### Do

```tsx
// @ts-expect-error: the fixture checks the compiler's message
const n: number = "1";
```

## `ts/no-array-constructor` — No Array constructor with several arguments

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-array-constructor.md

### What it checks

Arrays are built with literals; `new Array(n)` with one argument (a length) is allowed.

**Why:** `new Array(a, b)` and `new Array(n)` mean different things, and the literal says what it
means.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const xs = new Array(1, 2, 3);
```

##### Do

```ts
const xs = [1, 2, 3];
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const xs = new Array(1, 2, 3);
```

##### Do

```tsx
const xs = [1, 2, 3];
```

## `ts/no-duplicate-enum-values` — No two enum members share a value

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (which value is right needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-duplicate-enum-values.md

### What it checks

Each member of an enum given a literal value has a different value.

**Why:** Two members with one value are indistinguishable at run time, which is usually a copy-paste
slip.

### How to fix

1. Give each member its own value.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 1,
}
```

##### Do

```ts
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 1,
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
enum Color {
  Red = 1,
  Green = 2,
}
```

## `ts/no-empty-object-type` — No empty interfaces or {} types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right replacement — `object`, `unknown` or `Record<string, never>` — depends on intent)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-empty-object-type.md

### What it checks

Code doesn't declare an empty interface or use the type `{}`.

**Why:** `{}` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, which is almost never what an
empty-looking type was meant to say.

### How to fix

1. For any object, use `object`.
2. For any value, use `unknown`.
3. For an object with no keys, use `Record<string, never>`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Options {}
type Empty = {};
```

##### Do

```ts
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Anything = unknown;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Options {}
type Empty = {};
```

##### Do

```tsx
type Options = Record<string, never>;
type Anything = unknown;
```

## `ts/no-explicit-any` — No explicit any

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (`unknown` may need narrowing code where the value is used)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-explicit-any.md

### What it checks

Types are not written as `any`.

**Why:** `any` silently disables checking for everything it touches; `unknown` keeps the checks and
forces a narrowing.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function parse(input: any) {
  return input;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function parse(input: unknown) {
  return input;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function parse(input: any) {
  return input;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function parse(input: unknown) {
  return input;
}
```

## `ts/no-extra-non-null-assertion` — No repeated non-null assertions

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-extra-non-null-assertion.md

### What it checks

A non-null assertion `!` is not repeated.

**Why:** `x!!` means the same as `x!`; the second `!` is a typo.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const n = value!!;
```

##### Do

```ts
const n = value!;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const n = value!!;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const n = value!;
```

## `ts/no-misused-new` — No constructors declared in interfaces, and no `new` methods in classes

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the intended constructor signature needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-misused-new.md

### What it checks

An interface doesn't declare a method named `constructor`, and a class doesn't declare a method
named `new`.

**Why:** Both look like constructors but are ordinary methods; constructors in types are written
`new (): T`.

### How to fix

1. In an interface, describe a constructor with `new (…): T`.
2. In a class, use `constructor(…)`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Point {
  constructor(): void;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
interface PointConstructor {
  new (): object;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Point {
  constructor(): void;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface PointConstructor {
  new (): object;
}
```

## `ts/no-namespace` — No TypeScript namespaces

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (moving a namespace's members into a module changes every import)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-namespace.md

### What it checks

Code is organised with ES modules, not `namespace` or `module` blocks; `declare module "x"` and
`declare global` are allowed.

**Why:** Namespaces predate ES modules and don't work with modern bundlers and tooling as well.

### How to fix

1. Move the namespace's members to a module of their own.
2. Export them, and import them where the namespace was used.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
namespace Geometry {
  export const pi = 3.14;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
export const pi = 3.14;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
namespace Geometry {
  export const pi = 3.14;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
export const pi = 3.14;
```

## `ts/no-non-null-asserted-optional-chain` — No non-null assertion after an optional chain

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (removing `!` widens the type to include `undefined`, which later code may not handle)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-non-null-asserted-optional-chain.md

### What it checks

An optional chain (`a?.b`) is not followed by a non-null assertion (`!`).

**Why:** The two contradict each other: `?.` allows `undefined`, and `!` asserts it never happens.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const name = user?.name!;
```

##### Do

```ts
const name = user?.name;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const name = user?.name!;
```

##### Do

```tsx
const name = user?.name;
```

## `ts/no-require-imports` — No require() calls

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (an import may need the module's default or named exports chosen by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-require-imports.md

### What it checks

Modules are loaded with `import`, not `require()`.

**Why:** `require()` is untyped and invisible to TypeScript's module checks.

### How to fix

1. Replace the call with an `import` of the names the code uses.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const fs = require("node:fs");
```

##### Do

```ts
import fs from "node:fs";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const fs = require("node:fs");
```

##### Do

```tsx
import fs from "node:fs";
```

## `ts/no-this-alias` — No aliasing this to a variable

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the callbacks that use the alias must become arrow functions by hand)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-this-alias.md

### What it checks

`this` is not stored in a variable such as `self` or `that`; destructuring it is fine.

**Why:** Arrow functions keep the outer `this`, so an alias only adds a name to keep track of.

### How to fix

1. Turn the callbacks that use the alias into arrow functions.
2. Use `this` directly and remove the alias.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const self = this;
button.onclick = function () {
  self.save();
};
```

##### Do

```ts
button.onclick = () => {
  this.save();
};
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const self = this;
button.onclick = function () {
  self.save();
};
```

##### Do

```tsx
button.onclick = () => {
  this.save();
};
```

## `ts/no-unnecessary-type-constraint` — No extends any or extends unknown on a type parameter

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (in a .tsx arrow function `<T>` alone parses as JSX and needs `<T,>`)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unnecessary-type-constraint.md

### What it checks

A type parameter isn't constrained to `any` or `unknown`.

**Why:** Every type extends both, so the constraint says nothing.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function id<T extends unknown>(x: T) {
  return x;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function id<T>(x: T) {
  return x;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function id<T extends unknown>(x: T) {
  return x;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function id<T>(x: T) {
  return x;
}
```

## `ts/no-unsafe-declaration-merging` — No interface that merges with a class of the same name

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether to rename or to move the members into the class needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-declaration-merging.md

### What it checks

An interface doesn't share its name with a class in the same scope.

**Why:** The merged interface adds members to the class's type that the class never initialises, and
the compiler can't tell.

### How to fix

1. Move the interface's members into the class, or rename the interface.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
interface Point {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
interface PointLike {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
interface Point {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
interface PointLike {
  z: number;
}
class Point {
  x = 0;
}
```

## `ts/no-unsafe-function-type` — No Function type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the right signature needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unsafe-function-type.md

### What it checks

The built-in `Function` type is not used as a type.

**Why:** `Function` accepts any function and its calls are unchecked, like `any` for functions.

### How to fix

1. Write the function's real signature, e.g. `(event: Event) => void`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let handler: Function;
```

##### Do

```ts
let handler: (event: Event) => void;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let handler: Function;
```

##### Do

```tsx
let handler: (event: Event) => void;
```

## `ts/no-unused-expressions` — No expression statements that do nothing

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether a call, an assignment or nothing was meant needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unused-expressions.md

### What it checks

Every expression statement does something: a call, an assignment, an update, `await`, `yield`,
`delete` or `void`. Directives such as `"use strict"` are allowed.

**Why:** An expression whose value is thrown away is usually a forgotten call or assignment.

### How to fix

1. Add the call or assignment that was meant, or remove the statement.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
function close(conn: Connection) {
  conn.close();
}
```

## `ts/no-unused-vars` — Every declared name is used

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (removing a declaration can drop the side effects of its initialiser)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-unused-vars.md

### What it checks

Every variable, function, class, type, interface, enum, import, parameter and caught error is used
somewhere. Parameters before the last used one are allowed (`args: after-used`).

**Why:** An unused declaration is dead code or a sign the code doesn't do what it was meant to.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vars` | `string` | `"all"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `args` | `string` | `"after-used"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrors` | `string` | `"all"` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `ignoreRestSiblings` | `boolean` | `false` | *not described in the rule file* |
| `varsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `argsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `caughtErrorsIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |
| `destructuredArrayIgnorePattern` | `string` | *none* | *not described in the rule file* |

### How to fix

1. Check the initialiser has no side effect that matters.
2. Remove the declaration, or use it where it was meant to be used.
3. For a parameter that must stay for its position, prefix it with `_` and set `argsIgnorePattern: "^_"`.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs";
export const load = (path: string) => readFile(path);
```

## `ts/no-wrapper-object-types` — Primitive types, not wrapper object types

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/no-wrapper-object-types.md

### What it checks

Types use `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `symbol`, `bigint` and `object`, not the wrapper objects
`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `Symbol`, `BigInt` and `Object`.

**Why:** The wrapper types describe boxed objects almost no code uses, and accept values the
primitive types reject.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
let label: String = "a";
```

##### Do

```ts
let label: string = "a";
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
let label: String = "a";
```

##### Do

```tsx
let label: string = "a";
```

## `ts/prefer-as-const` — as const instead of repeating a literal as its type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/prefer-as-const.md

### What it checks

A literal cast to its own literal type (`"a" as "a"`) uses `as const` instead.

**Why:** `as const` says the same thing once, and stays right when the literal changes.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
const mode = "dark" as "dark";
```

##### Do

```ts
const mode = "dark" as const;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
const mode = "dark" as "dark";
```

##### Do

```tsx
const mode = "dark" as const;
```

## `ts/prefer-namespace-keyword` — namespace, not module, for a TypeScript namespace

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/prefer-namespace-keyword.md

### What it checks

A TypeScript namespace is declared with `namespace`, not `module`; `declare module "x"` is
unaffected.

**Why:** `module Foo {}` is the old spelling and is easy to confuse with an external module
declaration.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
module Shapes {
  export const sides = 4;
}
```

##### Do

```ts
namespace Shapes {
  export const sides = 4;
}
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
module Shapes {
  export const sides = 4;
}
```

##### Do

```tsx
namespace Shapes {
  export const sides = 4;
}
```

## `ts/triple-slash-reference` — No /// <reference path> directives

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `manual` (the matching import needs the module path and what it provides)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/triple-slash-reference.md

### What it checks

Files are connected with `import`, not `/// <reference path="…" />`.

**Why:** Reference directives predate ES modules and hide dependencies from bundlers and other
tools.

### How to fix

1. Replace the directive with an `import` of the module it pointed to.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
/// <reference path="./globals.d.ts" />
export const x = 1;
```

##### Do

```ts
import "./globals";
export const x = 1;
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
/// <reference path="./globals.d.ts" />
export const x = 1;
```

##### Do

```tsx
import "./globals";
export const x = 1;
```

## `ts/type-only-imports` — Names used only as types are imported with type

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-ts` · **Languages:** TypeScript, TSX
- **Fix:** `suggest` (a type-only import is erased, so code that relied on the module's side effects changes)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:ts/conventions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/ts/type-only-imports.md

### What it checks

An imported name that the file uses only in type positions is marked `type`.

**Why:** Type-only imports are erased at compile time, which keeps runtime imports honest and helps
bundlers drop unused modules.

### Examples

#### TypeScript

##### Don't

```ts
import { Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

##### Do

```ts
import { type Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

#### TSX

##### Don't

```tsx
import { Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

##### Do

```tsx
import { type Config, load } from "./config";
export const c: Config = load();
```

### Differences from the source

Only within the file, without type information: a name used as a value anywhere is left alone.
Default and namespace imports are reported without a fix.

## `yaml/document-start` — A YAML document starts with ---

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `auto`
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/conventions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/document-start.md

### What it checks

Every YAML document begins with an explicit `---` line. Comments and directives may come before it. Markdown front matter is not checked: its `---` belongs to the Markdown file.

**Why:** An explicit start marks where a document begins, so a file can grow to hold several documents, and tools that concatenate YAML files keep the boundaries.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
name: build
on: push
```

##### Do

```yaml
---
name: build
on: push
```

## `yaml/gha-action-schema` — GitHub Actions action metadata matches its schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a misshapen input or run step has several possible meanings; the author picks the one they intended)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-action-schema.md

### What it checks

An `action.yml` matches SchemaStore's schema for action metadata: `name`, `description` and `runs` are present, and the inputs, outputs and steps have the keys and forms GitHub reads.

**Why:** GitHub reads an action's metadata only when a workflow uses it, so a misspelt `steps:` or `using:` breaks every workflow that calls the action, not the action's own repository.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and what the schema expects.
2. Add the missing key, or correct the key or the value.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=action.yml
name: Setup
description: Set the toolchain up
runs:
  using: composite
  step:
    - run: ./setup.sh
      shell: bash
```

##### Do

```yaml path=action.yml
name: Setup
description: Set the toolchain up
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - run: ./setup.sh
      shell: bash
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `github-action.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/github-action.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`.

## `yaml/gha-pin-sha` — GitHub Actions are pinned to a commit SHA

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (finding the commit a tag points to needs the network, and the engine never uses it (L5))
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-pin-sha.md

### What it checks

A `uses:` in a GitHub Actions workflow or composite action names a full 40-character commit SHA, not a tag or branch. Local actions (`./…`) and `docker://` images are not checked.

**Why:** A tag or branch can be moved to different code at any time, so a compromised or careless upstream changes what your workflow runs; a commit SHA can't change.

### How to fix

1. Look up the commit the tag points to, for example with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> <tag>`.
2. Replace the tag with the 40-character SHA and keep the tag as a comment: `uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.2.2`.
3. Let Dependabot or Renovate update the pinned SHAs.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
```

##### Do

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
```

## `yaml/gha-workflow-schema` — GitHub Actions workflows match their schema

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (a misshapen job or step has several possible meanings; the author picks the one they intended)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/github-actions` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/gha-workflow-schema.md

### What it checks

A GitHub Actions workflow matches SchemaStore's schema for workflows: every key of a trigger, a job and a step is one GitHub reads, with a value of the form it takes.

**Why:** GitHub rejects a malformed workflow only when it is pushed, and a misspelt key such as `runs_on` or `timeout-minute` fails the whole workflow file, so the mistake shows up as a red run instead of in review.

### How to fix

1. Read the message: it names the key and what the schema expects, and suggests the key meant when the name is misspelt.
2. Correct the key or the value.
3. Run `codelaw check` on the file again until it is clean.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs_on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
```

##### Do

```yaml path=.github/workflows/ci.yml
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
```

### Notes

The schema is SchemaStore's `github-workflow.json` schema, shipped with the pack in `data/schemas/github-workflow.json` with its descriptions removed; nothing is fetched. YAML is read as YAML 1.2, as GitHub reads it, so `on:` is a key. `oneOf` is read as `anyOf`.

## `yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans` — No yes/no/on/off as unquoted values

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `suggest` (quoting keeps the YAML 1.2 meaning (a string); if a boolean was meant, write `true` or `false` instead)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans.md

### What it checks

A value is not a bare `yes`, `no`, `on` or `off` (in any of their capitalisations). Quote it if it is text, or write `true` or `false` if it is a boolean. Keys are not checked, so a GitHub Actions `on:` is fine.

**Why:** YAML 1.2 reads these words as strings, but YAML 1.1 loaders, still common (PyYAML, Ruby's Psych, many tools built on them), read them as booleans: `country: no` becomes `false`.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
country: no
```

##### Do

```yaml
country: "no"
```

##### Do

```yaml
enabled: true
```

### Differences from the source

The idea comes from the YAML 1.1 and 1.2 specifications. `y` and `n` are not reported: the YAML 1.1 type repository lists them, but the common 1.1 loaders don't treat them as booleans.

## `yaml/no-ambiguous-numbers` — No numbers that YAML 1.1 and 1.2 read differently

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the octal or base-60 meaning or the YAML 1.2 meaning was intended needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `warn`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-ambiguous-numbers.md

### What it checks

A value is not an unquoted integer with a leading zero (`0755`) or an unquoted base-60 form (`22:22`, `1:30:00`).

**Why:** YAML 1.1 reads `0755` as octal (493) and `22:22` as the number 1342; YAML 1.2 reads them as 755 and the string "22:22". The same file means different things to different loaders — the classic case is port mappings in `docker-compose.yml`.

### How to fix

1. For an octal number, write it as `0o755`; for a decimal one, drop the leading zero.
2. For text such as a port mapping or a time, quote it: `"22:22"`.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
mode: 0755
ports:
  - 22:22
```

##### Do

```yaml
mode: 0o755
ports:
  - "22:22"
```

### Differences from the source

The idea comes from the YAML 1.1 and 1.2 specifications.

## `yaml/no-duplicate-keys` — No key twice in one YAML mapping

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (which of the two values was meant can't be known from the file)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-duplicate-keys.md

### What it checks

Each key appears once in a mapping, block or flow. Quoted and plain spellings of a key are the same key.

**Why:** YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, but many loaders accept duplicates and keep only the last value, so the first one is silently lost.

### How to fix

1. Decide which value the key should have.
2. Delete the other entry, or give it a key of its own.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
service:
  image: nginx
  restart: always
  image: caddy
```

##### Do

```yaml
service:
  image: caddy
  restart: always
```

## `yaml/no-undeclared-alias` — Every alias refers to an anchor defined before it

- **Pack:** `@codelaw/rules-data` · `codelaw-rules-data` · **Languages:** YAML
- **Fix:** `manual` (whether the anchor is missing, misspelt or defined too late needs the author)
- **Severity when named:** `error` · **Turned on by:** `codelaw:data/recommended` at `error`
- **Page:** https://github.com/arpitarya/codelaw/blob/main/docs/rules/yaml/no-undeclared-alias.md

### What it checks

An alias `*name` refers to an anchor `&name` defined earlier in the same document.

**Why:** An alias with no anchor before it is an error: YAML loaders refuse the whole file, and anchors don't carry over from one document to the next.

### How to fix

1. Find the anchor the alias meant.
2. Move the anchored node above the alias, fix the spelling, or add the anchor.

### Examples

#### YAML

##### Don't

```yaml
production:
  <<: *defaults
  host: example.com
defaults: &defaults
  port: 443
```

##### Do

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  port: 443
production:
  <<: *defaults
  host: example.com
```

## Engine rules

### `codelaw/no-rules` — No rule pack and no local rule is configured

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw init` to install the rule packs for the languages in this repo, or add a rule under `.codelaw/rules/`.

### `codelaw/not-utf8` — File is not valid UTF-8 and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Re-encode the file as UTF-8, or exclude it in `codelaw.toml`.

### `codelaw/file-too-large` — File is larger than `[files] max_file_size` and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Exclude the file, or raise `[files] max_file_size` in `codelaw.toml`.

### `codelaw/generated` — File is marked generated and was skipped

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the generator instead, or set `[files] lint_generated = true`.

### `codelaw/internal-error` — A rule failed on this file

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Report the rule and file to the rule's maintainer; the rest of the run is unaffected.

### `format/unformatted` — File is not formatted

Severity `warn` · fix `auto`

1. Run `codelaw format` (or `codelaw fix`) on the file.

### `format/failed` — The formatter left the file as it was

Severity `info` · fix `manual`

1. If the file does not parse, correct the syntax error and run `codelaw format` again.
2. Otherwise the formatted text failed verification; add the file to `[format] exclude` and report it with the file attached.

### `codelaw/file-changed-during-run` — File changed on disk during the run, so the fix was not written

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw fix` again once the file is no longer being edited.

### `codelaw/write-failed` — The fixed file could not be written, so it is unchanged

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Make the file writable (its permissions, a read-only disk, a full disk), then run `codelaw fix` again.

### `codelaw/suppression-needs-reason` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment has no reason

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Write the reason after a colon: `codelaw-ignore <rule>: <reason>`.

### `codelaw/unused-suppression` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment suppresses nothing

Severity `info` · fix `auto`

### `graph/no-deprecated-usage` — A deprecated symbol is used

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Replace the use with the replacement `.codelaw/deprecations.toml` names (or the deprecation marker's message gives).
2. An existing use may stay until its deadline only through `.codelaw/baseline/graph--no-deprecated-usage.toml`, which a person adds with `codelaw baseline add`.

### `codelaw/stale-baseline` — A baseline entry allows more findings than its file has

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Run `codelaw baseline prune` (or `codelaw fix`, which prunes too) to lower the entry; lowering is always safe.

### `codelaw/expiring-exception` — An exception (a baseline entry, a deprecation, a `codelaw-ignore`) expires within its warning window

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the findings the exception covers before its `expires` date: on that day they are reported again and the exception is an error.
2. To keep it longer, a person moves `expires` later with `codelaw baseline add --expires …` (a baseline entry) or edits the comment; `codelaw baseline check` flags an extended deadline for review.

### `codelaw/expired-exception` — An exception reached its `expires` date and no longer covers anything

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Fix the findings it covered; they are reported again at their rule's own severity.
2. Then remove the exception: `codelaw baseline prune` (or `codelaw fix`) lowers a baseline entry, and the `codelaw-ignore` comment is deleted by hand.

### `codelaw/exception-without-expiry` — An exception has no `expires` date while `[exceptions] require_expiry` is on

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Add `expires = "YYYY-MM-DD"` (the first day it no longer holds): `codelaw baseline add --expires …` rewrites a baseline entry; a `codelaw-ignore` takes `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` before its colon.

### `codelaw/exception-author` — An exception's `added_by` is not an email address, or not the git author of the change

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Set `added_by` (`by=` in a `codelaw-ignore`) to your own git email, `git config user.email`; `codelaw baseline add` writes it for you.

### `codelaw/unknown-suppression` — A `codelaw-ignore` comment names a rule that does not exist

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Correct the rule id, or remove the comment.

### `graph/untested-function` — A new or edited function is reached by no test file

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Write a unit test that imports the function (or its module, for a function the module does not export) and calls it: a test needs judgment, so codelaw does not write one.
2. If the function should never need its own test (a thin wrapper, generated code), exempt it in `.codelawignore` with `forever: <reason>`; to defer the test, give the line `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` and `on_touch=…` and a reason.

### `graph/function-coverage` — A new or edited function's line coverage is under `[coverage] min`

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Add test cases that run the lines the coverage report shows as missed, regenerate the lcov report in the same job, and run `codelaw check --coverage <report>` again: a test needs judgment, so codelaw does not write one.
2. If the function cannot reasonably be covered, exempt it in `.codelawignore` with a reason, `expires=` or `forever`, and `on_touch=`.

### `codelaw/stale-coverage` — The coverage report does not match this file, so its coverage is not judged

Severity `warn` · fix `manual`

1. Regenerate the lcov report from the code being checked — in the same CI job, after the tests and before `codelaw check` — and pass it with `--coverage` or `[coverage] report`.

### `codelaw/stale-ignore` — A `.codelawignore` line matches no file or function

Severity `warn` · fix `auto`

### `codelaw/incomplete-ignore` — A `.codelawignore` line is missing a field or contradicts itself, so it exempts nothing

Severity `error` · fix `manual`

1. Give the line what the message names: a reason after a colon (always, with `expires=` or `forever`), `expires=YYYY-MM-DD` or `forever` (`[coverage.ignore] require_expiry`), and `on_touch=error|warn|keep` unless it is `forever` (`[coverage.ignore] require_on_touch`).
2. `forever` takes no `expires=`, `warn_days=` or `on_touch=`; a glob takes no `on_touch_scope=function`.
